Four duties attach to him personally as the "responsable du moyen de communication" rather than to the employer, because they concern the act of publishing: date every offer (L5332-1); no listing containing a foreign-language text (L5331-4, which applies even where the job genuinely needs English — a real constraint in a resort); no upper age limit and no reference to any L1132-1 characteristic (L5331-2, L5321-2); and hold the name and address of any anonymous advertiser, producible to the DREETS or France Travail on simple request (L5332-2 with L5332-4). The first three carry only a 3rd-class contravention. The fourth carries no stated penalty but is the one an inspector will actually ask him for.

His model is well-chosen legally, and two of its features are obligations rather than preferences. Free for candidates is L5321-3, which bans any direct or indirect payment from a jobseeker for placement services — 100% of revenue has to come from employers, permanently. Employers paying for listings is the express carve-out in L5331-1 to the ban on selling offers. His silent curation survives L5321-2 as long as the criterion is working conditions and never a discrimination ground, and it is worth writing those criteria down so the file shows what the decision rested on.

The two things his audience makes urgent. On minors: there is no rule about advertising to them, but hospitality is the sector where the substantive bans bite, and L4153-6 forbids putting a minor on bar service in an on-premises drinks establishment unless the house is agréé and the minor is over sixteen in an RNCP-registered training programme — a listing that advertises otherwise is describing work that cannot lawfully be done, which is L5331-3 territory. On pay: nothing requires a salary today, but any figure stated is one of the three enumerated heads of the misleading-offer délit; and the EU directive's transposition deadline passed on 7 June 2026, with France's bill reaching the Conseil des ministres on 10 September 2026 and still awaiting both chambers. A pay-range field built now, optional, flipped to required on promulgation, is the cheapest thing on this list.
must_do: Log an express insertion request for every single listing — identified employer account, exact submitted text, exact published text, timestamp, every later edit with its author. This is the one artefact that decides whether L5334-1 names the restaurant or names him. Never scrape, never import a feed, never publish an offer he wrote himself.
Stamp a visible publication date on every listing (L5332-1, non-nullable field), and decide the policy on re-dating a 'boosted' listing before a customer asks for it.

Make French the authoritative version of every listing. The submission form must reject an English-only offer; an EN toggle is a translation alongside the French, never instead of it (L5331-4 — needing English for the job is not a defence).

Collect and store the legal name and address of every employer at onboarding, not at listing time, and build a fast lookup so a DREETS or France Travail request under L5332-4 can be answered the same day.

Add a listing review step before publication that flags age limits and L1132-1 references — 'jeune', 'bonne présentation', 'habitant la vallée', a named nationality, a gender. He is the publisher of whatever a brasserie types.

For any listing open to under-18s in a débit de boissons, capture whether the establishment holds the agrément, and gate the hours field so no under-18 listing can advertise work past midnight (L4153-6, L3163-2).

Add an optional pay-range field to the listing form now, and design it to become mandatory on promulgation of the transposition loi. Never build a field asking a candidate their current or past salary — that question is on its way to being prohibited.

Publish mentions légales (LCEN art. 6), CGU, a contact point, a way to report a listing, and give an employer a written reason when a listing is pulled. None of this requires a public rating and none of it breaks the silent-standard model.
Set a minimum age of 16 on candidate accounts. It sits above the CNIL's parental-consent threshold of 15 and matches L4153-1's employment floor, and it removes the parental-consent question entirely.
Never charge a candidate anything, and never let the homepage's 'free' claim outlive that fact — L5321-3 forbids the charge and L5331-5 criminalises the stale claim, at 1 an and 37 500 €.

Hold the bright line if the product grows: decide freely about EMPLOYERS, never about CANDIDATES. Shortlisting, ranking or pre-screening individuals is the step that turns L5321-2 into an operational duty and the code's closure power (L5323-1) into a live risk.

Get this reviewed by a French avocat en droit du travail before launch — specifically the L5331-1 wrinkle below and the placement-status question. This brief is research, not advice, and he is 19 with a criminal exposure attached to the product.
unknowns: L5331-1's carve-out reads 'insertion, à titre onéreux, ... dans une publication ou un autre moyen de communication PAYANT'. A literal reader could argue a free-to-read website is not a paid medium and so the carve-out does not cover it. Every French job board operates as he intends and the settled reading is that the ban targets trafficking in the offers themselves, but I found no authority squarely on the point and this is the one article where his exact model meets the text head-on. Worth the lawyer's first hour.

Whether a job board falls inside the L5321-1 definition of 'activité de placement' as a pure publisher. The wording ('services visant à rapprocher les offres et les demandes d'emploi') is broad enough to catch it, which would make the Titre II duties — notably L5321-2's non-discrimination obligation toward employers and jobseekers alike — directly applicable rather than merely prudent. I found no source settling it for listings sites.

Whether the prior declaration for private placement organisations still exists. Search material indicated it was repealed by loi n°2010-853 du 23 juillet 2010 with the implementing rules abrogated by décret n°2012-539 du 20 avril 2012, but guichet-entreprises.fr no longer resolves and I could not open any page confirming it. Treat as unverified.

The 450 € figure for a contravention de 3e classe. R5334-1 refers to 'l'amende prévue pour les contraventions de la 3e classe' without an amount; the amount lives in article 131-13 3° du code pénal, and I could not open a page carrying that text. The article number is right; the figure is unconfirmed.

The mentions légales penalty figures. The service-public page returned 1 an and 75 000 € for an entrepreneur individuel while general search material also cited 375 000 € for companies. I did not open a second page to reconcile them.

Whether an offer must be withdrawn once the post is filled. A search summary asserted it; I found no such provision in L5331-1 to L5334-1 and did not treat it as sourced. The practical route to the same conclusion is L5331-3 1°, 'le caractère effectivement disponible', which makes a stale listing a misleading-offer risk regardless.

The exact per-article mapping of DSA obligations that survive the micro-enterprise exemption. The Arcom page groups them rather than mapping each; I read articles 15(2), 19 and 29 as the exempted set but did not verify against the regulation itself — EUR-Lex refused every fetch I attempted, in French and English, HTML and PDF.

The final shape of the French pay-transparency law: thresholds, phasing, and the penalty regime are all still in the hands of the Sénat and the Assemblée nationale under procédure accélérée. The Conseil d'État avis of 23 July 2026 describes the bill as deposited, not the law as enacted. This should be re-checked before launch, not taken from this brief.

Whether the convention collective HCR (IDCC 1979) imposes anything on the content of job advertisements. I did not research the branch agreement, and hospitality minimum wage grids will matter to any pay-range field he builds.

research.lane: Lane 3 — RGPD / data protection for a curated hospitality job board in France (Megève / Haute-Savoie), operated by a 19-year-old sole trader. Covers CNIL recruitment doctrine, retention, controller status, information duties and legal basis, DPO/DPIA, special categories, and the silent employer-blacklist question — plus the Code du travail "placement" regime that turned out to sit underneath all of it.

findings.claim: He is legally an 'organisme privé de placement' the moment the site habitually brings offers and job-seekers together — this is the finding that reframes the whole lane, because it pulls a Code du travail regime on top of the RGPD.
findings.detail: L5321-1 defines placement by function, not by business model. Publishing offers and letting the two sides contact each other IS 'rapprocher les offres et les demandes d'emploi', done 'à titre habituel', without becoming party to the employment relationship — which is exactly his product as described. He does not need to select, match, or take a fee per hire to be inside this definition; not becoming party to the contract is part of the definition, not an escape from it. Consequence: articles R5323-8 to R5323-11 (annual prefectural return, collection limits, no NIR, non-discrimination, six-year data ceiling) bind him from day one.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, as a pure publisher. Drift into selecting or matching does not trigger this — he is already in scope.
findings.source_quote: L'activité de placement consiste à fournir, à titre habituel, des services visant à rapprocher les offres et les demandes d'emploi, sans que la personne assurant cette activité ne devienne partie aux relations de travail susceptibles d'en découler.

findings.claim: (b) THE RULE HE IS THINKING OF: data on job-seekers held by private placement bodies may not be kept beyond six years from the date it was recorded. Article R. 5323-11 du code du travail.
findings.detail: Note the two details that matter. First, the clock runs from 'leur enregistrement' — the date of recording — NOT from the last contact with the candidate, which is the CNIL's separate CV-library rule. Second, it is a hard ceiling, not a permission: the RGPD minimisation principle and the CNIL's shorter recommended durations run inside it. Six years is the outer wall, never the default.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. It is drafted for 'les seuls organismes privés de placement', which is what L5321-1 makes him.
findings.penalty: No specific fine attaches to R5323-11 itself; over-retention is sanctioned as an RGPD breach — art. 83(5) RGPD (up to €20m / 4% of worldwide turnover) since it engages art. 5(1)(e) storage limitation.
findings.source_quote: Les données relatives aux personnes à la recherche d'un emploi enregistrées dans un traitement de données mis en œuvre par les seuls organismes privés de placement ne peuvent être conservées au-delà d'un délai de six ans à compter de leur enregistrement.

findings.claim: (b) Inside that six-year ceiling, the CNIL sets two much shorter operative durations, and its 2026 retention référentiel says in terms that both apply to intermediaries, not just to employers.
findings.detail: I extracted and read the CNIL référentiel 'Les durées de conservation — gestion des ressources humaines' (rows dated 29/01/2026) rather than trusting a summary. Two rows govern him: (1) CV-library / 'vivier de candidats' — active base 'Jusqu'à 2 ans à compter du dernier contact avec le candidat non retenu', and only for candidates who consented or did not object; (2) unsuccessful candidates' application files — intermediate archive of five years from the date the post was filled, for evidential purposes in a discrimination action, and this row's legal basis is stated as an obligation, not a recommendation. The référentiel writes the scope as applying 'tant pour les intermédiaires que les employeurs'.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. The two-year CV-library rule is the one that will actually shape his database; the five-year evidential archive is the one people forget and then cannot defend a discrimination claim.
findings.penalty: Art. 83(5) RGPD — up to €20m or 4% of worldwide annual turnover.
findings.source_quote: Jusqu'à 2 ans à compter du dernier contact avec le candidat non retenu

findings.claim: The five-year evidential archive rests on a Code du travail limitation period: article L. 1134-5 fixes five years for an action in reparation of discrimination.
findings.detail: The CNIL guide states the rule and the article number: the five-year period runs 'à compter de la révélation de la discrimination'. The retention référentiel expresses the practical start point differently — from the date the post was filled. I read both CNIL documents directly; I did not open the statute itself, because Legifrance refuses automated fetches.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY.
findings.source_quote: l'article L. 1134-5 du code du travail fixe à cinq ans le délai de prescription de l'action en réparation du préjudice résultant d'une discrimination

findings.claim: (c) CONTROLLER, not processor, and not joint controller with the restaurants. The CNIL's recruitment guide answers this for job boards by name.
findings.detail: Fiche n°3 of the CNIL Guide Recrutement takes 'l'exploitant d'une plateforme web (jobboard) mettant en relation employeurs et candidats' as a worked example and places him in the responsable de traitement column, for the processing relating to creating and managing the personal accounts his services require. The reasoning given is that he alone decides the site's creation, its objectives and its technical arrangements — account creation, how long data transits the site, security measures such as password robustness for both candidates and recruiters. The restaurant becomes a separate, independent controller at the moment it pulls a CV into its own files: 'Dès lors qu'un cabinet de recrutement ou un employeur direct récupèrent les CV des candidats pour les intégrer dans leur propre base, ils deviennent responsables de traitement'. Joint control is expressly described as rare in recruitment, and the guide's only worked example of it is an international group with a coordinating entity — not a platform and its paying customers.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY: separate controller. He owes candidates the full controller package himself; he does NOT need an art. 26 joint-controller arrangement with each restaurant, and he must not sign an art. 28 processing contract that mislabels him as the restaurants' processor. Joint control would become arguable only if he and a restaurant jointly designed a selection tool or evaluation grid — i.e. only on drift into matching.
findings.source_quote: peut être considéré comme responsable du traitement relatif à la création et gestion des comptes personnels nécessaires aux services qu'il propose

findings.claim: The CNIL warns that the label is not his to choose — a supervisory authority can requalify it whatever the contract says.
findings.detail: Fiche n°3: if an organisation decides in fact the why and the how, it is a controller 'même s'il est désigné comme sous-traitant dans un contrat'; the authorities 'ne sont pas liées par les qualifications choisies par les parties'. The guide also requires the analysis to be written down and justifiable in advance. This matters because the tempting commercial move — telling restaurants 'you are the controller, I only host' — would be requalified.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Write the qualification analysis down before launch; it is part of the accountability record.

findings.claim: (d) LEGAL BASIS is not one basis but three, one per purpose — and the CNIL changed its position on the CV library: it is now consent, not legitimate interest.
findings.detail: The guide's mapping table gives: (1) running the site and finding relevant profiles — 'utilisation de site web proposant des offres d'emploi sur Internet aux candidats' — legitimate interest; (2) receiving and filing an application the candidate sent — contract, as pre-contractual measures taken at the candidate's own initiative, and the guide insists the processing must be 'mis en œuvre à la seule initiative du candidat'; (3) keeping a CVthèque / vivier so profiles can be shown or contacted later — consent, which must be 'libre, spécifique, explicite et univoque'. The guide flags this last point as a deliberate change from the earlier HR référentiel, which had recommended legitimate interest. Authentication cookies on the candidate area sit on legitimate interest. He may not cumulate bases for one purpose — one purpose, one basis.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. His product is a CV library by construction: profiles sit on the site so restaurants can contact them. That is the consent purpose, and it needs a separate, unbundled, explicit opt-in — not a tickbox merged into account creation or T&C acceptance.
findings.source_quote: Le choix de la base légale du consentement pour fonder les traitements destinés à la constitution d'une CVthèque constitue une évolution des recommandations de la CNIL

findings.claim: (d) Consent cannot be used for anything that affects the candidate's chances of getting a job — so it is the right basis for the CV library and the wrong one for everything else.
findings.detail: The guide states the boundary directly: processing carried out in the recruitment operations themselves cannot rest on consent where a refusal could affect the candidate's chances of obtaining a job or a type of job. The imbalance between candidate and recruiter makes consent unfree there.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Practical rule: 'do you want to be visible to employers / kept in the pool?' = consent, revocable, refusable without penalty. 'Send this application to this restaurant' = contract, no consent tickbox needed and none should be offered.

findings.claim: (d) The information owed at account creation and at application is the article 13 list PLUS three extra duties that come from the Code du travail, not from the RGPD.
findings.detail: RGPD art. 13 items, per the CNIL guide's own enumeration: identity and contact details of the controller; DPO contact details where one exists; the purpose; the legal basis, and where it is legitimate interest, what that interest actually is; whether supplying each field is obligatory or optional and what happens if it is not supplied; the recipients; any transfer outside the EU and its safeguard; the retention period; how to exercise access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection and portability; the right to complain to the CNIL; and the existence of any automated decision-making or profiling. On top of that, articles L. 1221-6 to L. 1221-9 du code du travail add: information may only serve to assess capacity for the job offered; the candidate must be expressly informed BEFOREHAND of the recruitment-aid methods and techniques used on them; and no information may be collected by a device not previously disclosed to them. The CNIL allows layered notices so the whole thing is not dumped on one screen.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. The Code du travail limb is the one a generic privacy-policy template will miss — 'expressly informed beforehand' is stronger than 'available in our policy'.
findings.penalty: Art. 83(5) RGPD — up to €20m or 4% of worldwide annual turnover (arts. 12-22 are in the higher tier).
findings.source_quote: aucune information concernant personnellement un candidat ne peut être collectée par un dispositif qui n'a pas été porté préalablement à sa connaissance

findings.claim: (e) DPO: NOT required. None of the three mandatory triggers in article 37(1) RGPD is met by a regional job board.
findings.detail: Art. 37(1) makes designation compulsory only where (a) the controller is a public authority; (b) core activities consist of regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or (c) core activities consist of large-scale processing of art. 9 special categories or art. 10 criminal-offence data. He is private; a job board that publishes offers and passes applications is not systematic monitoring; and he must not be processing special categories at all (see the next finding). One alpine region is not 'large scale'. I read this through the CNIL's hosted RGPD text rather than the EUR-Lex original, which would not render for me.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY: no DPO. This flips if he ever starts large-scale behavioural profiling of candidates. Voluntary designation stays available and is a cheap credibility signal, but it converts into binding art. 38-39 obligations once made — do not designate casually.

findings.claim: (e) AIPD/DPIA: YES — and the CNIL's recruitment guide names a jobboard operator as an example of processing that triggers it.
findings.detail: Fiche n°10 sets out the two routes to a mandatory AIPD. Route two is meeting at least two of the EDPB's nine criteria, and the guide's own worked list of examples under that route ends with: 'traitements utilisés par l'exploitant d'une plateforme web de type jobboard mettant en relation employeurs et candidats et proposant divers services'. The guide also notes that the EDPB treats employees as vulnerable persons because of the power imbalance, and says the candidate-recruiter relationship 'peut, selon les contextes, être présumée comme au moins aussi déséquilibrée'. The AIPD must be done BEFORE the processing starts, and if it cannot reduce the high risks to an acceptable level he must consult the CNIL before launching.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, before launch. This is the single most concrete pre-launch compliance artefact he owes, and it is the one a 19-year-old founder will not know exists.
findings.penalty: Art. 83(4) RGPD — up to €10m or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (art. 35 sits in the lower tier).
findings.source_quote: traitements utilisés par l'exploitant d'une plateforme web de type jobboard mettant en relation employeurs et candidats et proposant divers services

findings.claim: (e) Yes, the CNIL's formal list of processing requiring a DPIA names recruitment explicitly — but under the heading of profiling, which is the drift threshold.
findings.detail: I extracted and read the list PDF (deliberation of 11 October 2018) rather than relying on a summary. Entry three is 'Traitements établissant des profils de personnes physiques à des fins de gestion des ressources humaines', criteria 'évaluation ou notation' plus 'personnes dites vulnérables', and its worked examples include 'traitement visant à faciliter le recrutement, notamment grâce à un algorithme de sélection'. The recruitment guide adds a second example squarely aimed at platforms: 'utilisation d'un traitement algorithmique prédictif permettant d'identifier sur une plateforme les offres d'emploi en adéquation avec les compétences affichées sur le CV du candidat'.
findings.applies_to_him: Route one (the formal list) is the DRIFT trigger: the day he adds a recommendation engine, a scoring system, or automatic candidate-to-offer matching, the AIPD becomes mandatory by list, not by argument. Route two (the nine criteria) already catches him today as a jobboard.
findings.source_quote: traitement visant à faciliter le recrutement, notamment grâce à un algorithme de sélection

findings.claim: (e) The CNIL's exemption list does NOT rescue him. It covers an organisation's own internal HR, not a platform's candidate database.
findings.detail: I read the exemption list PDF. The relevant entry exempts 'Traitements, mis en œuvre uniquement à des fins de ressources humaines... pour la seule gestion du personnel des organismes qui emploient moins de 250 personnes, à l'exception du recours au profilage' — payroll, training, expense reimbursement, working-time control. That is an employer managing its own staff. A job board processing third-party candidates is not within it, and the list's own preamble warns that exemption from an AIPD does not exempt from any other RGPD obligation and that where there is doubt, do one anyway.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Do not let anyone tell him 'micro-entreprise, so exempt' — the exemption is about headcount of the organisation whose OWN staff is being managed.

findings.claim: (e) The registre des activités de traitement (art. 30 RGPD) IS mandatory for him regardless of size, and it is not optional for micro-entreprises.
findings.detail: The CNIL guide states the register applies 'à tous les organismes, publics comme privés quelle que soit leur taille', and to all professionals collecting personal data non-occasionally in the course of their activity — which is precisely a job board. It is an internal document, not filed with the CNIL, but produced on inspection.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY.
findings.penalty: Art. 83(4) RGPD — up to €10m or 2% of worldwide annual turnover.

findings.claim: (f) NEVER collected or inferred: the six article 9 categories. Health, union membership and racial/ethnic origin are all in the prohibited set, and the prohibition covers inference, not just a form field.
findings.detail: Fiche n°19 lists the closed set: alleged racial or ethnic origin; political opinions; religious or philosophical convictions; trade-union membership; health; sex life or sexual orientation; plus genetic and biometric data used to uniquely identify someone. Processing is prohibited in principle under art. 9(1) RGPD and art. 6 of the loi Informatique et Libertés, and the guide makes clear that 'traitement' here includes collection, recording, transmission, use and access — so a free-text field where a candidate volunteers a health condition is already processing. Escaping the ban needs BOTH an art. 9(2) exception AND a valid art. 6 legal basis, cumulatively. The CNIL also treats a RQTH (recognised disabled-worker status) as health data.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Practical consequence for a hospitality site aimed at young workers: no free-text 'tell us about yourself' box that invites health or personal disclosure, and a documented rule that volunteered sensitive information is deleted, not filed.
findings.penalty: Art. 83(5) RGPD — up to €20m or 4%. Separately, art. 226-16 et seq. code pénal: five years' imprisonment and €300,000 fine.
findings.source_quote: Le traitement des données sensibles... est en principe interdit

findings.claim: (f) PHOTO: not a sensitive datum, but the Défenseur des droits says requiring one can only be exceptional — and it recommends stripping photos from applications altogether.
findings.detail: I extracted and read the Défenseur des droits guide 'Pour un recrutement sans discrimination'. On requiring a photo: 'De fait, exiger par exemple une photo sur un CV ne peut être qu'exceptionnel.' Its recommended de-biasing measure is to anonymise applications by removing personal information unconnected to skills, listing precisely 'nom, prénom, adresse, âge, situation de famille et photo'. The mechanism is that physical appearance ('apparence physique') is itself a prohibited discrimination criterion under L. 1132-1 — so a mandatory photo builds a discrimination exposure into the product. The CNIL guide confirms appearance requirements are lawful only as an 'exigence professionnelle essentielle et déterminante' under L. 1133-1, the textbook case being modelling or acting — not a commis de cuisine.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Make the photo strictly optional, never a required field, never a completeness score, and never a filter restaurants can search on.
findings.penalty: Discrimination in hiring: art. 225-2 code pénal.
findings.source_quote: exiger par exemple une photo sur un CV ne peut être qu'exceptionnel

findings.claim: (f) DATE OF BIRTH: age is a prohibited discrimination criterion but is NOT an article 9 sensitive datum — so the test is necessity under L. 1221-6, and for his young audience there is one real justification.
findings.detail: The CNIL guide says explicitly of the discrimination criteria that not all of them are sensitive data: 'Pour exemple, le sexe ou l'âge ne sont pas des données dites sensibles.' So the governing test is the lien direct et nécessaire of L. 1221-6, not the art. 9 prohibition. Two things pull in opposite directions for his site. Against collecting it: the Défenseur des droits lists age among the fields to strip for bias reduction, and L5331-2 du code du travail bans publishing an offer stating an upper age limit. For collecting it: his audience is young people entering the trade, and articles D. 4153-20 et seq. forbid employing under-18s on certain dangerous work — kitchen work being an obvious live case — so knowing whether a candidate is a minor can be genuinely necessary. Note separately that R5323-8 requires him to report job-seeker numbers broken down by sex and age to the préfet.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Recommended shape: collect 'are you under 18?' (a yes/no needed for the minor-work rules and the prefectural return) rather than a full date of birth, and never expose age as a search filter for restaurants.
findings.source_quote: Pour exemple, le sexe ou l'âge ne sont pas des données dites sensibles.

findings.claim: (f) The CNIL has already enforced on over-collection in recruitment, and the list of what it struck down maps directly onto fields a hospitality signup form would casually include.
findings.detail: In a formal mise en demeure the CNIL found unjustified the collection of information about a candidate's family members, the candidate's place of birth, over-granular nationality where aggregated categories would do, and past salary amounts. The company complied and the procedure was closed. The recruitment guide separately bans asking for a social security number or bank details at application stage, and article R5323-9 du code du travail independently forbids a private placement body from collecting the NIR at all.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Place of birth and past salary are the two that a naive form design will include.

findings.claim: (f)+(b) Article R. 5323-9 bars him from collecting the NIR (numéro de sécurité sociale) outright, and R. 5323-10 subjects collection, use, retention and transmission to the non-discrimination rule.
findings.detail: R5323-9 permits a private placement body to collect job-seekers' personal data only so far as necessary to the placement activity, 'à l'exception du numéro d'inscription au répertoire national d'identification des personnes physiques'. R5323-10 then binds the whole data lifecycle to articles L. 1132-1 to L. 1132-4 and the loi du 6 janvier 1978. The significance is that non-discrimination here is not only an employment-law duty — it is written into the data-processing rule, so a discriminatory filter is simultaneously an unlawful processing.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY.
findings.source_quote: à l'exception du numéro d'inscription au répertoire national d'identification des personnes physiques

findings.claim: (g) THE SILENT BLACKLIST IS THE WEAKEST PART OF THE PLAN. If the churn record identifies a named patron or gérant, it is personal data, and it is a 'liste d'exclusion' in the CNIL's sense — a category the CNIL surrounds with transparency duties that are the exact opposite of 'enforced at the door, silently'.
findings.detail: Two steps. First, is it personal data? The CNIL's definition page says company contact details are not, in principle, personal data — a generic switchboard number and a contact@ address for a legal person fall outside. But a single-site restaurant is usually identified through a named individual, and the moment the record reads 'Chez X — gérant M. Dupont — churns staff', it relates to an identified natural person and the RGPD applies in full. Second, what does that oblige? The CNIL's fiche n°15 on exclusion lists is the governing doctrine, and every one of its requirements bites: the only available legal basis is legitimate interest, subject to a documented balancing test; entry must rest on 'des motifs objectifs opposables à la personne concernée, faisant abstraction de tout jugement de valeur ou d'appréciation subjective' and of a certain gravity — 'did not feel right about them' fails, a documented pattern might pass; the criteria must be defined in advance and disclosed; and the information must be given at two moments — when someone is actually entered on the list AND before the list is consulted. Retention must be limited and proportionate to the gravity of the facts, with an update-and-deletion procedure. Exclusion must not be fully automated. And an AIPD is mandatory.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, the moment he starts recording it. 'Quietly' is the part that does not survive: the CNIL requires disclosed criteria and notification of the person listed. He can keep the DECISION private (he need not publish ratings or league tables) but he cannot keep the CRITERIA and the FACT OF LISTING secret from the listed party.
findings.penalty: Art. 83(5) RGPD — up to €20m or 4% (transparency and lawfulness, art. 5 and arts. 12-14, sit in the higher tier).
findings.source_quote: des motifs objectifs opposables à la personne concernée, faisant abstraction de tout jugement de valeur ou d'appréciation subjective

findings.claim: (g) The churn blacklist independently lands on the CNIL's formal mandatory-AIPD list — profiling that can lead to exclusion from a contract.
findings.detail: The list PDF includes 'Traitements impliquant le profilage des personnes pouvant aboutir à leur exclusion du bénéfice d'un contrat ou à la suspension voire à la rupture de celui-ci', criteria 'évaluation ou notation' and 'croisement ou combinaison d'ensembles de données'. Refusing or withdrawing a paid listing on the strength of a churn record is exclusion from the benefit of a contract, decided by evaluating a person. This is route one — mandatory by list, no balancing argument available.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY if he keeps the record at all. This is a second, independent AIPD trigger on top of the jobboard one.
findings.penalty: Art. 83(4) RGPD — up to €10m or 2%.
findings.source_quote: Traitements impliquant le profilage des personnes pouvant aboutir à leur exclusion du bénéfice d'un contrat ou à la suspension voire à la rupture de celui-ci

findings.claim: (g) Where the churn signal comes from candidates rather than from the employer, article 14 RGPD applies — he must inform the employer's representative that he holds data about them, within one month.
findings.detail: Art. 14 governs data not obtained from the data subject: the controller must supply the art. 13 information set plus the categories of data and the source, within one month of obtaining it. If candidates tell him 'this place burns through staff' and he records it against a named gérant, that is indirect collection about that person. I read this through the CNIL's hosted RGPD text; the EUR-Lex original would not render for me.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY if he records employer-side reputational data sourced from workers. A crucial practical consequence: this duty is what makes an anonymous worker-reporting channel legally awkward, because informing the employer erodes the reporter's protection.

findings.claim: (g) SAFER DESIGN: keep the churn signal as data about the ESTABLISHMENT, never about a named person, and the RGPD problem largely dissolves.
findings.detail: This is my reading of the boundary the CNIL's own definition draws, not a rule I found stated for this case. If the record is 'SIRET 123… — 4 listings in 12 months, 3 re-listings of the same post' with no natural person named and no free-text judgement, it is information about a legal person and about his own commercial relationship with it, which the CNIL says is not in principle personal data. The risk re-enters through identifiability: for a one-person business the establishment and the gérant may be the same identifiable individual, and the CNIL's test is identifiability, not intent.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, as the design choice to make before the first record is written. Structured fields and objective counts; no free-text comment boxes — the CNIL's own advice on exclusion lists is to prefer a dropdown over free-text.

findings.claim: FREE FOR CANDIDATES IS NOT A BUSINESS CHOICE — IT IS A CRIMINAL PROHIBITION. Charging job-seekers carries six months' imprisonment and a €3,750 fine.
findings.detail: Article L. 5321-3 forbids any direct or indirect payment being required of job-seekers in return for placement services, with narrow exceptions for entertainment artists and sports agents. Article L. 5324-1 attaches the penalty. Note 'indirecte': a premium candidate tier, a paid CV-boost, a paid application-priority feature, or an affiliate kickback routed through the candidate would all be at risk, not just a straight fee. The article text was returned to me condensed rather than fully verbatim, hence medium rather than high.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. His stated model already complies — the point is that he must never be talked into monetising the candidate side later.
findings.penalty: Six months' imprisonment and €3,750 fine — art. L. 5324-1 code du travail.
findings.source_quote: Aucune rétribution, directe ou indirecte, ne peut être exigée des personnes à la recherche d'un emploi en contrepartie de la fourniture de services de placement

findings.claim: HIS CURATION HAS A LEGAL CEILING HE HAS NOT SEEN: article L. 5321-2 forbids refusing placement service to an EMPLOYER — not only to a candidate — on a discrimination ground.
findings.detail: The article has two limbs and both hit his model. First: no placement service may be refused to a job-seeker OR to an employer on one of the L. 1132-1 grounds. His 'decent conditions' standard is not an L. 1132-1 ground, so curating on it is lawful — but the same door that lets him refuse a house for churning staff would be unlawful if the real reason were the owner's origin, religion, sex or age, and a purely discretionary, unwritten, unreviewable door is exactly the structure in which such a refusal cannot be disproved. Second limb: no job offer may contain a reference to any of those characteristics — and he is the one publishing the offers.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. This is the strongest practical argument for writing his admission criteria down even though he wants the standard enforced silently: written objective criteria are what let him prove a refusal was about conditions, not about the person.
findings.source_quote: Aucun service de placement ne peut être refusé à une personne à la recherche d'un emploi ou à un employeur fondé sur l'un des motifs de discrimination énumérés à l'article L. 1132-1.

findings.claim: PUBLISHING THE OFFERS CARRIES ITS OWN CRIMINAL EXPOSURE: a misleading job advertisement is punishable by one year's imprisonment and a €37,500 fine.
findings.detail: Article L. 5331-3 prohibits publishing, by any means of communication accessible to the public, a job offer containing false or misleading statements, in particular on: (1) the existence, actual availability, origin, nature and description of the job; (2) the remuneration and ancillary benefits offered; (3) the place of work. Article L. 5334-1 sets the penalty at one year and €37,500. For seasonal alpine hospitality this is not theoretical — the recurring abuses in that sector are exactly accommodation promised and not provided, hours and pay misstated, and the resort named rather than the actual valley. A curated site that vets houses on conditions is implicitly warranting the accuracy of what it publishes.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, as a pure publisher. The text targets the act of causing an offer to be published, so a vetting platform cannot treat ad content as purely the restaurant's problem.
findings.penalty: One year's imprisonment and €37,500 fine — art. L. 5334-1 code du travail.
findings.source_quote: Il est interdit de faire publier... une insertion d'offres d'emploi... comportant des allégations fausses ou susceptibles d'induire en erreur

findings.claim: Three more publishing rules bind him mechanically: every offer must be dated, no offer may state an upper age limit, and no offer may be written in a foreign language.
findings.detail: L. 5332-1: 'Toute offre d'emploi publiée ou diffusée est datée.' — a dated timestamp on every listing, which is a product requirement, not a policy. L. 5331-2: publishing an offer mentioning an upper age limit required of the applicant is prohibited, save where a statutory age condition applies — this is the one his 'aimed at young people entering the trade' positioning could trip, if a restaurant writes 'under 25' or 'jeune équipe, 18-25'. L. 5331-4: no offer may carry a text drafted in a foreign language; where the post can only be named by a foreign term with no French equivalent, a detailed French description must accompany it — relevant in an international ski resort where 'chef de rang', 'runner', 'ski bum season staff' English listings are common.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. These are cheap to build in: a mandatory publication date field, a validation rule on age wording, and a French-language requirement in his listing form.
findings.source_quote: Toute offre d'emploi publiée ou diffusée est datée.

findings.claim: His paid-listing model is expressly carved out of the ban on selling job offers — but only because it is a paid insertion in a paid medium.
findings.detail: Article L. 5331-1 prohibits selling job offers or job applications, whatever the medium used, then adds that this does not prevent the paid insertion of offers or applications in a publication or other paid communication medium. So restaurants paying to have offers listed, and paying more for visibility, sits inside the exception. What would NOT sit inside it is selling the offers or the candidate applications themselves as a data product — for example selling the CV database to a third party. The page returned the article to me in English rather than verbatim French, hence medium confidence on the exact wording.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. His revenue model is lawful as structured; the boundary is that he sells placement in the medium, never the offers or the applications as such.

findings.claim: If a restaurant wants to advertise anonymously, the law makes HIM the holder of its identity — article L. 5332-2.
findings.detail: An employer placing an anonymous job offer by any means of public communication must disclose its name or corporate name and its address to the publication director or the person responsible for the means of communication — which in his site's case is him. Where an intermediary places the insertion, that intermediary must supply the employer details to the publication director. Practically: he may run blind listings, but he must hold and be able to produce the real identity behind each one.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Build the identity field as mandatory in the back office even when the public listing is blind.
findings.source_quote: fait connaître son nom ou sa raison sociale et son adresse au directeur de la publication ou au responsable du moyen de communication

findings.claim: He owes an annual statistical return to the préfet, before 31 March, on his placement activity.
findings.detail: Article R. 5323-8 requires a private-law body carrying on a placement function to send the préfet each year, before 31 March of the following year, on a form fixed by ministerial order: the turnover attributable to placement for the past year, related where applicable to total turnover; and the number of job-seekers, broken down by sex and age, who were received during the year, placed during the year, and registered in the body's files at 31 December. This is a genuine obligation almost no small French job board knows about, and it is the practical reason he will need sex and age as aggregate fields even while minimising them elsewhere.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, with the first return due before 31 March of the year after launch.
findings.source_quote: Le chiffre d'affaires relatif au placement, réalisé sur l'année écoulée, rapporté s'il y a lieu au chiffre d'affaire total

findings.claim: Breaching the placement principles exposes him to administrative closure of up to three months, independently of any fine.
findings.detail: Article L. 5323-1 empowers labour-inspection officials to record breaches of Chapter I (articles L. 5321-1 to L. 5321-3 — the placement definition, the non-discrimination-in-service rule, and the no-fee-from-candidates rule), and allows the administrative authority, after a formal notice, to order the closure of the body for a period not exceeding three months where placement is carried on in breach of those provisions or where public order is harmed.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. For a seasonal alpine business a three-month closure spanning a ski season is an existential penalty, larger in practice than most fines.
findings.penalty: Administrative closure up to three months — art. L. 5323-1 code du travail.

findings.claim: Beyond RGPD administrative fines, French criminal law attaches five years' imprisonment and a €300,000 fine to serious data offences.
findings.detail: The CNIL's own penalties page sets out articles 226-16 (processing without complying with required formalities/conditions), 226-17 (failure to implement required security measures), 226-18 (fraudulent, unfair or unlawful collection) and 226-22 (unauthorised disclosure) of the code pénal, each at five years and €300,000; negligent disclosure drops to three years and €100,000; obstructing CNIL supervision is one year and €15,000. I read the CNIL page but received the article texts as quoted fragments in a summary rather than the full statutory text.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Worth stating plainly because founders assume RGPD exposure is civil/administrative only.
findings.penalty: Five years' imprisonment and €300,000 fine — arts. 226-16 to 226-22 code pénal.

findings.claim: Hiring discrimination carries three years' imprisonment and a €45,000 fine under article 225-2 code pénal — I could not open a primary source for the figures.
findings.detail: Search results attributed to Défenseur des droits decisions state three years and €45,000 for natural persons and €225,000 for legal persons, and identify art. 225-2 (3°) as refusing to hire and 225-2 (5°) as subordinating a job offer to a discriminatory condition. The CNIL recruitment guide, which I did read, cites 'Article 225-1 et 225-2 du code pénal' as the framework but does not state the amounts. Legifrance refuses automated fetches, so I did not read the article text and I am not asserting the figures as verified.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY in principle, via L5321-2 and the publishing rules — but treat the amounts as unconfirmed.
findings.penalty: Claimed: three years and €45,000 (natural persons), €225,000 (legal persons) — UNVERIFIED.

findings.claim: FLAG, NOT A FINDING: the Digital Services Act may require him to give a restaurant a reasoned explanation when he removes or demotes its listing — which would collide head-on with silent curation. I could not verify it.
findings.detail: A site that stores and publicly disseminates information supplied by its business users looks like an 'online platform' under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065. My recollection is that article 17 requires a clear and specific statement of reasons to the affected recipient when a provider restricts the visibility of, removes, demotes, or suspends an account over illegality or incompatibility with its terms — and that article 19 exempts micro and small enterprises only from articles 20 to 28, which would leave article 17 applying to him. I could not confirm this: EUR-Lex returned an empty document to me on four separate attempts and economie.gouv.fr returned 403. A French government page did confirm that micro-enterprises (under 10 staff, under €2m) and small enterprises (under 50 staff, under €10m) are exempted from 'diverses mesures (rapports de transparence, système interne de traitement des réclamations)' — but that is not the same as article 17, and I am not asserting the article numbers or their content as read. Note this is separate from the RGPD analysis and does not change any finding above. The related Platform-to-Business Regulation (EU) 2019/1150, which requires disclosure of ranking parameters including paid-visibility effects, is probably NOT engaged, because its definition of online intermediation services turns on business users offering goods or services to consumers and a job offer is not that — but I did not verify this either.
findings.applies_to_him: Unverified. Worth a dedicated check before he builds the 'pay more for better visibility' feature and the silent de-listing process, because both are precisely what these two instruments regulate.

research.bottom_line: The RGPD answers are mostly reassuring; the finding that actually changes his plan is not an RGPD finding at all. By the definition in article L. 5321-1 du code du travail, a site that habitually brings job offers and job-seekers together IS an activité de placement — becoming a party to no employment contract is part of the definition, not an escape from it. So he is an organisme privé de placement from day one, which layers a Code du travail regime under everything: a six-year ceiling on job-seeker data (R. 5323-11), a ban on collecting the NIR (R. 5323-9), an annual statistical return to the préfet before 31 March (R. 5323-8), a criminal prohibition on ever charging candidates (L. 5321-3, six months and €3,750 under L. 5324-1), and administrative closure of up to three months for breach (L. 5323-1). On the RGPD questions proper: he is a separate CONTROLLER, not a processor and not a joint controller — the CNIL's recruitment guide works a jobboard operator through as an example and places it there, with the restaurant becoming an independent controller the moment it pulls a CV into its own files. No DPO is required. An AIPD IS required, before launch, and on two independent grounds: the CNIL's guide names 'l'exploitant d'une plateforme web de type jobboard' as an example of processing meeting the EDPB criteria, and his employer blacklist separately lands on the CNIL's formal mandatory list as profiling that can exclude someone from the benefit of a contract. Legal basis splits three ways — legitimate interest for running the site, contract (pre-contractual measures at the candidate's own initiative) for receiving applications, and CONSENT for the CV library, which is a recent and deliberate CNIL change from the old legitimate-interest position and which his product needs as an unbundled explicit opt-in. Retention: two years from last contact for the CV pool, a five-year evidential archive against discrimination claims that the CNIL's 2026 référentiel says applies to intermediaries as well as employers, all of it inside the six-year statutory wall. The one part of his design that does not survive contact with the law is the silent blacklist. It is a 'liste d'exclusion' in the CNIL's sense, and the CNIL's doctrine demands the opposite of silence: objective criteria with no value judgement, defined in advance, disclosed, and the listed party informed both when they are entered and before the list is consulted. He can keep the DECISION private — no ratings, no public scores, no declarations, exactly as he wants — but he cannot keep the CRITERIA and the fact of listing secret from the house concerned. The cleanest fix is to hold the churn signal as structured objective counts against the establishment's SIRET rather than against a named gérant, with no free-text comments, which keeps most of it outside personal-data territory. Writing his admission standard down is also his best protection under L. 5321-2, which forbids refusing placement service to an employer on a discrimination ground: an unwritten, unreviewable door is precisely the structure in which he could not disprove such an allegation. Finally, two exposures he has almost certainly not considered, both flowing from being the publisher rather than the matchmaker: a misleading job advertisement is one year's imprisonment and €37,500 (L. 5331-3 and L. 5334-1) — and the recurring abuses in seasonal alpine hospitality are exactly misstated accommodation, hours, pay and location; and every offer must be dated, must not state an upper age limit, and must not be written in a foreign language.
must_do: Run an AIPD (DPIA) BEFORE launching, not after. Two independent triggers: the CNIL guide names jobboard operators under the nine-criteria route, and the employer blacklist is on the CNIL's formal mandatory list as profiling leading to exclusion from a contract. Use the CNIL's free PIA tool. If the AIPD cannot reduce the high risks to an acceptable level, he must consult the CNIL before going live.

Build the registre des activités de traitement (art. 30 RGPD) before launch — mandatory regardless of size, one entry per purpose: site/account management, receipt and transmission of applications, CV library, employer relationship, employer churn record.

Split the legal bases explicitly and build the consent flow correctly: legitimate interest for running the site, contract for handling an application the candidate sent, and a separate unbundled explicit opt-in for being kept visible in the CV pool. Never merge the CV-pool consent into account creation or T&C acceptance, and make refusal cost the candidate nothing.

Write the article 13 notice to cover the RGPD list AND the Code du travail limb: the candidate must be expressly informed BEFOREHAND of any recruitment-aid method or technique used on them, and nothing may be collected by a device not previously disclosed. Layer the notice rather than dumping it on one screen.

Set and automate three retention clocks: two years from last contact for the CV pool; five years from the date a post was filled for the evidential archive against discrimination claims; and a hard six-year stop from the date of recording (R. 5323-11) that nothing may outlive. Automate the deletion — a retention policy nobody executes is worse than none.

Restructure the employer churn record before the first entry is written: objective structured counts against the establishment's SIRET (listings per year, re-listings of the same post), no named gérant, no free-text comment boxes, dropdowns only. If any named individual survives in it, the full CNIL exclusion-list regime applies, including notifying them.

Write the admission and de-listing criteria down, publish them in the terms for restaurants, and keep the individual decisions private. This is what makes the curation defensible under L. 5321-2 (no refusal of service to an employer on a discrimination ground) and under the CNIL's exclusion-list doctrine, without publishing a single rating or score.

Never monetise the candidate side, in any form — no premium tier, no paid CV boost, no paid application priority, no affiliate revenue routed through the worker. L. 5321-3 catches indirect payment too; L. 5324-1 is six months and €3,750.

Build four validation rules into the listing form: a mandatory publication date on every offer (L. 5332-1); a block on upper-age wording (L. 5331-2); French-language text, with a French description where only a foreign job title exists (L. 5331-4); and a mandatory back-office employer identity and address field even for blind listings (L. 5332-2).

Put a factual-accuracy check into the vetting he is already doing — accommodation, hours, pay and actual place of work — and a contractual warranty from the restaurant. A misleading offer is one year and €37,500 under L. 5331-3 / L. 5334-1, and these are the exact fields seasonal alpine listings get wrong.

Make the photo field strictly optional, never required, never part of a profile-completeness score, and never a filter restaurants can search on. Collect 'under 18: yes/no' rather than a full date of birth — enough for the minor-work restrictions and the prefectural return, without exposing age as a selection criterion.

Never collect or infer the six article 9 categories, never collect the NIR (R. 5323-9 bars it outright for placement bodies), and never collect place of birth, family details or past salary — the CNIL has already issued a mise en demeure over exactly those. Write a documented rule that volunteered sensitive information is deleted rather than filed.
Diarise the annual return to the préfet before 31 March (R. 5323-8): placement turnover, and job-seeker numbers by sex and age — received, placed, and on file at 31 December.

Do NOT sign any contract with a restaurant that labels him their processor (sous-traitant). The CNIL says the authorities are not bound by the parties' chosen label and can requalify. Document the controller analysis in writing before launch.

Get the DSA question answered properly before building the paid-visibility feature and the de-listing process — it is the one open item that could directly contradict the silent-curation design, and I could not verify it.
unknowns: Digital Services Act (Reg. 2022/2065): whether article 17's statement-of-reasons duty applies to him when he removes or demotes a restaurant's listing, and whether the article 19 micro/small-enterprise exemption covers it. EUR-Lex returned an empty document on four attempts and economie.gouv.fr returned 403. This is the highest-value open item, because it bears directly on whether silent de-listing is lawful.

Platform-to-Business Regulation (EU) 2019/1150: whether a job board counts as an 'online intermediation service'. My reading is that it probably does not, because the definition turns on business users offering goods or services to consumers and a job offer is not a consumer transaction — but I did not open the text. If it did apply, its ranking-transparency rule would force him to disclose that paid visibility affects ranking, and its article 4 would require reasons and notice before terminating a business user.

Whether any prior declaration or authorisation is required to start a placement activity. I found the downstream duties (R. 5323-8 to R. 5323-12) by opening each article, but found no prior-declaration article and did not locate a definitive chapter listing. R. 5323-1 and R. 5323-3 both returned 404 on the Code du travail numérique. Treat 'no prior declaration required' as unproven rather than established — worth one call to the DREETS Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes.

Exact figures for the hiring-discrimination penalty under art. 225-2 code pénal (reported as three years / €45,000 for natural persons, €225,000 for legal persons). Legifrance refuses automated fetches and the CNIL guide cites the article without the amounts.

Exact verbatim French of L. 5321-1 and L. 5331-1 — both were returned to me in English translation by the fetch tool, though L. 5321-1's French text did come through in a second retrieval. The substance is not in doubt; the precise wording of L. 5331-1's paid-insertion exception should be re-read before he designs the paid-visibility tiers on top of it.

Whether the micro-entreprise or société choice changes anything here. Nothing I read distinguished them for these obligations, but I did not search for it specifically — and the criminal penalties differ (legal persons face multiplied fines under the code pénal).

How the placement regime interacts with him being 19. Nothing in R. 5323-8 to R. 5323-11 or L. 5321-1 to L. 5321-3 sets an age condition, but I did not check whether any capacity or professional-qualification requirement attaches to running a placement body.

research.lane: Lane 4 — status as an online platform (hébergeur/éditeur, L111-7 ranking transparency, DSA minimum, B2B consumer law, CGU/CGV, exposure for harm at a listed job)
research.bottom_line: Curating WHO may list does not make him an éditeur — what makes him an éditeur is authoring or rewriting the offers themselves. So the door policy is safe; the copy is not. Three things are genuinely load-bearing for him. (1) Paid visibility must be labelled as paid, in the listing itself, not buried in a page nobody reads — this is the one rule his revenue model is built to collide with, and the misleading-practice route (2 ans / 300 000 €) reaches him whether or not a jobseeker counts as a "consommateur". (2) "Silent" de-listing collides with the DSA: a hosting provider that restricts content on terms-based grounds owes the affected party a statement of reasons (art. 17), which micro platforms are NOT exempt from. He can keep it private, but not silent — or he must move the standard out of moderation and into contract renewal, where no statement is owed. (3) His biggest exposure if a candidate is harmed is not the hosting regime — the hosting safe harbour survives voluntary moderation — it is the PROMISE. Advertising "only decent houses" is a claim about his service; the moment a listed house proves abusive, that claim is the hook, for the candidate and for the DGCCRF. Promise a process ("every house is visited and re-checked each season"), never an outcome ("good employers only"). Beyond that, as a micro platform the DSA is light: contact points, clear CGU, a notice-and-action button, reasons when he takes something down. Exempt from transparency reports, from the whole Articles 20-28 block, and from trader traceability. The code du travail is the sharper edge: offers must be dated, in French, free of false or discriminatory wording, and the penalties reportedly reach the diffuseur and not only the employer — which is exactly what a job board is. Two items need a lawyer's yes before launch, both flagged in unknowns: whether the diffuseur really is on the hook for offer content, and whether his site already meets the statutory definition of "placement".

findings.claim: Curating WHO may list does not by itself make him an éditeur — authorship of the content does
findings.source_quote: Hébergeur: « Personne physique ou dirigeant d'une personne morale qui stocke des écrits, des sons, des images ou des vidéos réalisés par des tiers ». Directeur de publication: « Personne en charge de la publication d'un contenu éditorial ».
findings.detail: The official distinction is drawn on who produced the material: storing writings 'réalisés par des tiers' is hosting; being 'en charge de la publication d'un contenu éditorial' is publishing. Admission control is a decision about counterparties, not about content. The page does not adjudicate curation specifically, hence medium confidence.
findings.applies_to_him: He stays a hébergeur for every offer an employer writes and submits through his form and that he publishes as submitted. He becomes an éditeur — full liability, no notice-and-takedown shelter — for anything he writes himself: rewritten job descriptions, his own summaries, headline copy, a 'coup de coeur' blurb, an editorial ranking he composes. The practical rule: the employer types the offer, he never touches the words. If he wants to normalise formatting, do it with structured fields (job title, contract type, salary, hours) filled by the employer, not with prose he drafts.
findings.penalty: n/a (qualification rule)

findings.claim: As a hébergeur he is liable only once notified and failing to act promptly
findings.source_quote: (paraphrase from the opened page) Hébergeur obligations: must provide accessible reporting mechanisms for illegal content; must remove flagged illegal content immediately or block access; must notify competent authorities. Liable when they fail to remove reported illegal content or act with knowledge content was illegal.
findings.detail: Liability attaches on knowledge plus inaction, not on publication. The same page gives the penalty figures for the hébergeur who fails: one year imprisonment and 250 000 € for a natural person, and for a legal entity a fine up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover. It also notes a retention duty for user identification data since 21 October 2025 (décret 2025-980 cited).
findings.applies_to_him: His protection is procedural, and he only has it if the procedure exists before the problem does: a visible reporting button, a logged inbox, a documented removal decision with a timestamp. Build the takedown log on day one — it is the evidence that he acted promptly. Also note the identification-data retention duty: he must keep enough to identify who posted each offer.
findings.penalty: Hébergeur failing to remove: 1 an d'emprisonnement + 250 000 € (personne physique); up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover (personne morale)

findings.claim: Voluntary own-initiative moderation does not, by itself, cost him the hosting liability exemption (DSA art. 7)
findings.source_quote: From a search summary, NOT an opened page: 'Providers of intermediary services shall not be deemed ineligible for the exemptions from liability referred to in Articles 4, 5 and 6 solely because they, in good faith and in a diligent manner, carry out voluntary own-initiative investigations.'
findings.detail: This is the 'Good Samaritan' clause and it is the direct answer to his central worry. EUR-Lex refused every fetch I attempted (HTML, PDF, ELI, OJ, both languages, both encodings — all returned empty or 410), so I could not read Article 7 myself. The European Commission's own DSA FAQ, which I did open, confirms only the general point that the DSA 'incorporates the existing liability exemption rules of the e-Commerce Directive' and does not address voluntary moderation.
findings.applies_to_him: If confirmed, his screening of employers is not a trap: filtering in good faith does not convert him into an éditeur under EU law. The exemption is still lost the moment he has actual knowledge of specific illegal content and leaves it up. Have a lawyer read Article 7 and Recital 18 (the 'active role' carve-out) against his exact workflow before he markets the curation.
findings.penalty: n/a (liability-exemption rule)

findings.claim: Minimum DSA compliance for a micro platform: contact points, clear CGU, notice-and-action, statement of reasons, criminal-offence notification
findings.source_quote: (from the opened Arcom page) Intermediary services, Articles 9-15: handling injunctions against unlawful content, designating contact points, appointing EU legal representatives, maintaining clear terms of service, publishing annual transparency reports. Hosting services, Articles 16-18: notification mechanisms for reporting, reasoned statements when moderating user content, notifying authorities of suspected criminal law violations.
findings.detail: Arcom is France's Digital Services Coordinator, so this is the regulator's own mapping. Stripping out what micro enterprises are exempt from (next finding), what remains for him is: a point of contact for authorities (art. 11), a point of contact for users (art. 12), terms and conditions in plain language (art. 14), a notice-and-action mechanism (art. 16), a statement of reasons when he restricts content (art. 17), and notification to authorities on suspicion of a criminal offence threatening life or safety (art. 18). No EU legal representative needed — he is established in France.
findings.applies_to_him: That is a weekend of work, not a compliance department: an email address for authorities, a contact form for users, CGU drafted in plain French, a 'signaler cette offre' button on every listing, a template reason-for-removal email, and a note in his procedures about when to call the procureur. None of it requires headcount.
findings.penalty: Up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover (see separate finding)

findings.claim: He is exempt from the heaviest DSA blocks: transparency reports, Articles 20-28, and trader traceability
findings.source_quote: « intermediary service providers that can be qualified as microenterprises or small enterprises (i.e. those employing fewer than 50 people and whose annual turnover or annual balance sheet total does not exceed €10 million) and that are not very large online platforms ... are exempt from certain obligations » under articles 15(2), 19, and 29.
findings.detail: The three exemption hooks map to: art. 15(2) — no annual transparency report; art. 19 — the entire online-platform block (Articles 20-28: internal complaint-handling, out-of-court dispute settlement, trusted flaggers, measures against abuse, dark-patterns rules, advertising transparency, recommender-system transparency, protection of minors) does not apply; art. 29 — the trader-traceability/'know your business customer' rules (Articles 30-32) do not apply. Arcom's separate page confirms micro and small enterprises need not register on the Commission's transparency database (art. 24(5)). My mapping of which articles each hook covers is my own reading, not Arcom's words — hence medium.
findings.applies_to_him: He is nowhere near 50 employees or 10 M€. He stays exempt for years. Concretely: no transparency report to publish, no formal appeal system to build, no trusted-flagger channel, no advertising-repository. He must re-check the moment headcount or turnover moves, and the exemption is lost instantly if he is ever designated a very large platform (45 million EU users — irrelevant here).
findings.penalty: n/a (exemption)

findings.claim: DSA breaches are sanctioned up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover
findings.source_quote: (from the opened page) Maximum fine: 6% of worldwide annual turnover from the preceding year. Repeated serious breaches may result in temporary service access restrictions.
findings.detail: The same page states the CGU duties in the regulation's own register: platforms must « informer leurs utilisateurs de toute modification importante de leurs conditions générales » and present terms « de manière simple, intelligible, aisément abordable et sans ambiguïté ».
findings.applies_to_him: On a micro-entreprise turnover, 6% is small in absolute terms — the real cost of a DSA breach for him is the Arcom file and the reputational hit in a small valley, not the fine. The CGU wording duty is the operative one: plain French, and he must notify users of significant changes rather than silently editing the page.
findings.penalty: Up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover of the preceding year

findings.claim: Paid ranking must be disclosed — this is exactly what the platform-transparency regime targets
findings.source_quote: From search summaries only — every economie.gouv.fr URL I tried returned HTTP 403: 'For each ranking result, they must specify whether it was influenced or not by a payment from the referenced provider' and platforms 'must indicate the criteria for referencing, ranking, and de-referencing in a specific, easily accessible section on all pages of the site.'
findings.detail: The regime sits at article L111-7 of the code de la consommation with its implementing articles D111-7 and following (I did not read Legifrance and do not claim to have). It requires an 'information loyale, claire et transparente' on ranking criteria and, per the DGCCRF, disclosure at the level of each result of whether a payment influenced it — plus disclosure of any contractual link, capital link or remuneration that influences ranking. The DGCCRF has been enforcing it hard: one of its campaigns found 73% of controlled companies non-compliant.
findings.applies_to_him: This is the rule his business model is designed to collide with. Selling 'better visibility' is lawful; selling it invisibly is not. The compliant design: a badge on each boosted listing ('Offre sponsorisée' / 'Mise en avant payante'), plus a permanently linked page stating the ranking criteria and that payment can influence position. If boosted offers sit in a separate band above organic results, the band must be labelled. He should not describe boosted placement in language that implies editorial endorsement ('notre sélection', 'recommandé') — that compounds the paid-ranking problem with a false-endorsement problem.
findings.penalty: Administrative fine under the code de la consommation — amount not verified (see unknowns)

findings.claim: Even if a jobseeker is not a 'consommateur', the misleading-practice rules still reach him
findings.source_quote: (from the opened page) « deux ans d'emprisonnement et 300 000 € d'amende »; enhanced penalty « jusqu'à 4 % du chiffre d'affaires moyen annuel » for large-scale or EU-wide infractions.
findings.detail: There is a real doctrinal gap: article L111-7 is owed to consumers, and a person looking for a job is not obviously acting as a consumer of a free service. The gap closes because deceptive-commercial-practice rules are expressly extended to practices aimed at professionals and non-professionals (code de la consommation, around L121-5 — article number not verified). The page I opened confirms the 2-years / 300 000 € figure and a turnover-percentage uplift; the fetch attributed the articles to L212-1, which is the unfair-terms article and is plainly a mis-read, so treat every article number in this finding as unverified. Search summaries gave the uplift as 10% of average annual turnover over three years for deceptive practices, versus 4% for unfair terms.
findings.applies_to_him: He cannot escape the paid-ranking disclosure by arguing candidates are not consumers. And the employers paying him ARE professionals buying a service, so a misdescribed visibility package is exposed from that side too. Disclose, and describe what a paid slot actually delivers ('position in the top block for 30 days') rather than an outcome ('more candidates').
findings.penalty: 2 ans d'emprisonnement + 300 000 € d'amende, raisable to a percentage of average annual turnover (figures verified; article numbers not)

findings.claim: The restaurants are professionals, not consumers — with one narrow exception that probably catches him
findings.source_quote: The DGCCRF fiche's own title, verified through search but not opened (403): « Petits professionnels : vous avez 14 jours pour vous rétracter en cas de contrat conclu hors établissement ». Summary: professionals with at most five employees whose contract object falls outside their main professional activity get the same protection, including 14 days to withdraw without penalty.
findings.detail: The base rule is that B2B contracts sit outside the consumer code: no 14-day withdrawal, no consumer unfair-terms list, no pre-contractual consumer information duty. The exception (code de la consommation article L221-3 — article number not verified) requires three conditions together: the contract is concluded HORS ÉTABLISSEMENT, its object is outside the buyer's main activity, and the buyer has five employees or fewer. Buying job advertising is outside a restaurant's main activity. Many Megève hotels and restaurants have five or fewer employees. And a 19-year-old founder selling locally will sign people at their own reception desk — which is exactly 'hors établissement'.
findings.applies_to_him: Two practical consequences. If he signs at the restaurant's premises, he should assume a 14-day withdrawal right applies and say so in the contract — an unmentioned withdrawal right typically extends, and an unmentioned one is a defect he cannot cure later. If he signs online through his own site, this is a distance contract rather than an off-premises one, and the exception as titled does not appear to reach it. Cheapest fix: sell through an online signup flow, and where he does sign on site, include a 14-day withdrawal clause and a withdrawal form. The cost of granting it voluntarily is a few refunds; the cost of owing it silently is unenforceable contracts.
findings.penalty: Not a penalty — the contract becomes challengeable and the withdrawal period extends

findings.claim: Job offers he publishes must be dated and in French and free of false or discriminatory wording
findings.source_quote: The offer must indicate « sa date de publication ou de mise en ligne » and « doit être rédigée en français » if the work occurs in France or if « l'auteur de l'offre ou l'employeur est français ». Penalties: « un an d'emprisonnement » et 37 500 € d'amende for false statements; « 3 ans d'emprisonnement » et 45 000 € d'amende for discrimination.
findings.detail: The page lists the required content — publication date, company presentation, job title and duties, contract type (CDI, CDD, apprenticeship), required qualifications, work location, professional credentials for regulated posts, application procedure — and prohibits false or misleading allegations about the post or the benefits offered, and wording generating discrimination (health, religion, sex, age, family situation). It cites code du travail articles L5321-2 and L5331-2 through L5334-1.
findings.applies_to_him: These are content rules for the offers on his site, so they are design constraints on his submission form, not just the employer's problem. Make publication date automatic and visible. Make the form reject free-text that is not in French. Build a blocklist check on the discriminatory formulations the page names ('sans enfants', 'nationalité française', 'âgé de 25 à 35 ans', gendered job titles). In hospitality the gendered-title trap is live: 'serveuse', 'chef de rang H/F' — enforce H/F in the template.
findings.penalty: False/misleading allegations: 1 an d'emprisonnement + 37 500 €. Discriminatory content: 3 ans d'emprisonnement + 45 000 €

findings.claim: Those code du travail penalties reportedly reach the DIFFUSEUR of the offer, not only the employer
findings.source_quote: From a search summary, not from the page I opened: 'Additionally, these sanctions may also be applied to job broadcasters.' When I re-fetched the page asking specifically about diffuseur liability, it answered that the document does not explicitly clarify whether sanctions apply to the diffuseur separately from the employer.
findings.detail: The underlying prohibition is framed as 'faire publier ... ou diffuser' — wording that catches whoever causes the publication, not only whoever wrote it (code du travail around L5331-2; I did not read Legifrance). If that reading holds, a job board is the archetypal diffuseur. This is the single most consequential unverified item in the lane and the one I would put in front of a lawyer first.
findings.applies_to_him: If confirmed, his exposure for offer content is criminal and direct, and it does not wait for a notification the way the hosting regime does. The mitigations are the same ones curation already gives him: an automated screen on the submission form, a human read before a first-time employer's offer goes live, a contractual warranty from the employer that the offer is accurate and lawful, an indemnity, and a documented takedown on notice. Note the asymmetry — this exposure exists whether he curates or lists everything, so curation does not create it.
findings.penalty: Same as the offer-content penalties: 1 an + 37 500 € (false), 3 ans + 45 000 € (discrimination) — if the diffuseur reading is confirmed

findings.claim: Charging employers for insertion is lawful; charging candidates is not
findings.source_quote: From a search summary, not verified on an opened page: 'the principle is one of free distribution of job offers and requests, while prohibiting their sale, regardless of the medium used. However, the paid insertion of offers (or requests) for employment in a publication or other form of paid communication (for example, a website) is authorized.'
findings.detail: This maps to code du travail L5331-1 (publicity and distribution of job offers is free and gratuitous, but paid insertion in a paying medium is authorised) and to the separate prohibition on charging jobseekers for placement services (around L5321-3).
