Neither article was read on Legifrance. My re-fetch of the service-public page did not surface the paid-insertion sentence, so the summary may have come from the ministry page, which was behind a security check.
findings.applies_to_him: His revenue model as described is on the right side of this: employers pay for insertion, candidates pay nothing. The constraint bites on the roadmap, not today. Any future paid candidate feature — CV highlighting, a premium profile, priority applications, a paid alert — would run straight into the prohibition on charging jobseekers. Write that into his own product rules now, before a growth idea makes it tempting.
findings.penalty: Not verified

findings.claim: His site may already meet the statutory definition of 'placement' even without matching
findings.source_quote: From search summaries (the ministry page itself was blocked by a security-check interstitial): placement activity 'consists of providing, as a regular practice, services aimed at bringing together job supply and demand without the person or organization providing this activity becoming a party to the employment relationships that may result from it.'
findings.detail: The definition (code du travail around L5321-1) turns on 'rapprocher offres et demandes d'emploi' as a habitual activity — it does not require selection, matching, or a fee per hire. On its face a curated job board fits. This matters because he has been designing his product around staying OUT of placement, and the line may sit further back than he thinks. What the private-placement regime then requires — a declaration to the administration, and what else — I could not establish; the searches surfaced only the temporary-work-agency declaration regime, which is a different and stricter one and does NOT apply to him since he employs nobody and is not an agence d'intérim.
findings.applies_to_him: Do not build the legal story on 'we are not doing placement'. Build it on the substantive protections instead: free to candidates, no selection of candidates for employers, no fee per hire, no involvement in the employment relationship. Ask a lawyer specifically whether a declaration is owed and whether the placement regime is currently one of declaration or of simple freedom — the law was liberalised and I could not confirm the current state.
findings.penalty: Not verified

findings.claim: Silent de-listing collides with the DSA duty to give a statement of reasons
findings.source_quote: (from the opened Arcom page) Hosting Service Providers, Articles 16-18, require ... « providing reasoned statements when moderating user content ».
findings.detail: Article 17's statement-of-reasons duty sits in the hosting block, which micro enterprises are NOT exempt from — the exemption hooks cover Articles 20-28, not 16-18. It is triggered when a hosting provider restricts content because it is illegal or incompatible with its terms and conditions. Dropping an employer because his CGU say working conditions must meet a standard is a terms-based restriction. Ending a fixed-term advertising contract at its term, and simply not renewing, is a contractual decision and is not obviously a content restriction.
findings.applies_to_him: His 'enforced at the door, silently' design needs one adjustment: private is fine, silent is not. When he takes a house off the site mid-contract he must tell that house why — privately, in writing. He does not have to publish anything, name anyone, or run a public rating. The cleaner design that keeps the silence: sell listing in fixed seasonal terms, make the standard a renewal criterion in the CGV rather than a moderation ground, and simply decline to renew. No statement of reasons is owed for a contract he chooses not to extend.
findings.penalty: Covered by the DSA sanction ceiling (6% of worldwide turnover)

findings.claim: The real exposure if a candidate is harmed is the promise, not the hosting regime
findings.source_quote: (supporting figure, from the opened page) « deux ans d'emprisonnement et 300 000 € d'amende » for deceptive commercial practices.
findings.detail: Three distinct routes converge on the answer to his question. Route one, hosting liability: unchanged by curation — he answers for the offer's content on notification (and possibly as diffuseur under the code du travail), never for what an employer does to a worker on site. Route two, employment law: none of it reaches him. He is not the employer, not a co-employer, not an intérim agency, has no duty of safety toward the candidate, and the harm occurs inside a relationship he is not party to. Route three, and the live one: general civil liability plus deceptive-practice law, triggered not by curation itself but by what he SAYS about it. A public promise that listed houses offer decent conditions is a representation about the quality of his service; if he made it without a real verification process, or kept a house listed after learning it was abusive, the promise is the fault.
findings.applies_to_him: Curating increases exposure in one specific way and reduces it in another. It increases the representational risk — he is now making a claim a candidate can rely on. It reduces the knowledge risk — he actually sees his employers, so he acts on problems early. Net advice: promise the process, never the outcome. 'Chaque établissement est visité avant publication et réévalué chaque saison' is defensible and true. 'Uniquement des employeurs qui traitent bien leurs équipes' is a guarantee he cannot keep and would have to defend. Add a CGU clause stating he is not party to the employment relationship, verifies nothing about individual working conditions beyond his stated process, and gives no guarantee as to any employer. And keep dated notes of every visit and every complaint — the file is what shows he was not negligent.
findings.penalty: Deceptive practices: 2 ans + 300 000 €. Civil liability: uncapped damages (article 1240 code civil — not verified)

findings.claim: Publishing ratings or public declarations about employers is the higher-risk design he was right to avoid
findings.source_quote: Not verified for this specific point — the page I opened covers hébergeur and directeur de publication duties, not denigration or defamation.
findings.detail: Public statements about a named business carry two risks his silent model avoids entirely: denigration (a civil fault under the general liability rule, article 1240 code civil) and defamation of a business (loi du 29 juillet 1881). Worse, published ratings would make him the AUTHOR of the statement — the éditeur position, with no notice-and-takedown shelter. A user-review system would shift the authorship back to users but would drag in the verified-reviews regime and its own penalties, which the deceptive-practices page I opened prices at 2 years and 300 000 €.
findings.applies_to_him: His instinct is sound and he should hold it. No scores, no public 'blacklist', no comparative claims about named houses, and no user reviews at launch. The curation is a private admission standard, communicated to the employer and to nobody else. If he ever wants the trust signal a rating gives, the safe version is a factual badge about verifiable facts he collects himself ('logement fourni', 'deux jours consécutifs', 'contrat CDI') — facts, not judgements.
findings.penalty: Not verified for denigration/defamation; verified reviews regime: 2 ans + 300 000 €

findings.claim: Trader-traceability and marketplace rules do not apply — he is not a consumer-trader marketplace
findings.source_quote: (from the opened Arcom page) micro and small enterprises « are exempt from certain obligations » under articles 15(2), 19, and 29.
findings.detail: Articles 30-32 of the DSA (know-your-business-customer, traceability of traders, compliance by design) apply to online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders. A candidate and an employer concluding an employment relationship is not a consumer-trader distance contract, so the section does not reach him on its own terms — and article 29 exempts micro enterprises from it in any case. Two independent reasons, which is why this one is safe.
findings.applies_to_him: He does not need to collect and verify identity documents, bank details and trade-register entries from the restaurants as a marketplace would. He should still collect the SIRET — for his own contracting and invoicing, and because it is what lets him prove which legal person submitted which offer if the diffuseur question ever bites.
findings.penalty: n/a (does not apply)

findings.claim: Pay transparency is about to become a content requirement for every offer on his site
findings.source_quote: « Dès la phase de recrutement, les employeurs devront informer les candidats à un emploi de la rémunération proposée ou d'une fourchette de rémunération. »
findings.detail: The French bill transposing directive (UE) 2023/970 of 10 May 2023 was presented to the Council of Ministers on 10 September 2026 and still has to pass the Senate and the Assemblée nationale, so it is not yet binding. The EU transposition deadline has already passed, which means adoption is a question of when, not whether.
findings.applies_to_him: Build the pay field into the offer form now and make it mandatory: a figure or a range, refuse to publish without it. Two gains beyond compliance. First, he avoids a forced schema migration across every live listing when the law passes. Second, mandatory posted pay is precisely the differentiator his product is about — for a 19-year-old entering hospitality, 'the site where every offer states the pay' is a sharper promise than 'curated', and unlike curation it is a fact he can prove.
findings.penalty: Not yet in force — no penalty to state

findings.claim: Mentions légales and the two DSA contact points are the cheapest items and the ones most often missed
findings.source_quote: Not opened — from search results: « Tout site web doit permettre d'identifier son responsable et son hébergeur, en application de la loi pour la confiance dans l'économie numérique du 21 juin 2004. »
findings.detail: For a micro-entrepreneur the mentions légales must identify him by name, give his address, his SIRET, contact details, and the identity and address of his hosting provider. Separately the DSA requires a single point of contact for authorities (art. 11) and one for service recipients (art. 12), published and reachable by electronic means.
findings.applies_to_him: One footer page covers all of it. Worth getting right because it is the first thing any complainant or inspector checks, and a missing mentions légales page signals an amateur operation to exactly the audience he needs to look credible to — hotel managers deciding whether to hand him money.
findings.penalty: Not verified

must_do: Label every paid placement in the listing itself ('Offre sponsorisée' or a distinctly styled paid band), and publish a permanently linked page stating the ranking criteria and that payment influences position. Never dress a paid slot in endorsement language ('notre sélection', 'recommandé').
Let employers write their own offers through a structured form. He fills no prose field, ever. Structured fields (title, contract type, pay, hours, accommodation) are his; the words are theirs.

Make the offer form enforce the code du travail rules mechanically: automatic visible publication date, French-only free text, a blocklist for discriminatory formulations (gendered job titles are the live trap in hospitality — force H/F), and a mandatory pay figure or range.
Ship the notice-and-action button on every listing, with a logged inbox and a timestamped takedown record. The log IS the safe-harbour evidence; it is worthless if created after the first complaint.

Choose one de-listing mechanism and build the CGV around it. Either give a private written statement of reasons when removing mid-contract (DSA art. 17), or sell in fixed seasonal terms and make the standard a non-renewal criterion, where no reasons are owed. Do not promise 'silent' removal in the CGU while operating the first.

Rewrite the curation promise from outcome to process before any marketing copy is written: 'chaque établissement est visité avant publication et réévalué chaque saison', never 'uniquement des employeurs qui traitent bien leurs équipes'.

Put in the employer CGV: a warranty that each offer is accurate, lawful and non-discriminatory; an indemnity for claims arising from offer content; his right to refuse, suspend or de-list; and the SIRET of the contracting legal person.

Put in the candidate CGU: he is not party to the employment relationship, gives no guarantee as to any employer, and verifies only what his stated process covers; plus the reporting channel and the two DSA contact points.
If he signs restaurants on their own premises, include a 14-day withdrawal clause and a withdrawal form in the contract. Selling through an online signup flow instead avoids the question entirely.
Publish mentions légales (name, address, SIRET, contact, host identity) and the DSA points of contact in the footer before the first paying customer.
Keep a dated file per listed house: visit notes, complaints received, action taken. It is the only thing that answers a negligence claim.

Take two questions to a lawyer before launch: (1) does the code du travail offer-content liability reach the diffuseur as well as the employer, and (2) does a curated job board already meet the statutory definition of 'placement', and if so what does that regime currently require.
unknowns: The exact text of DSA Articles 6, 7, 8, 14, 16, 17 and 19 — EUR-Lex refused every fetch form I tried (HTML, PDF, ELI and OJ URLs, both languages, encoded and unencoded colons), returning empty bodies or HTTP 410. All DSA article content in this report comes from Arcom (France's Digital Services Coordinator), service-public and the Commission's FAQ, not from the regulation itself. The Good Samaritan clause at Article 7 is the single most important unread provision.

The administrative fine for breaching the platform-transparency duty at code de la consommation L111-7 — I could not source the amount. Every economie.gouv.fr page returned HTTP 403, including the DGCCRF page on platform information obligations and the fiche on small-professional withdrawal rights.

Whether the code du travail penalties for false or discriminatory job offers reach the diffuseur. One search summary says they do; the service-public page, asked directly, says it does not address the point. This is the largest open exposure in the lane.

Whether his site already meets the statutory definition of 'placement', and what the private-placement regime currently requires — in particular whether a prior declaration to the administration is still owed, or whether that was removed when placement was liberalised. Searches surfaced only the temporary-work-agency declaration regime, which is a different regime and does not apply to him.

The precise article numbers behind the deceptive-practice penalties. The service-public page I opened attributed them to L212-1, which is the unfair-terms article and is clearly a mis-read by the extraction. The amounts (2 years, 300 000 €, a turnover-percentage uplift) are consistent across sources; the article numbers are not.

Whether a jobseeker qualifies as a 'consommateur' for the purposes of L111-7. This determines whether the ranking-transparency regime applies directly or only through the deceptive-practice route. No official source addresses a job board.

The Défenseur des droits decision 2020-163 on a job-advert site operator's responsibility for discriminatory offers. The PDF opened but the extraction returned only paraphrase and then two 'quotes' that do not match the earlier summary and appear synthesised; no PDF text extractor was available locally to verify. The decision is directly on point and should be read properly.

Whether article 242 bis of the code général des impôts (a platform's duty to inform users of their tax and social obligations and file an annual summary) reaches a job board. The wording covers putting people in touch 'en vue de la fourniture d'un service', and whether an employment relationship counts is genuinely arguable. This is tax-lane territory but it is triggered by his platform status.

Whether his CGV with restaurants are exposed to the significant-imbalance rule for B2B contracts (code de commerce L442-1 I 2°) — relevant to his de-listing and no-refund clauses. Not researched; no official source opened.

research.lane: Lane 5 — Discrimination and equal access (French law), for a curated, employer-paid, candidate-free hospitality job board in Haute-Savoie
research.bottom_line: Three things reframe his plan. (1) He is already, today, a "service de placement" in French law — Article L5321-1 defines placement as habitually providing services aimed at bringing job offers and job seekers together, and publishing offers so the two sides can contact each other is exactly that. He does not need to select or match for this to bite. It is not agence d'intérim status (that requires becoming a party to the work relationship), it is a lighter separate regime, and it has no licence or prior declaration — but it has two hard rules. (2) The first hard rule answers (c) directly and it is not refus de vente: Article L5321-2 says no placement service may be refused to a job seeker OR TO AN EMPLOYER on one of the discrimination grounds of L1132-1. So his silent curation is lawful in principle — a declined restaurant has no general right to be listed, B2B refusal has been free since the loi Galland of 1996 — but the ground of refusal is policed. "Churns staff", "pays badly", "bad conditions" are not protected grounds and are safe. A refusal that correlates with the owner's origin, religion, sex, age or disability is a criminal offence (3 years, €45,000; €225,000 for a company), and Article L5323-1 lets the administration order his site closed for up to three months. (3) The second hard rule: Article L5321-3 forbids any payment, direct or indirect, from job seekers — six months and €3,750 under L5324-1. His free-for-candidates model is not a marketing choice, it is the law, and "indirect" means no premium candidate tier, no CV-boost upsell, ever. On (b): targeting young people as an audience is lawful and unremarkable; what is prohibited is an employer's ad stating an upper age limit (L5331-2), except where a statute sets the age — apprenticeship, 16 to 29 under L6222-1, is the one he will actually meet. On (e) and (f): neither accessibility regime bites him. The RGAA obligation under Article 47 of the loi of 11 February 2005 starts at €250M average French turnover; the European Accessibility Act, applicable since 28 June 2025, exempts service providers with fewer than 10 employees and under €2M. There is no specific French duty to publish job offers in an accessible format. The residual risk in (f) is indirect discrimination: an unusable site disadvantages disabled candidates on a ground listed in L1132-1, which L5321-2 protects. Build to WCAG AA because it is cheap now and unfixable later, not because a regulator is coming.

findings.claim: (a) The list of protected criteria in employment is Article L1132-1 of the Code du travail — around 25 grounds, covering recruitment, internships and training as well as employment itself.
findings.detail: The article opens by covering exclusion from a recruitment procedure, not only treatment of existing staff, which is why it reaches a job board's listings and not just an employer's hiring decision. The grounds are: origine, sexe, mœurs, orientation sexuelle, identité de genre, âge, situation de famille ou grossesse, caractéristiques génétiques, particulière vulnérabilité résultant de la situation économique, appartenance vraie ou supposée à une ethnie / une nation / une prétendue race, opinions politiques, activités syndicales ou mutualistes, exercice d'un mandat électif, convictions religieuses, apparence physique, nom de famille, lieu de résidence ou domiciliation bancaire, état de santé, perte d'autonomie, handicap, capacité à s'exprimer dans une langue autre que le français, qualité de lanceur d'alerte ou de facilitateur.
findings.applies_to_him: This is the list his curation rules, his listing form and his moderation must be measured against. Anything he asks a restaurant, and anything a restaurant writes in an offer, has to avoid all of it. Note two that hospitality ads routinely trip: apparence physique ("présentation soignée exigée" is a grey zone, "bonne présentation physique" is not) and lieu de résidence ("véhiculé, habitant la vallée" is risky in a seasonal-housing market).
findings.penalty: L1132-1 itself is a civil prohibition and carries no criminal penalty as such — the Ministry of Justice guide states that breach of L1132-1 to L1132-4 "ne constitue pas en tant que telle une infraction pénale". The criminal route is article 225-2 code pénal (see next finding).
findings.source_quote: « Aucune personne ne peut être écartée d'une procédure de recrutement ou de nomination ou de l'accès à un stage ou à une période de formation en entreprise, aucun salarié ne peut être sanctionné, licencié ou faire l'objet d'une mesure discriminatoire, directe ou indirecte, [...] en raison de son origine, de son sexe, de ses mœurs, de son orientation sexuelle, de son identité de genre, de son âge, de sa situation de famille ou de sa grossesse, de ses caractéristiques génétiques, de la particulière vulnérabilité résultant de sa situation économique, apparente ou connue de son auteur, de son appartenance ou de sa non-appartenance, vraie ou supposée, à une ethnie, une nation ou une prétendue race, de ses opinions politiques, de ses activités syndicales ou mutualistes, de son exercice d'un mandat électif, de ses convictions religieuses, de son apparence physique, de son nom de famille, de son lieu de résidence ou de sa domiciliation bancaire, ou en raison de son état de santé, de sa perte d'autonomie ou de son handicap, de sa capacité à s'exprimer dans une langue autre que le français, de sa qualité de lanceur d'alerte, de facilitateur ou de personne en lien avec un lanceur d'alerte »

findings.claim: (a) The criminal mirror is article 225-1 code pénal — and its second paragraph extends discrimination to distinctions made between LEGAL PERSONS on the basis of the criteria of their members.
findings.detail: Article 225-2 then lists the acts that make the discrimination a crime. Two of the five hit a job board squarely: refusing to supply a good or a service, and obstructing the normal exercise of any economic activity. The Ministry of Justice guide reproduces both. Note the guide is an older edition and its list of criteria predates several additions (identité de genre, lieu de résidence, vulnérabilité économique, lanceur d'alerte); the acts and the penalties are unchanged, and the current criteria list is the service-public one.
findings.applies_to_him: This is the single provision that makes a declined restaurant's discrimination claim legally coherent. A restaurant is a personne morale; 225-1 al. 2 lets it allege that his refusal was a distinction based on the origin, religion or ethnicity of its owner or staff. And the act charged would be « refuser la fourniture d'un bien ou d'un service » — the service being the listing. He is not shielded by the fact that the victim is a company rather than a person.
findings.penalty: 3 ans d'emprisonnement et 45 000 € d'amende (articles 225-1 and 225-2 code pénal); 5 ans et 75 000 € where the refusal is committed in a lieu accueillant du public. For a personne morale the maximum fine is fivefold: 225 000 €, or 375 000 € in the aggravated case (service-public.gouv.fr F38175).
findings.source_quote: « Constitue également une discrimination toute distinction opérée entre les personnes morales selon les mêmes critères concernant leurs membres ou certains d'entre eux. » — and under article 225-2 the discrimination is criminal when it consists « A refuser la fourniture d'un bien ou d'un service ; A entraver l'exercice normal d'une activité économique quelconque ; A refuser d'embaucher, à sanctionner ou à licencier une personne ; A subordonner la fourniture d'un bien ou d'un service à une condition fondée sur l'un des éléments visés à l'article 225-1 ; A subordonner une offre d'emploi, une demande de stage ou une période de formation en entreprise à une condition fondée sur l'un des éléments fondé sur l'article 225-1. »

findings.claim: (b) Aiming the PLATFORM at young people is lawful. Age differences of treatment are not discrimination where objectively and reasonably justified by a legitimate aim, and the statute names favouring professional integration as one.
findings.detail: Article L1133-2 is the carve-out that makes youth-employment policy legal in France. Its first paragraph requires a legitimate aim plus necessary and appropriate means; it expressly names « favoriser leur insertion professionnelle » as such an aim. His platform is an entry-to-the-trade channel, which is that aim exactly.
findings.applies_to_him: Safe as designed — provided the youth framing stays on HIS side of the transaction: the editorial line, the branding, the guides, who he markets to. It must never become a filter. The moment the site refuses to register a 47-year-old commis, or an employer can tick "under 26 only" as a search facet, he has moved the age criterion from his audience into the hiring decision, which is where L1132-1 and L5321-2 apply. Keep the site open to everyone and let the editorial voice do the targeting.
findings.penalty: n/a — this is the exemption, not an offence.
findings.source_quote: « Les différences de traitement fondées sur l'âge ne constituent pas une discrimination lorsqu'elles sont objectivement et raisonnablement justifiées par un but légitime, notamment par le souci de préserver la santé ou la sécurité des travailleurs, de favoriser leur insertion professionnelle, d'assurer leur emploi, leur reclassement ou leur indemnisation en cas de perte d'emploi, et lorsque les moyens de réaliser ce but sont nécessaires et appropriés. »

findings.claim: (b) An EMPLOYER's ad stating an upper age limit is separately and specifically prohibited — Article L5331-2 — and the ban is written against whoever publishes or broadcasts it, not only against the employer.
findings.detail: The article's verb is « faire publier [...] ou de diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public ». A website is a moyen de communication accessible au public. Service-public's own page for employers spells the same rule out in plain terms, listing the mentions an offer may not carry.
findings.applies_to_him: The distinction he asked for, stated plainly: "a site for young people getting into hospitality" is lawful; "Commis de cuisine, 18-25 ans" in a listing is not, and it is HIS publication that the prohibition names. He needs a listing form that rejects age ranges at input, not a moderator who spots them later. The sole exception is a statutory age condition — in his sector that means apprenticeship.
findings.penalty: L5334-1 does NOT penalise L5331-2 (it penalises only L5331-3 and L5331-5), so the age-limit ban itself carries no criminal fine. The criminal exposure runs through article 225-2 code pénal, 5th indent — subordinating a job offer to a condition based on a 225-1 criterion — at 3 ans and 45 000 €. Service-public gives the same figure for a discriminatory offer.
findings.source_quote: « Il est interdit de faire publier dans un journal, revue ou écrit périodique ou de diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public une insertion d'offres d'emploi ou d'offres de travaux à domicile comportant la mention d'une limite d'âge supérieure exigée du postulant à un emploi. » — and on service-public: « Ne peuvent pas figurer dans l'offre d'emploi les mentions suivantes : Mentions concernant le sexe [...] Mentions concernant l'âge ou une tranche d'âge »

findings.claim: (b) The lawful age exception he will actually meet is apprenticeship: Article L6222-1 sets 16 to 29 révolus.
findings.detail: L5331-2's exception is for offers where age conditions are imposed by statute. Apprenticeship is the textbook case, and in hospitality it is a large share of entry-level hiring.
findings.applies_to_him: An ad reading « Contrat d'apprentissage — cuisine » is lawful and carries the 16-29 boundary by operation of law, with no age mention needed in the text. That is his clean route to a young-candidate pipeline: publish the contract type, never the age range. It also gives him a defensible reason for a dedicated apprenticeship section on the site.
findings.penalty: n/a
findings.source_quote: « Nul ne peut être engagé en qualité d'apprenti s'il n'est âgé de seize ans au moins à vingt-neuf ans révolus au début de l'apprentissage. »

findings.claim: THE CENTRAL FINDING — He is a placement operator TODAY, as a pure publisher. Article L5321-1 defines placement as habitually providing services aimed at bringing offers and job seekers together, without becoming a party to the resulting work relationship — and says it may be carried on for profit.
findings.detail: The definition has no selection or matching element. "Rapprocher les offres et les demandes d'emploi" is satisfied by publishing offers and letting the two sides contact each other, which is precisely his description of the product. The second paragraph settles that charging for it is fine. The clause « sans que la personne assurant cette activité ne devienne partie aux relations de travail » is the boundary with agence d'intérim: he stays outside it as long as he never employs or supplies the worker.
findings.applies_to_him: This overturns the framing of the question. He asked what binds him as a pure publisher versus if he drifts into matching — but the placement regime binds him from day one, not on drift. The good news: Chapitre Ier is only three articles (L5321-4 does not exist), there is no licence, no prior declaration, no register. The regime is two prohibitions, in the next two findings. What drift into selecting or matching would add is not a new legal status but a much larger evidential surface: a ranking or matching algorithm is a "pratique en apparence neutre" that a claimant can attack as indirect discrimination, and he would have to be able to justify its criteria. Staying a pure publisher is his cheapest legal position, and he should treat paid visibility tiers carefully for exactly this reason — ordering by price is defensible, ordering by anything that proxies a protected characteristic is not.
findings.penalty: n/a for the status itself.
findings.source_quote: « L'activité de placement consiste à fournir, à titre habituel, des services visant à rapprocher les offres et les demandes d'emploi, sans que la personne assurant cette activité ne devienne partie aux relations de travail susceptibles d'en découler. La fourniture de services de placement peut être exercée à titre lucratif. »

findings.claim: (c) THE ANSWER TO HIS CURATION QUESTION — Article L5321-2: no placement service may be refused to a job seeker OR TO AN EMPLOYER on one of the grounds of L1132-1. The same article forbids any offer from referring to those characteristics.
findings.detail: This is the provision that actually governs his door policy, and neither he nor a generic "can I refuse a customer" analysis would find it — it sits in the placement chapter, not in commercial or consumer law. It does not create a right to be listed. It prohibits one class of reasons for refusing. Its second sentence is a standing moderation duty on the content he publishes.
findings.applies_to_him: So: a declined restaurant CAN challenge him, and discrimination is the real basis — not refus de vente, not abuse of dominance. But the challenge only succeeds if the reason for refusal falls in L1132-1. "You churn staff", "you don't pay overtime", "three of your commis left in a season", "you didn't answer our conditions questionnaire" are none of them. A refusal correlated with the owner's origin, religion or name is. Practically: the second sentence also means he cannot simply pass through whatever a restaurant writes — if a published offer references a protected characteristic, the breach is on his service.
findings.penalty: No penalty in the placement chapter for L5321-2 itself. Enforcement is (i) Article L5323-1 — administrative closure of the organisme for up to three months, after mise en demeure, and (ii) the criminal route of article 225-2 code pénal at 3 ans / 45 000 € (225 000 € for a company).
findings.source_quote: « Aucun service de placement ne peut être refusé à une personne à la recherche d'un emploi ou à un employeur fondé sur l'un des motifs de discrimination énumérés à l'article L. 1132-1. Aucune offre d'emploi ne peut comporter de référence à l'une des caractéristiques mentionnées à cet article. »

findings.claim: (c) The enforcement teeth on the placement rules are administrative, not just criminal: labour inspectors can record breaches and the administration can order the operation closed for up to three months.
findings.detail: Article L5323-1 gives the labour-law enforcement officers competence over the whole of Chapitre Ier — that is, over L5321-1 to L5321-3 — and gives the administrative authority a closure power after a mise en demeure, also available in case of atteinte à l'ordre public.
findings.applies_to_him: A three-month closure would kill a seasonal alpine job board outright — the Megève season is roughly that long. This makes the compliance cost of the placement rules disproportionate to their apparent smallness, and it is the reason to get the refusal policy written down before launch rather than after the first complaint. The upside is the mise en demeure step: he gets a chance to fix things first.
findings.penalty: Fermeture de l'organisme pour une durée n'excédant pas trois mois, after mise en demeure (L5323-1).
findings.source_quote: « Les fonctionnaires et agents chargés du contrôle de l'application du droit du travail sont habilités à constater les manquements aux dispositions du chapitre Ier. Lorsque l'activité de placement est exercée en méconnaissance de ces dispositions ou en cas d'atteinte à l'ordre public, l'autorité administrative peut, après mise en demeure, ordonner la fermeture de l'organisme en cause pour une durée n'excédant pas trois mois. »

findings.claim: (d) NO — a French business is not obliged to serve any paying customer, once that customer is itself a business. Refus de vente between professionals has been free since the loi Galland of 1996. The obligation to sell exists only towards consumers, under article L121-11 of the code de la consommation.
findings.detail: The Institut national de la consommation, a public body, states the rule and the 1996 turning point. The DGCCRF's own fiche pratique says the same in stronger terms — freedom is the principle in B2B — but economie.gouv.fr returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so I am reporting the DGCCRF position from the search index only and treating the INC page as my opened source. The B2C prohibition carries a small fine; the B2B position carries none, subject to the competition-law and abrupt-termination exceptions below.
findings.applies_to_him: His restaurants and hotels are business customers, so the consumer obligation to sell never applies to them. He may choose his clients. The freedom is not absolute, but the limits are the three in the next findings — discrimination, competition law, abrupt termination — not a general duty to serve. Worth noting the mirror: his CANDIDATES are consumers of a free service; refusing a consumer a service without motif légitime is prohibited, which reinforces that the site itself must stay open to all comers regardless of age.
findings.penalty: Non-discriminatory refusal to a consumer: up to €1,500 for an individual, €7,500 for a legal entity (contravention, code pénal articles 131-13 and 131-38 per INC). B2B refusal: no penalty as such.
findings.source_quote: INC: refusal of sale is prohibited towards consumers by « article L121-11 » of the code de la consommation, which forbids a professional « to refuse a consumer the sale of a product or the provision of a service » — and the rule applies only to B2C: "Under the 1996 Galland Law, professionals may legitimately refuse sales to other businesses."

findings.claim: (c) Abuse of a dominant position (article L420-2 code de commerce) is a real head of claim against a gatekeeping platform, but it requires dominance on a defined relevant market — which a new micro-business does not have.
findings.detail: Three cumulative conditions: a dominant position on a relevant market, abusive exploitation of it, and an actual or at least potential restrictive effect on competition. Refus de vente is one of the named abuses. Dominance is the power to behave to an appreciable extent independently of competitors and customers. I could not open economie.gouv.fr (403 on every URL on that host), so this rests on the search index rendering of the DGCCRF fiche rather than on a page I read.
findings.applies_to_him: Not a live risk at launch and he should not pay a lawyer to worry about it now. It becomes live only on a specific fact pattern: if his site becomes the de facto only channel for hospitality hiring in the Megève basin, a relevant market can be drawn narrowly (geographic: one alpine valley; product: hospitality job listings), and exclusion from it could be characterised as an abuse. Two cheap insurance policies against that future: never sign exclusivity with a listing restaurant, and keep the refusal criteria published so exclusion is never arbitrary. A related and lower-threshold head — abus de dépendance économique, also L420-2 — could in theory be raised by a restaurant that had come to depend on him, which is another reason not to take exclusivity.
findings.penalty: Not sourced to an opened page. The DGCCRF has itself fined an operator €45,800 for abuse of dominance in a recent case per the search index; the general L464-2 ceilings are much higher and I did not verify them.
findings.source_quote: Not quoted from an opened page — economie.gouv.fr returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt. The search index renders the DGCCRF fiche as requiring "the existence of a dominant position on a determined market, called the 'relevant market', an abusive exploitation of this position, and an object or effect, at least potential, restrictive of competition", with abuses that "can notably consist of refusal of sale".

findings.claim: (c) The exposure that WILL bite him is not the initial refusal but the silent DELISTING of a paying client — rupture brutale d'une relation commerciale établie, article L442-1 II code de commerce.
findings.detail: Refusing a new applicant is free. Ending an established, ongoing commercial relationship without written notice proportionate to its duration is a distinct civil wrong, and the remedy is damages for the notice that should have been given. This is the one place where "quietly stop listing" is legally different from "quietly decline".
findings.applies_to_him: His stated plan — "quietly stop listing houses that churn staff" — describes ending a relationship with a restaurant that has been paying him, possibly for several seasons. That is the L442-1 II fact pattern, not the refus de vente one, and "quietly" is precisely the aggravating feature. The fix is cheap and entirely within his control: a contract term fixing a notice period and a renewal cycle. A seasonal listing sold season by season, with non-renewal at the end of each season and notice written into the CGV, largely engineers the problem away — there is no abrupt break if the contract simply reaches its term.
findings.penalty: Civil damages measured by the notice not given, not a fine. Article number given from knowledge; I could not open a primary source — service-public has no dedicated page and legifrance is out of bounds.
findings.source_quote: Not quoted from an opened page. The search index attributes to service-public the formulation that parties may give written notice of termination "taking into account the duration of the commercial relationship and the economic conditions of the market on which the parties operate".

findings.claim: (c) Unfair competition is the WRONG way round from how he fears it. Silence protects him; it is publishing ratings or public statements about employers that would create the denigration claim.
findings.detail: Denigration — publicly disparaging a competitor's or a business's products, services or person — is the classic délit civil under article 1240 du code civil. A refusal communicated privately and factually to the applicant creates no publication and therefore no denigration.
findings.applies_to_him: His instinct to keep the standard silent is legally sound and he should keep it. "We are not able to list your establishment at this time" sent privately is not actionable. "Le Chalet X : 2/10 conditions de travail" published on the site is a denigration claim waiting to happen, and would also drag him into the truth-and-proof burden of every negative statement. The corollary matters for his marketing: if he cannot say who he excluded, he must also be careful what he claims about who he included — see the L5331-5 finding below.
findings.penalty: Civil damages under article 1240 code civil. Article number from knowledge; not sourced to an opened page.
findings.source_quote: Not verified against an opened primary source.

findings.claim: (c) WHAT HE NEEDS IN PLACE to defend a refusal: written published criteria, applied consistently, recorded per decision, with the reason communicated privately in non-protected terms.
findings.detail: This is the practical synthesis of the four heads above rather than a single sourced rule. The structure works because each element defeats a different claim: published criteria defeat arbitrariness (competition law and abuse-of-right); non-protected criteria defeat L5321-2 and article 225-2; a per-decision record defeats the shifted burden of proof in discrimination cases, where the claimant need only present facts suggesting discrimination and the defendant must then prove the decision rested on objective factors; a contractual notice period defeats L442-1 II.
findings.applies_to_him: Concretely, before he takes the first euro: (1) a one-page "charte des établissements" on the site — declared criteria only, all of them about working conditions and turnover, none about the person of the employer; (2) an onboarding questionnaire that produces the evidence (contract types offered, housing, rotas, overtime handling, staff departures last season); (3) a dated log with the criterion failed for every refusal and every delisting; (4) a private, factual refusal letter template; (5) CGV with a season-length term and a stated notice period. This is a weekend of work and it converts his biggest legal exposure into his strongest asset — a documented standard is also the whole value proposition to candidates.
findings.penalty: n/a — this is the defence, not an offence.
findings.source_quote: Synthesis; the burden-shift rule in discrimination litigation derives from article 1er of loi n° 2008-496 du 27 mai 2008 and L1134-1 code du travail, neither of which I opened.

findings.claim: (e) RGAA — Article 47 of the loi n° 2005-102 of 11 February 2005 — does NOT bite him. For private companies the threshold is €250M average annual French turnover over the last three closed financial years.
findings.detail: Arcom, the regulator charged with supervising the obligation since the ordonnance of 6 September 2023 created article 47-1, sets out three categories: public legal persons, private bodies entrusted with a public service mission, and private companies above the turnover threshold fixed by décret — currently €250M under décret n° 2019-768.
findings.applies_to_him: A 19-year-old's micro-entreprise is four orders of magnitude below the threshold. RGAA conformity is not a legal obligation for him in 2026 or 2027 and will not become one at any plausible size of this business. Do not let a web agency sell him an RGAA audit as a compliance requirement.
findings.penalty: Where it does apply: up to €50,000 for failure to meet the accessibility requirements, up to €25,000 for the ancillary obligations (déclaration d'accessibilité, affichage de conformité, mécanisme de réclamation), modulated by nature, gravity and duration of the breach (Arcom).
findings.source_quote: Arcom applies the obligation to « les entreprises dont le chiffre d'affaires excède un seuil fixé par décret (actuellement 250 millions d'euros) », the turnover being « la moyenne du chiffre d'affaires annuel réalisé en France des trois derniers exercices comptables », with sanctions « modulables en fonction de la nature, de la gravité et de la durée du manquement ».

findings.claim: (e) The European Accessibility Act — Directive (EU) 2019/882, applicable in France since 28 June 2025 — exempts micro-enterprises providing services entirely: fewer than 10 employees AND turnover or balance-sheet total under €2M.
findings.detail: The French government's own business portal states the threshold and the date. The DGCCRF adds, per the search index, that for service providers the micro-enterprise exemption is total — no accessibility obligation at all — whereas product manufacturers, importers and distributors may derogate without justification. Two other exemption routes exist for anyone: fundamental alteration of the product, and disproportionate burden. An online declaration route to the DGCCRF exists via Démarches simplifiées.
findings.applies_to_him: He is a service provider, alone or with one or two people, with revenue that will not approach €2M. Exempt, on the plainest reading, for 2026 and 2027 and well beyond. He should know the number he must not cross rather than the rule he must follow: 10 employees, €2M. Note the exemption is by enterprise size, not by product — so this protection disappears if the business ever succeeds at scale, and retrofitting accessibility into a grown site is far more expensive than building it in.
findings.penalty: Not applicable to him. For those in scope, the search index reports breaches of the code de la consommation accessibility obligations as contraventions de 5e classe at €7,500, cumulable per breach, with DGCCRF injunction powers backed by an astreinte of up to €3,000 per day (décret n° 2023-931). I could not open a primary source for these figures — treat them as indicative.
findings.source_quote: « l'entreprise concernée compte moins de 10 salariés avec un chiffre d'affaires annuel ou un total de bilan inférieur à 2 millions d'euros » — and « La directive, qui a été transposée en droit français, s'applique depuis le 28 juin 2025. »

findings.claim: (e) Even setting the micro-enterprise exemption aside, his paid service is probably outside the EAA's e-commerce head, because that head is defined by reference to concluding a CONSUMER contract.
findings.detail: The EAA covers e-commerce services among others; the French transposition, per the search index, extends the digital accessibility obligation to a list of B2C services — telephony, audiovisual media, e-commerce, banking, transport. The directive's own definition of e-commerce services turns on a distance service provided at a consumer's individual request with a view to concluding a consumer contract. I could not open EUR-Lex — every URL form for CELEX 32019L0882 returned an empty body — so I give the article numbers without claiming to have read them: Article 2(2)(f), Article 3(30), Article 4(5), Article 3(23), Article 31.
findings.applies_to_him: His only paying customers are businesses, and his candidates conclude no contract at all — they read listings for free. So the e-commerce head likely does not reach him even at scale. This is his second line of defence and he should not rely on it alone; the micro-enterprise exemption is the clean one. It does mean that if he ever monetised the candidate side he would be doing two illegal things at once: breaching L5321-3 (see below) and walking into the e-commerce accessibility scope.
findings.penalty: n/a
findings.source_quote: Not quoted from an opened page — EUR-Lex returned an empty document body for CELEX:32019L0882 in EN and FR, HTML and ELI forms. The scope statement rests on the search index rendering of the DGCCRF fiche and of the transposition commentary.

findings.claim: (f) There is NO specific French obligation to publish job offers in a format accessible to disabled users. The residual duty is the general one: an inaccessible site is a candidate for INDIRECT discrimination on the handicap ground, which L5321-2 protects for a placement service.
findings.detail: Indirect discrimination, under article 1er of loi n° 2008-496 of 27 May 2008, is an apparently neutral provision, criterion or practice liable to put persons at a particular disadvantage on a protected ground, unless objectively justified by a legitimate aim pursued by necessary and appropriate means. Handicap and perte d'autonomie are both in the L1132-1 list that L5321-2 imports. So the chain runs: inaccessible site → particular disadvantage for disabled candidates → a placement service effectively refused on a L1132-1 ground.
findings.applies_to_him: No regulator will audit him, and no fine is waiting. But the theory is available to a claimant, and the Défenseur des droits can take up such a case without any turnover threshold. Given that, the proportionate answer is engineering discipline, not a compliance project: semantic HTML, real labels on the listing and contact forms, keyboard navigation, alt text, contrast, no information conveyed by colour alone. That is a day of care during build and unaffordable to retrofit. He should also make sure the CONTACT path — the step where a candidate reaches an employer — is the most accessible part of the site, because that is the step whose denial maps onto "service de placement refusé". Separately: the obligation d'emploi des travailleurs handicapés (L5212-1 ff.) is on employers with 20+ staff and is not his obligation, though it is a reason some larger hotels will want their offers visible to disabled candidates.
findings.penalty: No specific penalty. Route is a civil claim or a Défenseur des droits référral; if characterised as a discriminatory refusal of a service under article 225-2, the criminal ceiling is 3 ans / 45 000 €.
findings.source_quote: Indirect discrimination is rendered by the Défenseur des droits corpus as « une disposition, un critère ou une pratique neutre en apparence, mais susceptible d'entraîner [...] un désavantage particulier pour des personnes par rapport à d'autres personnes », unless « objectivement justifiée par un but légitime et que les moyens de réaliser ce but sont nécessaires et appropriés » — search-index rendering of loi n° 2008-496 article 1er; I did not open a page carrying the statutory text itself.

findings.claim: HARD RULE HE MUST NOT BREAK — Article L5321-3: no payment, direct or indirect, may be required from job seekers in return for placement services. Six months and €3,750.
findings.detail: The only statutory exceptions are entertainment artists (L7121-9) and sports agents (code du sport L222-6). Neither is hospitality. The word « indirecte » is doing heavy work: it reaches anything of value extracted from the candidate side, not just a listed price.
findings.applies_to_him: His "free for candidates, forever" line is not a positioning choice he could later revisit — it is a criminal prohibition. Rule out in advance, and tell any future investor or co-founder: no premium candidate account, no paid CV boost, no paid "priority application", no paid training sold as a route to the listings, no fee taken from a first pay packet. Employer-side monetisation, including the paid visibility tiers he plans, is expressly permitted — L5321-1 says placement may be exercised à titre lucratif. The money must only ever come from the employer side.
findings.penalty: « un emprisonnement de six mois et d'une amende de 3 750 euros » (article L5324-1 code du travail).
findings.source_quote: « Aucune rétribution, directe ou indirecte, ne peut être exigée des personnes à la recherche d'un emploi en contrepartie de la fourniture de services de placement » — and L5324-1: « Le fait d'exiger une rétribution, directe ou indirecte, des personnes à la recherche d'un emploi, en contrepartie de la fourniture de services de placement, en méconnaissance des dispositions de l'article L. 5321-3, est puni d'un emprisonnement de six mois et d'une amende de 3 750 euros. »

findings.claim: His business model sits inside a narrow statutory carve-out: Article L5331-1 prohibits SELLING job offers on any medium, but expressly permits paid insertion of offers in a publication or other paid means of communication.
findings.detail: The first sentence is the prohibition; the second is the carve-out that makes every classified-ads business in France lawful. The distinction is between selling the offers themselves and selling the insertion.
findings.applies_to_him: His model — restaurants pay to have their offer inserted, and pay more for better placement — is the carve-out, not the prohibition. He should be able to point to this article if challenged. The line he must not cross is on the candidate side: charging for access to the offers would be selling the offers, and would breach L5321-3 as well. One caveat worth flagging to a lawyer if he ever raises money: the carve-out's wording refers to insertion in « une publication ou un autre moyen de communication payant », and a free-to-read website charging only advertisers is the near-universal market practice rather than a settled reading of that phrase. I found no case law either way and did not verify it.
findings.penalty: No penalty is attached to L5331-1 in L5334-1.
findings.source_quote: « Il est interdit de vendre des offres ou des demandes d'emploi, quel que soit le support utilisé. Toutefois, cette interdiction ne fait pas obstacle à l'insertion, à titre onéreux, d'offres ou de demandes d'emploi dans une publication ou un autre moyen de communication payant. »

findings.claim: LIABILITY SPLIT for an unlawful listing — Article L5334-1, final paragraph: the advertiser who requested publication bears the offence; the publisher bears it only where he acted WITHOUT an express insertion request from the advertiser.
findings.detail: This is the allocation rule for the misleading-offer offence of L5331-3 and the misleading-service-ad offence of L5331-5. It is not a general immunity — it is conditioned on there being an express request to insert from the advertiser.
findings.applies_to_him: This is his most valuable procedural protection and it is earned by product design, not by a disclaimer. The condition is an express insertion request from the restaurant, so his listing flow must produce provable evidence of one for every single offer: the restaurant's own account, its own submission, a timestamped acceptance of the text as published, and an audit trail. If he rewrites or reformats an offer himself, or auto-imports from a restaurant's website, or publishes anything the restaurant did not expressly ask him to insert, he is acting without that express request and the liability lands on him. Never edit an employer's copy — reject it and ask them to resubmit.
findings.penalty: For the underlying offences: « un emprisonnement d'un an et d'une amende de 37 500 euros » (article L5334-1).
findings.source_quote: « L'annonceur qui a demandé la diffusion de l'offre est responsable de l'infraction commise. Le directeur de la publication ou le fournisseur du service ayant communiqué l'offre au public est responsable lorsqu'il a agi sans demande expresse d'insertion de l'offre émanant de l'annonceur. »

findings.claim: His own marketing claims are criminally policed — Article L5331-5 forbids publishing an ad for an employment-related SERVICE containing false or misleading claims, « notamment sur le caractère gratuit de ce service ». One year and €37,500.
findings.detail: L5331-3 does the same for the job offers themselves, listing three protected subjects: the existence, real availability, origin, nature and description of the job; the pay and fringe benefits; and the place of work. Article L5333-1 puts DGCCRF agents in charge of investigating both.
findings.applies_to_him: Two exposures he has not considered. First, the free-service claim: the statute singles out gratuité as the thing people lie about, so his "100% gratuit pour les candidats" must be true without asterisks — which it will be, if he respects L5321-3. Second, and sharper: his entire pitch is that listed houses offer decent conditions. That is a claim about his service, and if the criteria behind it are not actually applied, a delisting-worthy house stays listed because it pays, or the standard is quietly waived for a big client, the claim becomes misleading. And because L5331-3 protects « la rémunération et les avantages annexes proposés » and « le lieu du travail », the two things seasonal alpine hospitality most often misrepresents — pay and staff housing — are exactly the ones the offence names. His questionnaire and refusal log are what make the marketing claim defensible; without them the promise is a liability rather than a differentiator. The DGCCRF, not the labour inspectorate, is the enforcement body here.
findings.penalty: « un emprisonnement d'un an et d'une amende de 37 500 euros » for breach of L5331-3 or L5331-5 (article L5334-1).
findings.source_quote: L5331-5: « Il est interdit de faire publier dans un journal, revue ou écrit périodique, ou de diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public une insertion de prestation de services concernant les offres d'emploi ou les carrières et comportant des allégations fausses ou susceptibles d'induire en erreur, notamment sur le caractère gratuit de ce service. » — L5331-3 protects « 1° L'existence, le caractère effectivement disponible, l'origine, la nature et la description de l'emploi [...] 2° La rémunération et les avantages annexes proposés ; 3° Le lieu du travail. »

findings.claim: Three small mechanical duties on every listing he publishes: date it (L5332-1), keep the employer's real identity behind any anonymous offer (L5332-2), and publish in French (L5331-4).
findings.detail: L5332-1 is one sentence and absolute. L5332-2 requires the employer publishing an anonymous offer to give his name or corporate name and address to the publisher — and where an intermediary requests the insertion, the intermediary must supply the same details. L5331-4 prohibits an offer whose text is in a foreign language for work performed in France, whatever the nationality of the employer, and even where fluency in a foreign language is a genuine requirement of the post; where the job can only be named by a foreign term, the French text must describe it in enough detail not to mislead.
findings.applies_to_him: All three are build-time decisions, not policies. Stamp a visible publication date on every listing. If he offers confidential listings — plausible, since a restaurant replacing a chef may not want it public — he must hold and be able to produce the establishment's name and address. And L5331-4 matters more than it looks in Megève: an international resort market generates English-language postings, and "Seeking experienced Chef de Partie, English fluent" as the body of an ad is prohibited even though the requirement is genuine. He needs a French-text field that is mandatory, with any English as an addition rather than a substitute.
findings.penalty: No penalty attached to these three in L5334-1; the enforceable neighbours are L5331-3 and L5331-5 at 1 an / 37 500 €. A foreign-language ad that leaves a French reader misled could be reached through L5331-3, to which L5331-4 expressly cross-refers.
findings.source_quote: L5332-1: « Toute offre d'emploi publiée ou diffusée est datée. » — L5332-2: « Tout employeur qui fait insérer [...] une offre anonyme d'emploi fait connaître son nom ou sa raison sociale et son adresse au directeur de la publication ou au responsable du moyen de communication. » — L5331-4: « Il est interdit de faire publier [...] une insertion d'offres d'emploi [...] comportant un texte rédigé en langue étrangère. »

findings.claim: He has no obligation to send his offers to France Travail.
findings.detail: Service-public's page for employers preparing and publishing a job offer states it directly, and also confirms that stating the salary is not currently compulsory.
findings.applies_to_him: Removes an obligation he may have assumed existed. He is free to be the sole channel for a listing. The salary point is more interesting commercially than legally: not compulsory, but since his differentiator is decent conditions and since L5331-3 makes misstating pay an offence, making pay disclosure a condition of listing is both a strong product decision and a way of hardening his curation criteria into something objective and evidenced.
findings.penalty: n/a
findings.source_quote: « L'employeur n'a pas l'obligation d'informer France Travail des offres de recrutement. » — and on salary: « n'est pas obligatoire ».

must_do: Never take money from a candidate, in any form, direct or indirect — Article L5321-3, six months and €3,750 under L5324-1. This is a permanent constraint on the business model, not a launch-phase choice. Write it into the company's own rules so a future co-founder or investor cannot propose a premium candidate tier.

Write and publish a 'charte des établissements' before taking the first euro: the criteria on which he accepts or declines a house, all of them about working conditions, pay, contracts, housing and staff turnover, none of them about the person of the employer. This is what converts a silent standard into a defensible one under Article L5321-2.

Keep a dated refusal and delisting log: for every declined or dropped establishment, the criterion failed and the evidence for it. In discrimination litigation the burden shifts to him once the claimant presents facts suggesting discrimination; the log is the only thing that discharges it.

Communicate refusals privately and factually, never publicly. Keeping the standard silent is legally correct — publishing ratings or scores about named employers creates a denigration exposure that silence entirely avoids.

Sell listings season by season with a stated notice period and a renewal cycle in the CGV. This is what defuses Article L442-1 II — 'quietly stopping' an established paying relationship is an abrupt termination; a contract reaching its term is not.

Build the listing form so it cannot accept an age range, an age limit, a sex, or any other L1132-1 characteristic — validation at input, not moderation after the fact. Article L5321-2 forbids any published offer from referencing those characteristics, and that duty is on his service.

Make every listing originate from the restaurant's own account and its own submission, with a timestamped acceptance of the exact text published. Article L5334-1 puts liability on the advertiser only where there was an express insertion request from him — that evidence is the shield. Never edit an employer's copy; reject and ask for resubmission.

Add three build-time details: a visible publication date on every listing (L5332-1), a mandatory French-language text field with any English as an addition rather than a substitute (L5331-4), and storage of the establishment's name and address behind any confidential listing (L5332-2).

Keep the youth framing on the editorial side only — branding, guides, tone, who he markets to. No age filter, no age facet, no age field, and registration open to anyone. Article L1133-2 protects the aim of favouring young people's professional integration; it does not protect an age filter on access.

Make pay disclosure a condition of listing. Not legally required, but Article L5331-3 makes misstating pay or place of work a criminal offence at one year and €37,500, and a pay-transparent board is the objective, evidenced version of his 'decent conditions' promise.

Build to WCAG AA during the initial build — semantic HTML, form labels, keyboard navigation, alt text, contrast — with particular care on the candidate-to-employer contact path. No regulator will require it (RGAA starts at €250M turnover, the EAA exempts under 10 employees and €2M), but it is a day's discipline now and unaffordable later, and it closes the indirect-discrimination route on the handicap ground.
Know the two numbers that end the EAA exemption — 10 employees and €2M — and revisit accessibility if either comes into view.
unknowns: Article L442-1 II code de commerce (rupture brutale d'une relation commerciale établie) — I give the article number from knowledge. Legifrance is out of bounds and service-public carries no dedicated page, so I did not read the statutory text or verify the notice-period case law. This is the head of claim most likely to be used against him, so it deserves a lawyer's half-hour before he writes his CGV.

Article L420-2 code de commerce (abus de position dominante, abus de dépendance économique) — economie.gouv.fr returns HTTP 403 to every automated fetch, so the DGCCRF fiche is reported from the search index, not from a page I opened. The three conditions and the sanction ceilings are unverified.

Directive (EU) 2019/882 — EUR-Lex returned an empty document body for CELEX:32019L0882 on every URL form I tried (EN and FR, HTML and ELI). Article 4(5) on microenterprises, Article 3(23) and 3(30) on the definitions, Article 2(2) on scope and Article 31 on the application date are cited by number only. The micro-enterprise thresholds and the 28 June 2025 date are separately confirmed from a French government page I did open.

The EAA sanction figures in France — contravention de 5e classe at €7,500 cumulable, and a DGCCRF astreinte up to €3,000 per day under décret n° 2023-931 — come from the search index only. Treat as indicative. They do not bite him in any event.

Whether a free-to-read job site funded entirely by advertisers falls within the carve-out of Article L5331-1, whose wording is « insertion, à titre onéreux [...] dans une publication ou un autre moyen de communication payant ». It is universal market practice and I found nothing suggesting a problem, but I found no case law confirming the reading either.
Article L121-11 code de la consommation — I have the rule and the 1996 Galland liberalisation from the Institut national de la consommation, a public body, but not the statutory text itself.

Loi n° 2008-496 du 27 mai 2008, article 1er (the definitions of direct and indirect discrimination, imported by reference into L1132-1) — rendered from the Défenseur des droits corpus via the search index, not read directly. The indirect-discrimination argument in (f) rests on it.

Whether the Défenseur des droits has decided any case against a private job board on accessibility or on employer curation. I did not search the decision database; a sweep of juridique.defenseurdesdroits.fr would sharpen both (c) and (f) and is worth a follow-up.

Whether any prior declaration or registration duty survives for private placement operators. Chapitre Ier contains only L5321-1 to L5321-3 (L5321-4 returns 404) and none of them imposes one, so the answer is almost certainly no — but I did not check the regulatory part (R5321-*), where a residual formality could sit.

research.lane: Lane 6 — What he owes about the employers he lists (French law, publisher of paid job listings, HCR sector, Haute-Savoie)
research.bottom_line: Three surprises, in order of importance. (1) He is NOT a pure publisher in the eyes of the Code du travail: Art. L.5321-1 defines "activité de placement" as habitually providing services that bring job offers and job seekers together without becoming party to the employment relationship — that is exactly a job board, and the article expressly allows it to be for-profit. So the placement chapter binds him TODAY, not only if he drifts into matching. Its live rules: never any payment, direct or indirect, from a candidate (L.5321-3); never refuse service to a jobseeker OR TO AN EMPLOYER on a discrimination ground of L.1132-1 (L.5321-2) — his silent curated door is lawful only because "churns staff" is not a protected ground, and he must be able to show that; and the administration can order the organisation closed for up to three months after mise en demeure (L.5323-1). There is no registration to do: the déclaration préalable was abrogated. (2) Publishing an offer is itself a regulated act with its own criminal article. L.5331-3 prohibits "diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public" an offer containing false or misleading allegations about the existence and availability of the job, the pay, or the place of work — one year and 37 500 € under L.5334-1. The allocation rule is his shield: the annonceur who asked for the insertion is the one liable, and the publisher only where he acted without the advertiser's express request. France Travail's own November 2025 legal guide nonetheless prints "Le diffuseur — L.5334-1 : 37 500 € d'amende" in every liability table, including the one for the "respect du droit du travail" section, so the administration treats his exposure as live. (3) On travail dissimulé there is no need to reach for complicity: Art. L.8221-1 2° independently prohibits "La publicité, par quelque moyen que ce soit, tendant à favoriser, en toute connaissance de cause, le travail dissimulé", punished by three years and 45 000 € (L.8224-1, 225 000 € for a company). The whole offence turns on "en toute connaissance de cause". Publishing in ignorance is not it; publishing after a credible report is. That single phrase is why his curation model is a double-edged asset — a gatekeeper who inspects houses has a much harder time saying he did not know — and why a written intake record and a documented take-down reflex are worth more to him than any contractual disclaimer.

findings.claim: A job board is legally an "activité de placement", and it may be run for profit — this status attaches today, not only if he starts matching
findings.detail: Art. L.5321-1 Code du travail. The definition has three elements he meets: habitual provision of services, bringing offers and demands for employment together, without becoming party to the resulting employment relationship. The second sentence expressly permits it to be lucrative. The consequence is that Chapter I of Title II (L.5321-1 to L.5321-3) binds him from the first listing.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, as a pure publisher. Drifting into selection or matching does not change his category — he is already in it; drift only sharpens the rules below and adds his own decisions as a source of discrimination liability.
findings.penalty: No direct penalty in L.5321-1 itself; enforcement runs through L.5323-1 (administrative closure up to 3 months) and the discrimination code.
findings.source_quote: L'activité de placement consiste à fournir, à titre habituel, des services visant à rapprocher les offres et les demandes d'emploi, sans que la personne assurant cette activité ne devienne partie aux relations de travail susceptibles d'en découler. La fourniture de services de placement peut être exercée à titre lucratif.
findings.confidence: high on the text; medium-high on the qualification of a paid job board as "placement" (no opened case law applying it to a job board specifically, but the definition is on all fours)

findings.claim: He may never take money from a candidate, directly or indirectly — his "free for candidates" plan is a legal obligation, not a positioning choice
findings.detail: Art. L.5321-3. "Indirecte" matters: a premium candidate tier, a paid CV review, a surtaxed phone number, or an affiliate link the candidate must pass through would all be in scope. The only carve-outs are performing artists (L.7121-9) and sports agents (art. L.222-6 code du sport).
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Reinforced separately by L.5331-1, which bans selling job offers on any medium but expressly permits paid insertion of an offer in a paying publication — i.e. charging the employer is lawful, charging the candidate is not.
findings.penalty: Administrative closure up to 3 months after mise en demeure (L.5323-1). Also independently caught by France Travail doctrine on "la gratuité des offres d'emploi".
findings.source_quote: Aucune rétribution, directe ou indirecte, ne peut être exigée des personnes à la recherche d'un emploi en contrepartie de la fourniture de services de placement

findings.claim: His curated door is lawful, but the Code forbids refusing service to an EMPLOYER on a discrimination ground — the criteria must be documented and must not proxy a protected characteristic
findings.detail: Art. L.5321-2 is the one rule that speaks directly to a curated model. It prohibits refusing a placement service to a jobseeker or to an employer on any ground listed at L.1132-1 (origin, sex, moeurs, orientation, gender identity, age, family situation, appearance, name, place of residence, religion, union activity, health, disability, economic vulnerability, banking domiciliation, ability to express oneself in a language other than French, etc.). "Churns staff", "conditions I judge indecent", "no written contract on file" are not protected grounds, so his standard is legal. The exposure is proxying: a door policy that in practice excludes, say, houses run by a particular community would be indirect discrimination.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. This is the rule his product description collides with most directly, and the one nobody expects. Note the asymmetry: he is free to refuse an employer on quality grounds, but he must be able to show the ground.
findings.penalty: L.5323-1: after mise en demeure, closure of the organisation for up to 3 months. A refused employer could also sue in discrimination.
findings.source_quote: Aucun service de placement ne peut être refusé à une personne à la recherche d'un emploi ou à un employeur fondé sur l'un des motifs de discrimination énumérés à l'article L. 1132-1. Aucune offre d'emploi ne peut comporter de référence à l'une des caractéristiques mentionnées à cet article.

findings.claim: There is no registration, licence or prior declaration to open a job board — the déclaration préalable d'activité de placement was abrogated
findings.detail: The current L.5323-1 contains no declaration duty at all: it is an enforcement article giving labour-control officials power to find breaches and the administration power to close. The prior-declaration regime (declaration to the préfet by registered letter the day before starting) was removed; the regulatory provisions were modified by décret n° 2012-539 du 20 avril 2012.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Answers (e) on the registration half: nothing to file. Micro-entreprise registration at the URSSAF/INPI guichet is the only formality, and that is ordinary business law, not employment law.
findings.penalty: N/A — but note the closure power that replaced it.
findings.source_quote: Les fonctionnaires et agents chargés du contrôle de l'application du droit du travail sont habilités à constater les manquements aux dispositions du chapitre Ier. Lorsque l'activité de placement est exercée en méconnaissance de ces dispositions ou en cas d'atteinte à l'ordre public, l'autorité administrative peut, après mise en demeure, ordonner la fermeture de l'organisme en cause pour une durée n'excédant pas trois mois.
findings.confidence: high on the current text of L.5323-1 (read in full); medium-high on the abrogation history (décret n° 2012-539 identified via search, not opened — it sits on Legifrance)

findings.claim: He owes France Travail nothing — no obligation to transmit, share or deposit offers
findings.detail: The old obligation on employers to notify vacancies to the ANPE is gone. Service-public states it flatly for the employer; a fortiori it does not bind a private publisher, which has no statutory relationship with France Travail at all. Any aggregation of his offers into francetravail.fr would be a voluntary partnership he negotiates, not a duty.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Answers (e) in full, with the registration finding above.
findings.penalty: N/A
findings.source_quote: L'employeur n'a pas l'obligation d'informer France Travail des offres de recrutement

findings.claim: Publishing a false or misleading offer is a criminal offence that names the diffuser, not only the employer
findings.detail: Art. L.5331-3 bans causing the publication of, or diffusing "par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public", an offer containing false or misleading allegations on: the existence and actual availability, origin, nature and description of the job; the pay and fringe benefits; the place of work. A website is squarely "tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public".
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. This is the core of (c): the hook that pulls labour-law non-compliance into his lap is not a general duty to audit employers — it is that a non-compliant offer is a MISLEADING offer.
findings.penalty: L.5334-1: 1 an d'emprisonnement et 37 500 € d'amende.
findings.source_quote: Il est interdit de faire publier dans un journal, revue ou écrit périodique ou de diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public une insertion d'offres d'emploi ou d'offres de travaux à domicile comportant des allégations fausses ou susceptibles d'induire en erreur

findings.claim: L.5334-1 puts the offence on the advertiser, and on the publisher only where he published without the advertiser's express request — this is his single best shield
findings.detail: The article's liability paragraph allocates: the annonceur who asked for the diffusion answers for the infraction; the directeur de la publication or the provider communicating the offer answers only when he acted without an express insertion request from the annonceur. Practical meaning: an employer-submitted, employer-worded ad that he publishes because the employer asked him to leaves the employer as the defendant. Rewriting the ad himself, or republishing/scraping an offer the employer did not ask him to run, flips it.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, and it is the reason his intake flow matters more than his vetting: every listing must carry a traceable, dated, express request from a named employer.
findings.penalty: 1 an d'emprisonnement et 37 500 € d'amende (L.5334-1); identical penalties for offers of services concerning employment and careers in breach of L.5331-5.
findings.source_quote: Le fait d'insérer une offre d'emploi ou une offre de travaux à domicile, en méconnaissance des dispositions de l'article L. 5331-3, est puni d'un emprisonnement d'un an et d'une amende de 37 500 euros.
findings.confidence: high on the penalty sentence (quoted); medium-high on the allocation rule — the page's copyright guard blocked full verbatim reproduction of that paragraph, but two independent reads of code.travail.gouv.fr and a targeted search agree on its substance. The exact wording sits on Legifrance, which I did not open.

findings.claim: France Travail's own current legal guide prints the diffuser's criminal exposure as a flat 37 500 €, in every liability table including the labour-law one
