findings.detail: The guide "Repères juridiques sur les offres d'emploi" (France Travail, DCE, November 2025, 52 pp.) defines three roles — l'employeur, le rédacteur, le diffuseur — and repeats a liability matrix after each section. The diffuser's row reads L.5334-1 / 37 500 € for criminal liability, a 3rd-class contravention (R.5334-1) for administrative liability, and damages under art. 1240 code civil for civil liability. The rédacteur's row carries civil liability only. The same matrix appears under section 06 "Respect du droit du travail", i.e. the administration attaches diffuser exposure to SMIC, working-time and contract-type defects too.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Read together with the allocation rule above, the honest reading is: the statute gives him a defence, the administration's published doctrine does not advertise it. He should plan for the doctrine, not the defence.
findings.penalty: Diffuseur: 37 500 € (L.5334-1) + contravention de 3e classe (R.5334-1) + dommages et intérêts (art. 1240 c. civ.). Employeur: 1 an + 37 500 €.
findings.source_quote: Le diffuseur : ce terme désigne celui qui est responsable de la publication ou qui fournit le service de communication de l'offre. […] Le diffuseur — Article L.5334-1 du code du travail : -37 500€ d'amende.
findings.confidence: high — PDF downloaded and text extracted in full; note the guide itself miscites "R.5334-1" where it means L.5334-1 for the 1-year custodial penalty

findings.claim: The offer's content must comply with labour law — working time, contract type, SMIC — and France Travail states this as a rule about the OFFER, not about the employer
findings.detail: Section 06 of the guide opens with it, then works through: a "CDD puis CDI" mention is proscribed because it contradicts the conditions for using a CDD (L.1242-1, L.1242-2, requalification L.1245-1); a stated salary must be at least the SMIC; part-time below 24h/week needs a sourced derogation, and he must be able to produce the text authorising it. The statutory hook the guide cites for the salary and CDD rules is L.5331-3 — the misleading-offer article.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Answers (c): there is no free-standing duty to audit an employer's compliance, but there IS a duty not to publish an offer whose own terms are unlawful, because such an offer is by definition misleading. The check is on the four corners of the ad, not on the payroll.
findings.penalty: Via L.5331-3 / L.5334-1. The guide adds, for the employer: R.3233-1 (paying below SMIC, contravention de 5e classe, 1 500 €) and R.3124-3 (working-time breach, contravention de 4e classe, 750 €).
findings.source_quote: Le contenu des offres d'emploi doit respecter les règles applicables en matière de droit du travail (temps de travail, nature et clause du contrat, SMIC, etc.). Plus largement, les offres doivent respecter l'ensemble du droit, et notamment, le droit commercial et le droit des sociétés.

findings.claim: He may not publish an offer whose final employer is unknown, or for which no real post exists
findings.detail: France Travail's guide, citing L.5331-2 and L.5332-2, states the rule for third-party-deposited offers (recruitment firms, placement bodies). It is the closest thing in French law to a know-your-employer duty on a publisher: identity of the final employer, and reality of the vacancy. The article citation is loose in the guide, but the substance is reinforced by L.5331-3, which makes "l'existence, le caractère effectivement disponible" of the job a criminal misleading-allegation head.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Answers (a)'s real content: not "verify the SIRET" as such, but "know and record who the employer is, and that the post exists".
findings.penalty: Via L.5331-3 / L.5334-1 (1 an, 37 500 €) where the offer is thereby misleading.
findings.source_quote: Une offre doit porter sur un emploi disponible et une activité professionnelle rémunérée. L'emploi proposé doit être réel et l'employeur final doit être connu de France Travail. […] Il est strictement interdit de diffuser une offre pour laquelle il n'y a pas réellement de poste à pourvoir ou dont l'employeur final n'est pas connu.
findings.confidence: medium-high — the principle is stated plainly and echoed by L.5331-3; the guide's mapping to L.5331-2 and L.5332-2 is imprecise (L.5331-2 is the age-limit article)

findings.claim: There is NO statutory duty on a job-offer publisher to verify that a listing employer is a registered business — no SIRET check, no Kbis, no attestation de vigilance
findings.detail: I looked for one across the offer-publication chapter (L.5331-1 to L.5334-1), the placement chapter (L.5321-1 to L.5323-1), France Travail's 52-page legal guide, and the service-public pages on publishing an offer. None imposes employer verification on the diffuser. What exists instead is the know-the-employer/real-post rule above, and the DSA notice-and-action duties. The nearest verification regime — the obligation de vigilance — does not reach him (next finding).
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Answers (a) directly: the duty is evidentiary, not administrative. Verifying the SIRET is free and instant and he should do it anyway, but as risk management and as proof of his "en toute connaissance de cause" good faith, not as compliance with a named article.
findings.penalty: N/A
findings.source_quote: La offre doit être rédigée en français si le travail doit s'effectuer sur le territoire français […] L'offre d'emploi doit indiquer sa date de publication ou de mise en ligne
findings.confidence: medium — this is a reasoned absence across the sources I opened, not a sourced negative statement; a specialist could still point to a duty I did not find

findings.claim: The obligation de vigilance runs the OTHER WAY: the restaurant is the donneur d'ordre and he is the prestataire, so HE may have to hand THEM an attestation de vigilance
findings.detail: Art. L.8222-1 makes the donneur d'ordre — the party commissioning work, a service, or a commercial act — responsible for obtaining, at signature and every six months, the URSSAF attestation de vigilance plus proof of registration (extrait K/Kbis or RNE), for any contract of at least 5 000 € HT. In his product the restaurant buys advertising from him. The restaurant is therefore the donneur d'ordre; he is the cocontractant. Once a single house's annual spend with him reaches 5 000 € HT, it is the house that must collect his attestation, not the reverse.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, inverted. Answers (a)'s "attestation de vigilance URSSAF" sub-question: he does not owe it about them, and there is no legal basis to demand one from them. He should be ready to PROVIDE one — which means keeping his micro-entreprise URSSAF account current from day one.
findings.penalty: For the donneur d'ordre who fails: solidarité financière — joint liability for the contractor's taxes, social contributions, surcharges, repayment of public aid, and the concealed workers' pay (L.8222-2). Not his exposure here.
findings.source_quote: Le donneur d'ordre a une obligation de vigilance vis-à-vis de son sous-traitant […] L'obligation s'déclenche pour les contrats d'une valeur égale ou supérieure à 5 000 € […] À la conclusion du contrat, tous les 6 mois jusqu'à la fin de l'exécution
findings.confidence: high on the mechanism and threshold; high on the direction of the duty, which follows from who commissions whom

findings.claim: Advertising that knowingly favours travail dissimulé is its own criminal offence — he does not need to be an accomplice to be a defendant
findings.detail: Art. L.8221-1 lists three prohibitions, and the second is not about employing anyone: "La publicité, par quelque moyen que ce soit, tendant à favoriser, en toute connaissance de cause, le travail dissimulé." A job listing is publicity by a means. The third prohibition — knowingly using the services of someone doing concealed work — is not his risk, since he buys nothing from the restaurant. The offence turns entirely on the knowledge element.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. This is the whole of (b). Complicity analysis under art. 121-7 code pénal is largely academic next to it: the legislature has already written the publisher's version of the offence.
findings.penalty: L.8224-1: 3 ans d'emprisonnement et 45 000 € d'amende. For a company: 225 000 € (service-public F31490). Aggravated to 10 ans / 100 000 € where minors, vulnerable persons or bande organisée are involved.
findings.source_quote: Sont interdits : 1° Le travail totalement ou partiellement dissimulé […] ; 2° La publicité, par quelque moyen que ce soit, tendant à favoriser, en toute connaissance de cause, le travail dissimulé ; 3° Le fait de recourir sciemment, directement ou par personne interposée, aux services de celui qui exerce un travail dissimulé.

findings.claim: "En toute connaissance de cause" is the entire defence, and his curation model erodes it
findings.detail: L.8221-1 2° requires knowledge. A publisher who takes an ad at face value has not committed the offence. But he is not that publisher: he inspects houses, judges their conditions, and quietly delists those that churn staff. A prosecutor would read that as a business that inspects — and therefore knows. The asymmetry is that his silent standard gives him no public record of what he found, only a private one. The mitigation is not less vetting, it is better records: a dated intake file per house showing what he checked and what he was told, and an immediate delisting reflex the moment a credible report of undeclared work arrives.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, and it gets worse as the curation gets more thorough. This is analysis, not a sourced rule — no authority I opened addresses curated job boards.
findings.penalty: Same as above: 3 ans / 45 000 € (225 000 € for a company).
findings.source_quote: tendant à favoriser, en toute connaissance de cause, le travail dissimulé
findings.confidence: medium — the statutory knowledge element is certain; how a court would weigh a curator's inspection as evidence of knowledge is my reasoning, unsupported by opened case law

findings.claim: As a hosting service he must run a notice-and-action mechanism from day one — the micro-enterprise exemption does NOT cover it
findings.detail: Arcom, the French DSA coordinator, sets out the layers. A hébergeur stores information provided by a recipient at their request — his listings. Articles 16 to 18 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 apply to every hébergeur: a reporting mechanism, a statement of reasons for moderation decisions, and reporting suspected criminal offences to the judicial authorities. Micro and small enterprises (under 50 staff, under €10m turnover or balance sheet) are exempt only from articles 15(2), 19 and 29 — transparency reporting, the Section 3 platform obligations, and dispute-resolution interface rules. Article 16 is not on that list.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, at any size. Answers (d): yes, there is a notice-and-action procedure, and it is mandatory from his first listing.
findings.penalty: See the French sanctions finding below.
findings.source_quote: Hébergeur: services that stockent des informations fournies par un destinataire du service à sa demande […] Entities with moins de 50 personnes occupées et moins de 10 millions d'euros de chiffre d'affaires ou au total du bilan are exempt from articles 15(2), 19, and 29—but remain subject to other provisions.
findings.confidence: high on the exemption list and the hébergeur obligations; I could not open EUR-Lex itself (it returned empty bodies to both WebFetch and curl), so the paragraph-level wording of arts. 16-18 is unverified

findings.claim: No fixed statutory delay — the standard is immediate removal on actual knowledge, and the French sanctions are severe
findings.detail: Service-public sets out the French side: the host must provide reporting mechanisms "facilement accessibles à toute personne qui souhaite signaler une donnée illégale", and removal is owed as soon as the illicit character is known. A valid notification carries the content complained of, its URL, the notifier's contact details, and a good-faith declaration. The page cites Regulation 2022/2065 and décret n° 2025-980.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Answers (d) on the delay question: there is no 24-hour or 48-hour clock for general illicit content; the clock starts at knowledge and the duty is immediate. That is harsher than a fixed delay, not softer.
findings.penalty: Failure to remove promptly after notification: 1 an de prison et 250 000 € d'amende for a personne physique; for a company, a fine up to 6 % du chiffre d'affaires mondial annuel of the preceding year. Failure to alert the competent authorities: 1 an et 250 000 € (personne physique), 1 250 000 € (personne morale), plus a possible professional ban.
findings.source_quote: Dès qu'il a connaissance du caractère illicite du commentaire, le directeur de publication doit immédiatement le faire retirer.
findings.confidence: medium-high — the sanctions and notification elements are quoted from the page; the "immédiatement" sentence as printed concerns a directeur de publication rather than an hébergeur, so the wording of the host's own standard ("promptement" in the LCEN tradition) is not pinned verbatim

findings.claim: His curation is what could cost him the hosting shield and make him the éditeur of every ad
findings.detail: French law distinguishes the directeur de publication — "Personne en charge de la publication d'un contenu éditorial" — who answers for content directly, from the hébergeur, who "stocke des écrits, des sons, des images ou des vidéos réalisés par des tiers" and answers only from actual knowledge. Choosing WHICH advertisers may buy is a commercial gate and, on the better view, leaves him a host. Writing or materially rewriting ad copy, editorialising the ranking, or presenting a house with his own endorsement pushes him toward éditeur — and toward L.5334-1's "acted without the advertiser's express request" limb at the same time. The two shields fail together, which is why they should be protected by the same rule: he curates the door, the employer writes the ad.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, as a design constraint. Paid visibility tiers are the pressure point: selling "better visibility" is fine, writing the copy that fills it is not.
findings.penalty: Loss of the conditional liability shield — primary liability for every listing's content, under L.5334-1, the discrimination articles, and the press-style regime.
findings.source_quote: Directeur de publication : Personne en charge de la publication d'un contenu éditorial (exemple : un écrit, une image, une vidéo). Hébergeur : Personne physique ou dirigeant d'une personne morale qui stocke des écrits, des sons, des images ou des vidéos réalisés par des tiers
findings.confidence: medium — the éditeur/hébergeur distinction is quoted from an official source, but where a curated, paid job board falls on that line is my application of it; I found no opened authority on the point

findings.claim: The DSA's know-your-business-customer rule (art. 30) most likely does NOT apply to him
findings.detail: Arcom states that article 30's traceability of professional sellers applies to "plateformes en ligne permettant aux consommateurs de conclure des contrats à distance avec des professionnels" — marketplaces. A jobseeker is not a consumer, and an employment contract is not a distance consumer contract. So the DSA does not impose the identity-collection regime on him that it imposes on a marketplace.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, as a negative. It matters because art. 30 would otherwise be the single provision requiring him to collect and verify each employer's registration data — and it is the rule people assume covers job boards.
findings.penalty: N/A
findings.source_quote: Article 30 applies specifically to plateformes en ligne permettant aux consommateurs de conclure des contrats à distance avec des professionnels (marketplaces), requiring traçabilité des vendeurs professionnels.
findings.confidence: medium — the scope wording is from an opened official page, but the conclusion that job boards fall outside it is my reading; I could not open the regulation's own recitals to confirm

findings.claim: Fraudulent job ads carry heavy criminal qualifications against their authors, and there is a State reporting channel he should use
findings.detail: Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr sets out the standard pattern — fake offers used "pour soutirer de l'argent ou dérober des informations personnelles" (banking data, social security number) — and the offences: escroquerie (art. 313-1 code pénal), usurpation d'identité (art. 226-4-1), collecte frauduleuse de données à caractère personnel (art. 226-18). Reporting goes to PHAROS at internet-signalement.gouv.fr; victim support via France Victimes 116 006 and Info Escroqueries 0 805 805 817.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Answers (d)'s other half: when a report lands, taking the ad down is step one and reporting it is step two — and under the DSA, alerting the authorities to suspected criminal offences is itself an obligation (art. 18), separately sanctioned in French law at 1 250 000 € for a company.
findings.penalty: Escroquerie: 5 ans et 375 000 €. Usurpation d'identité: 1 an et 15 000 €. Collecte frauduleuse de données: 5 ans et 300 000 €. (Against the fraudster, not him.)
findings.source_quote: soutirer de l'argent ou dérober des informations personnelles

findings.claim: Every offer must be in French and must carry its publication date
findings.detail: Art. L.5331-4 bans diffusing an offer containing text drafted in a foreign language, and — this is the part that bites in a border resort — the rule applies to services performed on French territory "quelle que soit la nationalité de l'auteur de l'offre ou de l'employeur", and even where perfect command of a foreign language is a condition of the job. A foreign term with no French equivalent must be accompanied by a French description detailed enough not to mislead. Separately, service-public states the offer must show its publication or posting date (France Travail cites R.5332-1 et seq.).
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. Megève is an international resort with English- and Russian-speaking clientele; ads sent to him in English, or with an English job title and no French body, are the predictable failure. France Travail's tolerance: a partly foreign-language description is publishable only if the French part comes first, the two versions are identical, and the nature of the post justifies it.
findings.penalty: Via L.5334-1 for misleading content; the dating and formal defects carry a contravention de 3e classe under R.5334-1 per France Travail's liability table.
findings.source_quote: Il est interdit de faire publier dans un journal, revue ou écrit périodique ou de diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public une insertion d'offres d'emploi ou d'offres de travaux à domicile comportant un texte rédigé en langue étrangère.

findings.claim: Discriminatory wording in an ad is the highest-penalty content risk, and one article targets age limits specifically
findings.detail: Art. L.5331-2 bans publishing or diffusing an offer stating an upper age limit for the applicant, except where a legal provision imposes an age condition. Beyond that, L.1132-1's full list of protected grounds applies to ad wording, enforced through arts. 225-2 and 225-4 code pénal. France Travail's guide is unusually concrete about the traps for his sector: only "Débutant" and "Expérimenté" may be used (not "Junior"/"Senior" outside a job title); "Recherche étudiant" or "contrat étudiant" is discriminatory because no such contract exists; requiring a foreign language is discriminatory unless directly tied to the post, with only "Bilingue", "Courant", "Notions" and "Technique" admissible — and its worked example is a restaurant, where "Courant" is proportionate for a server and "Bilingue" is not.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY. His audience is young people entering the trade, which makes age-adjacent wording ("jeune équipe", "18-25", "étudiant") the live risk, and his sector makes language requirements the second one.
findings.penalty: 3 ans d'emprisonnement et 45 000 € d'amende for discrimination (arts. 225-2 / 225-4 code pénal), per service-public.
findings.source_quote: Il est interdit de faire publier dans un journal, revue ou écrit périodique ou de diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public une insertion d'offres d'emploi ou d'offres de travaux à domicile comportant la mention d'une limite d'âge supérieure exigée du postulant à un emploi.

findings.claim: The sector has one extended convention collective that binds every employer he lists: CCN HCR du 30 avril 1997, IDCC 1979
findings.detail: The Code du travail numérique gives the identity: "Convention collective nationale des hôtels, cafés restaurants (HCR) du 30 avril 1997", in force since 07/12/1997, extended. Conventional minima currently flow from avenant n°33 du 19 juin 2024, and the applicable floor is the higher of the SMIC and the conventional minimum. Branch bodies: UMIH (Union des Métiers et des Industries de l'Hôtellerie) and GHR on the employer side; AKTO is the OPCO handling apprenticeship funding for the branch.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY only as a content check on the ads (a stated wage below the branch minimum makes the offer misleading under L.5331-3) and as the natural spine of his curation standard. He is not bound by the convention himself — he employs nobody in the branch.
findings.penalty: Against the employer. Against him only derivatively, via L.5331-3 / L.5334-1 if the ad's stated terms are unlawful.
findings.source_quote: Convention collective nationale des hôtels, cafés restaurants (HCR) du 30 avril 1997 […] soit le SMIC prévu par la loi, soit le salaire minimum prévu par la convention collective […] Minima conventionnels issus de l'avenant n°33 du 19 juin 2024
findings.confidence: high on the convention's identity and the SMIC/minimum rule; medium-high on avenant n°33 being the current one as of today

findings.claim: Night work by under-18s in hotels and restaurants is permitted only between 22h00 and 23h30, by derogation from the labour inspector
findings.detail: Two regulation articles do the work. R.3163-1 lists the sectors where a derogation to the ban on night work by young workers may be granted under L.3163-2 and L.6222-26: hôtellerie, restauration, boulangerie, pâtisserie, spectacles, courses hippiques. R.3163-2 then sets the window for his sector. The derogation is granted by the inspecteur du travail, with a 30-day délai and silence vaut accord (procédure SVA), legal basis L.3163-2 and R.3163-5.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY as a curation and ad-screening rule, not as a duty on him. Directly answers (f): an ad aimed at an apprentice that advertises service until midnight or a closing shift is advertising something the employer cannot lawfully do — and under L.5331-3 that makes it a misleading offer. In a Megève winter season this is not hypothetical.
findings.penalty: Against the employer, under the young-worker provisions. Against him via L.5331-3 / L.5334-1 if he publishes it.
findings.source_quote: Dans les secteurs de l'hôtellerie et de la restauration, le travail de nuit des jeunes travailleurs ne peut être autorisé que de vingt-deux heures à vingt-trois heures trente.
findings.confidence: high — both R.3163-1 and R.3163-2 read in full, and the procedure confirmed on the service-public silence-vaut-accord register (entry 631, inspecteur du travail, 30 days, SVA)

findings.claim: Every maître d'apprentissage in the HCR branch must hold a valid "permis de former" BEFORE the apprenticeship contract is signed
findings.detail: A branch-specific obligation with no equivalent in the general Code: 14 hours of initial training for anyone who has never supervised an alternant or has not done so for five years, plus a 7-hour refresher every four years. The basis is avenant n°17 du 10 janvier 2013 to the extended HCR convention, in force since 2014. Without it AKTO refuses to fund the contract and the labour inspection can serve a mise en demeure.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY as the sharpest single curation criterion available to him, and the answer to (f)'s apprenticeship half. It is binary, verifiable by asking one question, and it separates houses that take young people seriously from houses that take them cheaply — which is precisely the line he says he wants to police silently.
findings.penalty: Refusal of OPCO funding; mise en demeure from the inspection du travail; and per UMIH, the contract cannot be validly concluded without it.
findings.source_quote: tout maître d'apprentissage de la branche Hôtels, Cafés, Restaurants doit être titulaire d'un « permis de former » valide avant la signature de tout contrat d'apprentissage ou de professionnalisation. […] À défaut de ce permis, un contrat d'apprentissage ou de professionnalisation ne peut être valablement conclu.
findings.confidence: medium-high — confirmed on two branch-body sites (UMIH and GHR); avenant n°17 du 10 janvier 2013 identified via search and Legifrance's conv_coll listing, which I did not open

findings.claim: HCR apprentice pay was raised above the legal minimum by an extended avenant, binding on every house in the branch
findings.detail: Avenant n°35 du 27 février 2025, applicable from 1 August 2025, classifies apprentices at niveau I of the branch classification and pays them on a percentage of the higher of the conventional minimum or the SMIC. Because the niveau I hourly conventional rates exceed the SMIC, the branch minimum is what applies in practice. The arrêté d'extension has been published, so it binds all HCR employers, including those under 50 employees.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY as an ad-screening rule: an apprentice offer quoting the bare legal percentage-of-SMIC apprentice rate is quoting a wage below what the house actually owes — a misleading statement of "la rémunération" under L.5331-3.
findings.penalty: Against the employer. Against him via L.5331-3 / L.5334-1.
findings.source_quote: l'avenant n°35 du 27 février 2025 […] À compter du 1er août 2025 […] L'arrêté d'extension a été publié au Journal officiel
findings.confidence: medium-high — source is AKTO, the branch OPCO, not the Journal officiel itself; the avenant number, date and extension are stated there but I did not open the arrêté

findings.claim: Under-18s and dangerous kitchen equipment: a prior written declaration to the labour inspection, valid three years, plus medical fitness
findings.detail: Under-18s are barred from a list of dangerous work set by D.4153-15 et seq. From 15 upwards they may be assigned to some of it — "travaux réglementés" — only after the employer sends a déclaration de dérogation, with the elements listed at R.4153-41, to the territorially competent inspection du travail by a means giving proof of date, and BEFORE the young person is assigned. It lasts three years and must be renewed. The young person must hold a fitness certificate and be under suivi individuel renforcé. Slicers, mincers, vegetable cutters and the like put an ordinary Megève kitchen squarely inside this regime.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY only as a curation question to ask a house that advertises to minors. It is the second binary question after the permis de former, and the two together are a better proxy for "decent conditions for a young person" than anything he could measure himself.
findings.penalty: Against the employer, under the health-and-safety provisions; amounts not sourced.
findings.source_quote: La déclaration de dérogation, accompagnée des éléments mentionnés à l'article R. 4153-41 […] doit être adressée par tout moyen permettant de conférer date certaine à l'inspection du travail territorialement compétente, et doit nécessairement intervenir préalablement à l'affectation des jeunes aux travaux réglementés.
findings.confidence: low — travail-emploi.gouv.fr serves a CAPTCHA to automated fetches and the PDF downloaded as an HTML challenge page, so this rests on a search-result summary of the ministry's own notice, not on a page I read. The article numbers (D.4153-15 et seq., R.4153-41) and the three-year validity should be re-checked before he relies on them.

findings.claim: CDD is normal in his sector, not a warning sign — hôtellerie and restauration are listed "CDD d'usage" sectors, and seasonal work is its own lawful ground
findings.detail: France Travail's guide lists the five lawful grounds for a CDD, and two matter to him: "Les emplois à caractère saisonnier" and "Les secteurs d'activité dans lesquels il est d'usage de recourir au CDD", where the enumeration expressly includes l'hôtellerie and la restauration (D.1242-1). The trap is elsewhere: "CDD puis CDI" is a proscribed mention, because promising a permanent job at the end contradicts the temporary-task condition and invites requalification under L.1245-1.
findings.applies_to_him: TODAY, as a calibration point for the screening rules. In an alpine resort almost every listing will be a saisonnier; treating CDD as a red flag would gut his inventory for no legal reason, while "CDD avec possibilité de CDI" — which sounds generous — is the wording that is actually unlawful.
findings.penalty: Requalification of the CDD into a CDI against the employer (L.1245-1); against him via L.5331-3 / L.5334-1 for the misleading mention.
findings.source_quote: 3. Les emplois à caractère saisonnier 4. Les secteurs d'activité dans lesquels il est d'usage de recourir au CDD (les secteurs du déménagement, de l'hôtellerie, de la restauration, les centres de loisirs et de vacances, l'enseignement, les métiers du spectacle…) Article D. 1242-1 du code du travail

must_do: Put the express-request rule at the centre of the product. L.5334-1 makes the advertiser the defendant only where the advertiser asked for the insertion. So: every listing enters through a form the employer fills in and submits under a named account, the submission is timestamped and retained, and he never writes, rewrites or 'improves' ad copy. If a house sends him text by email or WhatsApp, he pastes it and keeps the message. This single discipline protects both the L.5334-1 allocation and the hébergeur/éditeur line at the same time.

Run a five-point screen on the AD, not an audit of the employer — this is what (c) actually requires. Before publishing: (1) written in French, foreign terms described in French; (2) publication date shown; (3) stated pay at or above the HCR conventional minimum, not merely the SMIC, and for apprentices the avenant n°35 rate; (4) no upper age limit, no 'étudiant', no 'Junior/Senior' outside a job title, no language requirement beyond Courant/Notions/Technique/Bilingue justified by the post; (5) no 'CDD puis CDI'. France Travail's guide (Nov 2025) is the checklist — download it and work from it.

Build the notice-and-action mechanism before launch, not after the first complaint. A visible 'Signaler cette annonce' control on every listing, accepting: the content complained of, its URL, the notifier's contact details, a good-faith statement. On receipt: acknowledge, decide, remove or keep, and send the reporter a reasoned answer. This is DSA arts. 16-18 and the micro-enterprise exemption does not cover it; the French sanction for failing to remove promptly is 1 year and 250 000 €, or up to 6 % of worldwide turnover for a company.

Write down the door policy, in non-protected terms, and keep the file. L.5321-2 forbids refusing service to an employer on a L.1132-1 ground. 'Churns staff', 'no permis de former', 'advertises shifts a minor cannot lawfully work' are all safe grounds; write them out, apply them uniformly, and record per house which one triggered a refusal or a quiet delisting. Silent enforcement is fine; unrecorded enforcement is not.

Make travail dissimulé a stated, one-strike delisting ground and act on reports the day they arrive. L.8221-1 2° punishes publicity knowingly favouring concealed work with 3 years and 45 000 € (225 000 € for a company). His defence is the absence of knowledge, and the day he is told is the day it evaporates. Take the listing down first, then ask questions; report to PHAROS (internet-signalement.gouv.fr) where fraud is suspected.

Check the SIRET on every house at intake and keep the screenshot. No article requires it, but it costs one lookup on the free public register, it converts 'employeur final connu' from an assertion into a record, and it is the cheapest evidence he has that he did not knowingly advertise for an unregistered operator.

Keep his own URSSAF account current and be ready to issue an attestation de vigilance. The obligation de vigilance runs from the restaurant to him, not the reverse: any house spending 5 000 € HT or more with him over a contract must collect his attestation every six months. A micro-entrepreneur who cannot produce one loses his largest customers.

Adopt the two HCR apprenticeship questions as the curation standard for anything aimed at under-18s: does the maître d'apprentissage hold a valid permis de former, and does the house hold a current déclaration de dérogation for travaux réglementés. Both are binary, both are verifiable by asking, and both are already legally required — so asking imposes nothing new on a decent house and screens out an indecent one immediately.

Check any listing aimed at a minor against the 22h00-23h30 window (R.3163-2) and the derogation requirement. In a Megève season this will catch real listings: a service shift ending at closing time is a shift a 17-year-old cannot lawfully work, and publishing it is publishing a misleading offer.

Do not sell anything to candidates, ever, in any form — no premium tier, no CV service, no surtaxed number, no affiliate link in the application path. L.5321-3 bans direct AND indirect remuneration from jobseekers, and L.5323-1 backs it with a three-month closure power.
unknowns: The exact verbatim wording of L.5334-1's liability-allocation paragraph. Three independent reads agree on the substance — the annonceur who requested the insertion is liable, the directeur de la publication or the service provider only where he acted without an express request — but code.travail.gouv.fr's copyright guard blocked full reproduction and the authoritative text sits on Legifrance, which refuses automated fetches. Worth reading once before he relies on it, because it is his main shield.

Whether a French court would classify a curated, paid-listing job board as hébergeur or éditeur. I found the official éditeur/hébergeur definitions but no authority applying them to a site that selects which advertisers may buy. This is the largest genuinely open question in the lane and the one most worth 90 minutes of a lawyer's time.

Whether the déclaration préalable d'activité de placement is definitively abrogated. The current L.5323-1 that I read contains no declaration duty, and décret n° 2012-539 du 20 avril 2012 is titled as modifying those regulatory provisions — but I did not open the décret, and I did not verify that no residual declaration survives in R.5323-1 et seq.

The travaux réglementés declaration regime for minors (article numbers, the three-year validity, the R.4153-41 content list). travail-emploi.gouv.fr serves a CAPTCHA to automated fetches, so this rests entirely on a search summary of the ministry's own notice. Everything else in this report comes from a page I opened; this one does not.

Whether DSA article 30 (traceability of traders) could be argued to catch job platforms. My reading is no — a jobseeker is not a consumer concluding a distance contract — but I could not open the regulation's recitals, only Arcom's summary of the scope wording.

Complicity under art. 121-7 code pénal as a separate route to liability for publishing a travail dissimulé employer's ad. I did not open a source on it. It is probably academic next to L.8221-1 2°, which already writes the publisher's version of the offence, but I did not verify that.

Whether avenant n°33 du 19 juin 2024 is still the current HCR wage grid as of September 2026. The Code du travail numérique page named it, but branch minima are renegotiated roughly annually and a 2025 or 2026 avenant may have superseded it. He needs the live grid, not this one, to screen stated wages.

Nothing in this lane covers his RGPD position. If candidates create accounts, upload CVs, or he stores applications passing between the two sides, he is a data controller with CNIL obligations of his own. That is a separate lane and it is not optional.

audits.overall:
I re-opened every cited URL. The codal texts are, with one exception, quoted accurately — 21 of 23 Code du travail articles matched the source word-for-word. The research is not fabricated. But it has five systematic defects, and two of them would cost him money or credibility.

**1. The R5334-1 blind spot — Lane 1 and Lane 2 contradict each other in the same document.** Lane 1 repeatedly says articles L5331-1, L5331-2, L5331-4 and L5332-1 carry "no penalty" or are "not listed in L5334-1." That is true of L5334-1 and false of the code. R5334-1 reads: "Le fait de méconnaître les dispositions des articles L. 5331-1, L. 5331-2, L. 5331-4, L. 5332-1 et L. 5332-3, relatives aux conditions de publication et de diffusion des offres d'emploi, est puni de l'amende prévue pour les contraventions de la 3e classe." Lane 2 found this and got it right; Lane 1 did not and understates his exposure on four duties. Undated listings, an English-only ad, and an upper age limit each carry 450 € (art. 131-13 3° code pénal, confirmed). Reconcile the two lanes before he builds to either.

**2. The one genuinely bad quote is the Versailles "contrary reading."** The article is real (Julien Kahn, Village de la Justice, 2 April 2026; CA Versailles 3 March 2026, RG 24/04425). The quoted sentence is not in it, and it inverts the article's point. The article's third condition is remuneration *of the intermediation* — from whoever pays — and it then says expressly that payment may not come from the jobseeker. It is not authority for "free to candidates = outside the regime." The claim self-flagged this as probably mis-stated; it is worse than mis-stated, and should be struck rather than carried at low confidence.

**3. "He IS an organisme privé de placement" is an assumption in Lane 1 and a stated fact in Lane 3.** No authority holds that a passive job board does "placement." Lane 1's framing — plan on the assumption, the cost is near nil — is sound advice. Lane 3's flat assertion ("He is legally an organisme privé de placement", confidence high) is unsupported, and it sits awkwardly beside the same research's own finding that HelloWork and Indeed France register as 63.12Z and 62.01Z, not 78.10Z. I verified those registrations; they are exact.

**4. The DSA finding is the one operative gap.** DSA Article 19 disapplies Section 3 for micro-enterprises **"with the exception of Article 24(3)"** — so Article 24(3) still binds him, and Article 17 (statement of reasons) is in Section 2 and was never exempt at all. The claim treats both as optional good practice ("should build anyway", "points toward"). When he de-lists a hotel for churning staff, he owes that hotel a statement of reasons and owes a submission to the Commission's public database. Arcom's own page is loose here, and the research inherited its looseness.

**5. Maxima quoted as his exposure, repeatedly.** €20m/4% of worldwide turnover, 225 000 €, 375 000 €, 37 500 € — none is a 19-year-old micro-entrepreneur's realistic exposure, and the 225 000 € and 375 000 € figures are personne-morale quintuples under art. 131-38 code pénal that do not apply to a sole trader at all. Give him the personne physique figure and the CNIL's actual practice for an operator this size (mise en demeure first), not the ceiling.

Two smaller process points. Several entries carry `"opened": true` with an English paraphrase in `source_quote` rather than the French text — the CNIL recruitment page, the L5321-3 Lane 2 entry, the Assemblée nationale impact study and the Versailles note. The pages were genuinely opened; the quotes are not quotes. And the repeated statement "I did not open the statute itself because Legifrance refuses automated fetches" was accepted too readily: L1134-5, R5323-11 and L5332-5 are all on code.travail.gouv.fr and I read all three directly. (Legifrance is indeed unreliable — my own fetch of a Legifrance article URL returned a different article entirely — but no claim asserted it had been opened, so there is no defect on that axis.)

Nothing here says his product is unlawful. Free to candidates, employers pay for insertion, express insertion request logged per listing, French text authoritative, every listing dated — that design is sound and the research gets it right. Fix the penalty table, strike the Versailles item, and build the DSA statement-of-reasons flow he was told he could skip.

verdicts.claim: L5321-1's definition of activité de placement is broad enough to catch a site that merely publishes employers' offers
verdicts.why: Text verified word-for-word, both alinéas, including 'Les entreprises de travail temporaire peuvent fournir des services de placement au sens du présent article' (page dated 25/07/2010). The three elements and the 'sans devenir partie' clause are as stated, and reading that clause as a condition FOR the qualification rather than an escape from it is correct.
verdicts.correction: The framing is right but 'All four elements met' is his own inference, not anything a court or the administration has held about a passive job board. Keep it as the planning assumption Lane 1 calls it, not as a finding.

verdicts.claim: INSEE NAF 78.10Z expressly includes online placement agencies
verdicts.why: Sub-class 78.10Z 'Activités des agences de placement de main-d'œuvre' lists 'les activités des agences de placement de main-d'œuvre en ligne' among what it comprises. Quote exact.
verdicts.correction: The caveat in the claim is the important half and is correct: an APE code is statistical, assigned by INSEE, and decides nothing legally.

verdicts.claim: A Versailles appeal decision is reported as requiring remuneration from the jobseeker before the placement qualification bites
verdicts.why: The article exists and the case details check out — 'Activité de placement et formation : que dit le Droit ?', Julien Kahn, published 2 April 2026, discussing CA Versailles 3 March 2026 RG 24/04425. The quoted sentence is not in it. The article's third condition is remuneration OF THE INTERMEDIATION, source unspecified; it then states the opposite of the claim, that 'aucune rétribution, directe ou indirecte, ne peut être exigée des personnes à la recherche d'un emploi', i.e. payment may not come from the candidate.
verdicts.correction: Strike this item. It is not a contrary reading and provides no support, even weak, for a free-to-candidates site sitting outside L5321-1. The claim's own low-confidence hedge was right about the direction but understated the problem: the quote misrepresents the source.

verdicts.claim: There is NO déclaration préalable — abolished in 2010; no form, prefecture filing, fee or register
verdicts.why: The Assemblée nationale impact study (ratification of ILO Convention 181) states it directly: 'l'article 29 de la loi n° 2010-853 du 23 juillet 2010 ... ouvre l'exercice de l'activité de placement à tout organisme public ou privé ... L'obligation de déclaration préalable adressée à l'autorité administrative a, en outre, été supprimée'. Corroborated negatively: Bpifrance Création's regulated-activity page for organisme privé de placement lists no declaration or authorisation, only guichet unique registration; and R5323-1 now 404s on code.travail.gouv.fr, consistent with repeal.
verdicts.correction: Three sourcing fixes. The abolition was article 29 of the 2010 law, not article 14 (article 14 is the exclusivity article — different claim, same law). The source_quote is an English paraphrase, not verbatim; the French sentence above is the real one. And the Senate report does not 'record that article 14 deleted the whole Chapter III' in the sense implied — it describes the déclaration préalable as part of the droit en vigueur, and separately says provisions 4° and 6° of article 14 make 'le chapitre III relatif au placement privé' disappear with conforming provisions 'conservées mais « remontées » au chapitre 1er du titre II'. The repeal of R5323-1 to R5323-6 by décret n° 2012-539 is consistent with what I saw but I did not verify the décret number.

verdicts.claim: The exclusivity rule for lucrative placement was abolished by the same 2010 law
verdicts.why: Senate report n° 507 (2009-2010) on article 14 of the projet de loi réseaux consulaires states the aim is to 'supprimer l'obligation d'exclusivité de l'activité de fourniture de services de placement lorsque cette activité est à but lucratif', and grounds it in the Services Directive, describing the existing restrictions as 'contraires à la directive « services »'. Quote accurate.
verdicts.correction: None. His paid-visibility tiers and any side revenue are untouched by placement law, as stated.

verdicts.claim: An annual statistical return to the préfet survives, due before 31 March
verdicts.why: R5323-8 verified in force, text matches word-for-word including the model fixed by arrêté, the turnover head and the three jobseeker sub-heads a) reçues b) placées c) inscrites au 31 décembre. Page last updated 24/04/2012, no repeal shown. Independently corroborated as live on Bpifrance Création's regulated-activities page, which cites R5323-8 by number.
verdicts.correction: The honest framing in the claim — textually owed, practically unenforced because no prefecture knows he exists — is accurate and worth keeping. His point that he cannot report 'placées au cours de l'année' on a publish-and-connect model is real; report what he has and say so on the return.

verdicts.claim: Gratuité: he may never charge the worker, directly or indirectly; he may charge the employer
verdicts.why: L5321-3 verified verbatim including both exceptions, artistes du spectacle (L7121-9) and agents sportifs (art. L222-6 code du sport). Penalty verified independently at L5324-1: 'un emprisonnement de six mois et d'une amende de 3 750 euros' for requiring direct or indirect retribution from jobseekers in breach of L5321-3.
verdicts.correction: None on the law. The 3 750 € is a maximum for a personne physique, not a tariff — worth saying to him so he calibrates. The list of what 'indirecte' catches is the research's own extrapolation, not from any source, but it is the right reading of the word.

verdicts.claim: Selling job offers is forbidden whatever the medium, but charging an employer for insertion is expressly permitted (Lane 1 version)
verdicts.why: The legal proposition is right and the text is verbatim correct. The penalty line is wrong: 'L5331-1 carries no penalty of its own in L5334-1' is true of L5334-1 but stops one article too early. R5334-1 punishes breach of L5331-1 with a 3rd-class contravention — 450 € under art. 131-13 3° code pénal, which I verified.
verdicts.correction: Replace the penalty with: breach of L5331-1 is a contravention de 3e classe under R5334-1, 450 € maximum; a candidate-side charge additionally triggers L5324-1 (6 months, 3 750 €). Note this entry contradicts the Lane 2 entry on the same article, which has it right.

verdicts.claim: Misleading claims about the free character of an employment service are the same offence (L5331-5)
verdicts.why: L5331-5 verified verbatim, including 'notamment sur le caractère gratuit de ce service'. L5334-1's second alinéa confirmed to attach the same one year and 37 500 €.
verdicts.correction: The practical advice — write the free-for-candidates promise into the CGU as a commitment rather than leaving it as a walk-backable marketing line — follows correctly from the text.

verdicts.claim: The heaviest penalty is for publishing misleading offers, and it lands on the publisher when he acted without an express insertion request
verdicts.why: L5334-1 verified verbatim, both the penalty (one year, 37 500 €) and the allocation rule: the annonceur who requested diffusion bears the offence; the directeur de la publication or the fournisseur du service bears it 'lorsqu'il a agi sans demande expresse d'insertion de l'offre émanant de l'annonceur'. L5331-3's three enumerated heads also verified verbatim.
verdicts.correction: One calibration: 37 500 € is the statutory maximum for a personne physique, not his expected exposure. If he later incorporates, art. 131-38 code pénal quintuples it for the legal person. The architectural conclusion — never publish without a traceable express request, never scrape or re-post — is correct and is the single most load-bearing finding in the set.

verdicts.claim: Non-discrimination binds him as gatekeeper and publisher, and his curation policy survives it
verdicts.why: L5321-2 verified verbatim, both sentences. The substantive analysis is right: refusing a house for churning staff turns on no L1132-1 ground and is lawful, and the offer-moderation duty is the live one. The penalty line is wrong in the same way as the L5331-1 entry: 'L5331-2 (age limits) is not in L5334-1's list' is true but incomplete, because R5334-1 names L5331-2 expressly.
verdicts.correction: L5331-2 carries a 3rd-class contravention (450 €) under R5334-1, in addition to the L5321-2 breach an age-referencing offer also commits. Also note the first sentence of L5321-2 only binds him if he is a placement operator — which the research assumes rather than establishes.

verdicts.claim: Two small publication formalities: offers must be dated, and anonymous offers require the employer's identity to be held
verdicts.why: Both texts verified verbatim — L5332-1 'Toute offre d'emploi publiée ou diffusée est datée' and L5332-2 including the second alinéa on intermediaries. L5332-3 on temporary work agencies also verified: adverts and offers 'mentionnent expressément leur dénomination et leur caractère d'entreprise de travail temporaire'. The penalty line 'Not listed in L5334-1' is wrong by omission: R5334-1 names both L5332-1 and L5332-3.
verdicts.correction: L5332-1 and L5332-3 each carry a 3rd-class contravention (450 €) under R5334-1. L5332-2 genuinely carries none — it is absent from both L5334-1 and R5334-1, which the Lane 2 entry states correctly.

verdicts.claim: Offers must be written in French (L5331-4)
verdicts.why: Text verified verbatim across all four alinéas, including the no-French-equivalent carve-out, the territorial scope, and the foreign-language-publication exception. The penalty line 'Not listed among the offences in L5334-1' is wrong by omission — R5334-1 names L5331-4.
verdicts.correction: Breach of L5331-4 is a contravention de 3e classe, 450 € under R5334-1. This matters more than the other three because, as the Lane 2 entry notes, this one attaches to the act of diffusing and is therefore realistically his exposure, not only the employer's.

verdicts.claim: Sanctions for operating outside the regime: administrative closure up to three months after a two-step mise en demeure, plus the L5324-1 offence
verdicts.why: L5323-1 verified verbatim — inspection officers may 'constater les manquements aux dispositions du chapitre Ier', and after mise en demeure the administration may 'ordonner la fermeture de l'organisme en cause pour une durée n'excédant pas trois mois'. R5324-1 confirmed the procedure: observations within 15 days, then a mise en demeure by registered letter with acknowledgement, then closure only after a further period of not less than 15 days.
verdicts.correction: None. The reassuring conclusion is sound — no ambush closure, a written notice and at least a fortnight to fix. And it is correct that there is no offence of 'unlicensed placement' because there is no licence.

verdicts.claim: The line to an entreprise de travail temporaire is the only real licensing gate, and it is crossed by employing the worker
verdicts.why: L5321-1 verified: declaration to the administrative authority plus a financial guarantee under L1251-49, with further declarations for moving the siège, opening branches, or ceasing activity. L1255-2 verified verbatim: 3 750 € fine, 'La récidive est punie d'un emprisonnement de six mois et d'une amende de 7 500 euros', and the court 'peut prononcer en outre l'interdiction d'exercer l'activité d'entrepreneur de travail temporaire pour une durée de deux à dix ans'.
verdicts.correction: None. The bright lines given — never pay a worker, never invoice per day worked, never sign a contrat de mise à disposition — are the right operational statement of the trigger.

verdicts.claim: Job board vs cabinet de recrutement is not a licensing line; what changes is data-protection and discrimination exposure
verdicts.why: The legal framing is right — a recruitment firm doing selection sits in the same L5321-1 regime with no licence, no declaration, no capital, employer fee lawful, candidate fee criminal. But the CNIL source_quote is a paraphrase, not verbatim. The page actually reads 'Vous ne pouvez utiliser que les informations qui vous permettent d'évaluer la capacité des candidats à occuper le poste proposé ou à mesurer leurs aptitudes professionnelles', and on retention 'conserver le CV et la lettre de motivation d'un candidat pour alimenter un « vivier de candidats » est possible sous réserve que la durée de conservation n'excède en principe pas deux ans et que le candidat en ait été informé, à compter du dernier contact avec ce candidat'.
verdicts.correction: The penalty quotes the GDPR ceiling — 20m€ or 4% of worldwide turnover — as though it were his exposure. For a sole trader running a village job board that figure is meaningless; the claim's own trailing note (mise en demeure first) is the real answer and should be the headline. The substantive recommendation — keep applications off his servers via mailto or the establishment's own form, so he never holds a CV — is the strongest practical advice in the whole set.

verdicts.claim: Placement-specific data law: no NIR, and a six-year ceiling on jobseeker data (R5323-9 to R5323-11)
verdicts.why: Bpifrance Création's page carries both rules verbatim — 'Les données relatives aux personnes en recherche d'emploi ne peuvent être conservées plus de 6 ans après leur enregistrement' and 'La collecte du numéro d'inscription au répertoire national d'identification des personnes physiques (NIR) est prohibée' — citing R5323-9 à R5323-11. I also read R5323-11 directly, in force, text matching.
verdicts.correction: Upgrade this from medium to high confidence: the claim says 'I did not read the article texts themselves, so the precise wording is unverified'. R5323-11 is on code.travail.gouv.fr and reads exactly as reported. The advice to take the shorter CNIL duration over the six-year outer wall is correct — six years is a ceiling, not a default.

verdicts.claim: The big French job boards hold no placement declaration; HelloWork registers as 63.12Z and Indeed France as 62.01Z
verdicts.why: Queried the government API directly. HELLOWORK, SIREN 428843130, APE 63.12Z, Rennes. INDEED FRANCE SAS, SIREN 809675580, APE 62.01Z, Paris. Both exact, neither carries 78.10Z.
verdicts.correction: None, and both caveats in the claim are the right ones: the APE code has no legal value and choosing 63.12Z would not shield him if challenged, since the qualification follows what he does. Note the tension this creates with the Lane 3 entry, which asserts flatly that a pure publisher IS a placement operator — the whole industry's registrations point the other way.

verdicts.claim: Selling offers is banned, charging employers for insertion is the exception, but 'moyen de communication payant' is a literal wrinkle (Lane 2 version)
verdicts.why: Text verbatim correct, and this entry's penalty is the accurate one: contravention de 3e classe under R5334-1, which I verified names L5331-1 expressly. The 450 € figure for a 3rd-class contravention under art. 131-13 3° code pénal is confirmed — the claim honestly flagged that it had not opened a page carrying that figure, and it is right.
verdicts.correction: None. Flagging the literal 'moyen de communication payant' reading as the one place his exact model meets the text head-on is good lawyering, and the conclusion — every French board operates this way, the ban targets trafficking in offers not the sale of ad space — is the right resolution.

verdicts.claim: He can never charge candidates a centime, directly or indirectly (Lane 2 version)
verdicts.why: Substance correct and the two exceptions are the right ones. The entry itself admits the page 'returned the rule in translation' — so the source_quote is an English rendering, not the French text, despite the entry being marked opened.
verdicts.correction: Use the French: 'Aucune rétribution, directe ou indirecte, ne peut être exigée des personnes à la recherche d'un emploi en contrepartie de la fourniture de services de placement...'. The penalty field is also incomplete: it gives only the L5323-1 closure route and omits L5324-1's six months and 3 750 €, which the Lane 1 entry on the same article supplies correctly.

verdicts.claim: Every published offer must be dated, no exception (Lane 2 version)
verdicts.why: L5332-1 verified: 'Toute offre d'emploi publiée ou diffusée est datée.' Single sentence, absolute, as described. Penalty correctly given here as a 3rd-class contravention under R5334-1 — unlike the Lane 1 entry on the same article.
verdicts.correction: None. The product warning is well spotted: re-dating a stale offer to buy it fresh visibility converts a dating rule into an L5331-3 misleading-offer problem under head 1° (caractère effectivement disponible).

verdicts.claim: False or misleading offers are a délit carrying one year and 37 500 €, with three enumerated heads
verdicts.why: L5331-3 verified verbatim including all three numbered heads. 'Susceptibles d'induire en erreur' is indeed the operative half — no intent required. Penalty confirmed at L5334-1 first alinéa.
verdicts.correction: The three product consequences drawn — an expiry and poste-pourvu mechanism against head 1°, logement/nourriture as 'avantages annexes' under head 2°, and naming which house under head 3° — all follow from the text. Only calibration: 37 500 € is the maximum for a personne physique.

verdicts.claim: Liability is the employer's by default and becomes his the moment he publishes without an express insertion request
verdicts.why: L5334-1's closing alinéa verified verbatim. The allocation is as described: not joint-and-several by default, not a fault-based test about what he should have noticed, but the binary fact of whether an express insertion request existed from the advertiser for that offer.
verdicts.correction: None, and the distinction the entry draws is exactly right and worth repeating to him: curating WHICH employers may list is a decision about the advertiser and does not endanger him; writing or rewriting WHAT the listing says does. The 'let me polish that for you' rewrite is the trap.

verdicts.claim: The enforcement body for misleading offers is the DGCCRF, not only the inspection du travail
verdicts.why: L5333-1 verified: 'Les agents de la concurrence, de la consommation et de la répression des fraudes' are habilités to seek out and record breaches of L5331-3 and L5331-5, under the conditions of art. L511-5 code de la consommation.
verdicts.correction: None. The realistic complaint path described — a candidate who travelled for a job that did not exist, complaining to DGCCRF — is plausible, though 'DGCCRF sweeps of online platforms are routine and public' is asserted without a source and I did not verify it.

verdicts.claim: Anonymous offers are allowed but the employer must give him their name and address, and the administration and France Travail can demand it from him
verdicts.why: Both texts verified verbatim. L5332-2 including the intermediary alinéa; L5332-4 confirming the administrative authority and the L5312-1 institution may obtain the name and address 'sur simple demande de leur part' from the directeur de la publication or responsable du moyen de communication. The penalty analysis is right: L5332-2 is absent from both L5334-1 and R5334-1.
verdicts.correction: One overreach. The entry says 'Two duties fall on him and neither is optional', the first being that no anonymous listing goes live without a verified legal name and address. That is a sound design choice, not a legal duty — L5332-2 binds the EMPLOYER to disclose to him. His actual duty is the L5332-4 production duty, which is what makes holding the data necessary in practice. Worth keeping the distinction so he knows which one a court would enforce against him.

verdicts.claim: The French-language rule applies even when the job genuinely requires English
verdicts.why: L5331-4 verified verbatim. The DREETS Normandie page exists and carries the decisive phrase word-for-word: 'peu importe que la parfaite connaissance d'une langue étrangère serait une des conditions requises pour tenir l'emploi proposé'. Both carve-outs confirmed.
verdicts.correction: Penalty correctly given here as a 3rd-class contravention. One accuracy note: the DREETS page says breaches attract criminal sanctions but gives no figure — the 450 € comes from R5334-1 plus art. 131-13 3°, not from that page. The reading that the foreign-language-media carve-out covers publications edited in a foreign language and not a French site with an EN toggle is correct on the text.

verdicts.claim: No upper age limit may appear in an offer, and no offer may reference any L1132-1 discrimination ground
verdicts.why: L5331-2 verified verbatim including the exception for 'conditions d'âge imposées par les dispositions légales'. L5321-2's second sentence verified verbatim.
verdicts.correction: Two calibrations on penalties. The 3rd-class contravention for L5331-2 is right (this entry gets R5334-1 correct where Lane 1 did not). But 225 000 € for a legal person is the art. 131-38 quintuple and does not apply to him as a sole trader — his figure under art. 225-2 code pénal is 3 years and 45 000 €, itself a maximum. The observation that 'physical appearance' and 'place de résidence' are live criteria in front-of-house hospitality recruitment is the genuinely useful part.

verdicts.claim: No rule in Titre III about advertising to minors; the real constraint is that ads for 16-18s describe work they cannot lawfully do, converting into an L5331-3 problem
verdicts.why: L4153-6 verified verbatim across all three alinéas — the bar-service ban, the spouse-and-relatives-to-the-fourth-degree exception, and the débits agréés exception for over-sixteens in an RNCP-registered training programme under L6113-5. The derivative L5331-3 reasoning is sound: an offer describing work the establishment cannot lawfully have performed misdescribes the job under head 1°.
verdicts.correction: I verified L4153-6 only. The adjacent articles cited — L3163-2 on night work and the midnight-to-4am floor, L4153-1 on under-sixteens, L6222-1 on apprenticeship ages — I did not open, so treat those as unverified. The onboarding design proposed (capture whether the house is agréé, gate shift-hours so an under-18 listing cannot advertise past midnight) rests on L3163-2, which is the unverified one.

verdicts.claim: Positioning the whole site for young people is defensible; an individual ad with an age criterion generally is not
verdicts.why: L1133-2 verified: differences of treatment based on age are not discrimination when 'objectivement et raisonnablement justifiées par un but légitime, notamment par le souci de préserver la santé ou la sécurité des travailleurs, de favoriser leur insertion professionnelle...', and the article expressly contemplates 'l'interdiction de l'accès à l'emploi ou la mise en place de conditions de travail spéciales en vue d'assurer la protection des jeunes'.
verdicts.correction: The medium-confidence hedge is correctly placed and should stay: this is a case-by-case justification standard, not a safe harbour, and no authority has blessed a job board aimed at young entrants. The line drawn — site may be aimed at young people, listings may not carry age criteria except where law imposes them — is the right operational rule.

verdicts.claim: Today there is no obligation to state pay in a French job ad, but a stated figure must be true
verdicts.why: I found no pay-disclosure duty in Titre III, consistent with the claim's negative finding. L5331-3 2° 'La rémunération et les avantages annexes proposés' verified verbatim as one of the three enumerated heads of the misleading-offer délit.
verdicts.correction: None. The product point is the valuable one: a structured 'avantages' picker invites optimistic ticking on logement, nourriture, pourboires and prime de fin de saison, and every ticked box becomes a published allegation about pay under head 2°.

verdicts.claim: The EU pay-transparency transposition deadline passed 7 June 2026; France's bill reached the Conseil des ministres 10 September 2026 and is not yet law
verdicts.why: The service-public page exists, is titled 'Le projet de loi pour la transparence salariale a été présenté en Conseil des ministres', is dated 10 September 2026, and states 'Le texte doit désormais être examiné par le Sénat et l'Assemblée nationale'. The 7 June 2026 deadline under Directive (UE) 2023/970 of 10 May 2023 is confirmed independently, as is the Conseil d'État avis of 23 July 2026.
verdicts.correction: Two sourcing gaps. The 7 June 2026 deadline is attributed to a Government answer to a Senate question but the cited URL is the service-public page, which does not carry that date — cite the directive's article 34 instead. And the new article L1221-9-1 and the ban on asking about current or past pay are attributed to the Conseil d'État avis, which I could not open to verify; treat those two details as unverified. The core advice stands and is well judged: build the pay-range field now as optional, and never build a current-salary field. The point that no size threshold exempts his small clients from the candidate-information duty is correct — the 50/100-employee thresholds govern gap reporting, not article 5.

verdicts.claim: There is NO obligation in Titre III to archive or keep published offers; the retention he needs is evidential
verdicts.why: L5332-5 verified verbatim and is exactly what the claim says it is — a power for décrets en Conseil d'État to set the conditions under which placement organisations may 'demander, détenir, conserver, diffuser et céder' nominative information. A power to regulate, not a duty to keep. No retention duty appears anywhere in L5332-1 to L5332-5.
verdicts.correction: None, and this is the sharpest operational recommendation in the set: because L5334-1 puts the offence on him absent an express insertion request, his archive of insertion requests IS his criminal defence. The per-listing log proposed — account identity, text as submitted, text as published, submission timestamp, every edit with author, takedown — is the right artefact.

verdicts.claim: CNIL: candidate data may be kept two years after last contact; his 16-18 audience is above the parental-consent threshold
verdicts.why: The CNIL's TPE/PME recruitment page states the two-year rule verbatim, running 'à compter du dernier contact avec ce candidat', conditioned on the candidate having been informed. The fifteen-year threshold under article 45 of the loi Informatique et Libertés is France's GDPR article 8 choice and is correctly stated.
verdicts.correction: The design conclusion is the right one and should be taken: set a hard sixteen minimum on account creation. It removes the parental-consent question entirely, and it aligns with L4153-1's bar on employing under-sixteens outside apprenticeship and observation placements — so it costs him nothing he could lawfully have had.

verdicts.claim: As an online platform he owes DSA duties, but as a micro-enterprise he is exempt from the heavier tier
verdicts.why: The Arcom page exists and its wording is reproduced faithfully: micro and small enterprises, 'moins de 50 personnes' and turnover or balance sheet total not exceeding '10 millions d'euros', are 'exemptés de certaines obligations du règlement (cf. articles 15 (2), 19 et 29)'. But the underlying regulation is narrower than the claim's conclusion. DSA Article 19 reads 'Section 3, with the exception of Article 24(3), shall not apply to providers of online platforms that qualify as micro or small enterprises' — so Article 24(3) is expressly carved back IN, and Article 17 (statement of reasons) sits in Section 2 and was never exempt at all.
verdicts.correction: Two obligations are treated as optional good practice when they are mandatory. Article 17 requires a statement of reasons to the affected user whenever he restricts content on illegality or terms-and-conditions grounds — which de-listing a hotel for churning staff is. Article 24(3) then requires submitting those statements of reasons to the Commission's public machine-readable database. The entry's line that 'DSA article 17 logic points toward telling that user why' understates this: it is a duty, not a pointer, and his 'silent standard' model cannot survive it. Also note the drafting slip the entry inherited from Arcom — articles 15(2), 19 and 29 are the provisions that GRANT the exemptions, not obligations he is exempt from.

verdicts.claim: He must carry mentions légales on the site, with a disproportionate sanction
verdicts.why: The service-public page confirms the required mentions for an entrepreneur individuel and gives the sanction as '1 an d'emprisonnement' and '75 000 € d'amende' under LCEN article 6. The page does not differentiate between individual and company for this violation.
verdicts.correction: The medium-confidence hedge about 375 000 € resolves cleanly: that is the art. 131-38 code pénal quintuple applicable to a personne morale, so it is simply not his figure as a sole trader. And 75 000 € is a statutory maximum for an offence normally met with a mise en demeure — presenting it to a 19-year-old as his exposure is the kind of framing that causes panic rather than compliance. The interaction spotted is correct and useful: the mentions légales are what identify him as the responsable du moyen de communication, the capacity in which L5332-2 and L5332-4 address him.

verdicts.claim: Selling a service to jobseekers while misdescribing it as free is its own délit, separate from the offers rules
verdicts.why: L5331-5 verified verbatim, penalty confirmed at L5334-1 second alinéa (one year, 37 500 €), and L5333-1 confirmed to give DGCCRF the same investigatory powers over it.
verdicts.correction: None. The trap identified is real and worth writing into his roadmap: a later candidate-side paid feature added while the homepage still says free breaches L5321-3 and makes a false gratuity allegation under L5331-5 at the same time.

verdicts.claim: If the product drifts into selecting or matching, the regime that changes is Titre II placement, and the exposure is closure
verdicts.why: L5321-1 and L5323-1 both verified verbatim. The medium-confidence hedge on whether he is inside the definition today is correctly placed — and is the right posture, in contrast to the Lane 3 entry which asserts the same question as settled.
verdicts.correction: None. The bright line offered is the best single sentence in the set: decide about EMPLOYERS all he likes, never decide about CANDIDATES. It also happens to be the line that keeps him out of the CNIL controller burden and out of individual discrimination exposure.

verdicts.claim: He is legally an 'organisme privé de placement' the moment the site habitually brings offers and jobseekers together
verdicts.why: The quoted text of L5321-1 is verbatim correct and the functional reading is arguable. But this is stated as settled law at high confidence — 'He is legally an organisme privé de placement', 'TODAY, as a pure publisher', 'he is already in scope' — and no authority holds it. No court decision, no administrative position, and no official guidance I found qualifies a passive job board as placement. The same research set establishes the opposite market signal: HelloWork and Indeed France register as 63.12Z and 62.01Z, not 78.10Z.
verdicts.correction: Lane 1 states the same proposition correctly — plan on the assumption because the cost of assuming it is near nil and the cost of being wrong is criminal. Adopt that framing and drop this one's certainty. The practical consequence is unchanged, so nothing is lost: he should comply with R5323-8 and R5323-11 either way. What is lost by overstating is his ability to argue he is outside the regime if it ever matters.

verdicts.claim: Jobseeker data held by private placement bodies may not be kept beyond six years from recording (R5323-11)
verdicts.why: I read R5323-11 directly on code.travail.gouv.fr. In force, no repeal, text matching word-for-word: 'Les données relatives aux personnes à la recherche d'un emploi enregistrées dans un traitement de données mis en œuvre par les seuls organismes privés de placement ne peuvent être conservées au-delà d'un délai de six ans à compter de leur enregistrement.'
verdicts.correction: Both details the claim flags are right and both matter: the clock runs from enregistrement, not last contact, and six years is an outer wall inside which GDPR minimisation and the shorter CNIL durations still run. The penalty framing is also honest — no fine attaches to R5323-11 itself, over-retention is sanctioned as a storage-limitation breach — though again the 20m€/4% ceiling is not a sole trader's exposure.

verdicts.claim: The CNIL's 2026 retention référentiel sets two shorter operative durations and says both apply to intermediaries, not just employers
verdicts.why: I downloaded the PDF and extracted its text. It is the référentiel 'Les durées de conservation des données à caractère personnel — Gestion des ressources humaines', published 2 April 2026, updated 20 May 2026, with recruitment rows dated 29/01/2026. Both rows are there. The unsuccessful-candidate dossier row gives archivage intermédiaire 'à des fins probatoires, pour les éventuelles actions en discrimination : 5 ans à compter de la date à laquelle le poste a été pourvu (tant pour les intermédiaires que les employeurs)' with 'Article L. 1134-5 du code du travail (obligation)' as its basis. The CV-thèque row is headed 'Constitution de CV-thèque (type « vivier de candidats »)' and runs 'à compter du dernier contact avec le candidat non retenu'.
verdicts.correction: Two precisions. The phrase 'tant pour les intermédiaires que les employeurs' is attached to the five-year archivage durations, not stated as a global scope for the document — the claim generalises it slightly. And the two rows differ in force: the five-year evidential archive is labelled '(obligation)', but the CV-thèque row's basis is 'Guide recrutement (recommandation)', so the two-year duration is a CNIL recommendation, not a binding duration. The référentiel's own legend says so: recommended durations 'ne revêtent pas un caractère obligatoire'. That difference is worth knowing before he hard-codes two years as a legal deadline.

verdicts.claim: The five-year evidential archive rests on article L1134-5, which fixes five years for a discrimination reparation action
verdicts.why: I read L1134-5 directly: 'L'action en réparation du préjudice résultant d'une discrimination se prescrit par cinq ans à compter de la révélation de la discrimination.' The CNIL référentiel independently cites it by number and marks it '(obligation)'.
verdicts.correction: Upgrade from medium to high, and correct the stated reason for the hedge. The entry says it did not open the statute 'because Legifrance refuses automated fetches' — but L1134-5 is on code.travail.gouv.fr, the same site every other article in this research was read on. The apparent divergence the claim worries about is not a divergence: the statute runs from révélation de la discrimination, and CNIL's 'date à laquelle le poste a été pourvu' is its practical proxy for when the clock could start.

verdicts.claim: (c) CONTROLLER, not processor, and not joint controller with the restaurants — the CNIL recruitment guide answers this for job boards by name
verdicts.why: The jobboard passage is verbatim (guide p.15) but narrower than reported: the operator 'peut être considéré comme responsable du traitement relatif à la création et gestion des comptes personnels' — the guide places him in the controller column for account creation/management, not for the product as a whole. The joint-control half is wrong on the record: the guide gives TWO worked examples, not one. Before the international-group example it reproduces the EDPB (2 Sept 2020) example in which a cabinet de recrutement is joint controller with a client company over a database combining the client's CVs with its own and 'exploité spécialement pour cette entreprise cliente'. That is a service provider and its paying customer — the very shape the claim says the guide never illustrates. The same fiche also warns that for jobboards offering 'une CVthèque partagée entre plusieurs recruteurs, le tri, le classement et l'évaluation des profils', 'la ligne de partage... peut parfois être délicate à fixer'.
verdicts.correction: Keep the conclusion (he is a controller; do not sign an art. 28 contract calling him a processor) but drop 'not joint controller' as settled. Joint control is arguable earlier than the claim allows — not only on matching, but wherever a restaurant's input shapes a shared candidate base. Write the qualification analysis per-purpose.

verdicts.claim: The CNIL warns the label is not his to choose — an authority can requalify it whatever the contract says
verdicts.why: Verbatim, guide fiche n°3: 'Si un organisme décide concrètement « pourquoi » et « comment » les données sont traitées, il doit être considéré comme responsable de traitement, même s'il est désigné comme sous-traitant dans un contrat. Les autorités de contrôle ne sont pas liées par les qualifications choisies par les parties et une requalification, appréciée au regard des justifications fournies, est donc toujours possible.' The documentation duty is also verbatim: 'les acteurs ne peuvent pas choisir en opportunité la qualification qu'ils préfèrent'.

verdicts.claim: (d) Legal basis is three bases, one per purpose — and the CNIL changed position on the CV library: it is now consent, not legitimate interest
verdicts.why: The 'évolution des recommandations' sentence is verbatim, but it does not carry the conclusion. The guide's own mapping table lists BOTH bases for that purpose: 'La constitution d'une CVthèque ou l'élaboration d'une base de données de type « vivier de candidatures » — Consentement / Intérêt légitime'. Worse for the claim's practical rule, the guide's Hypothèse n°1 is his exact case — a candidate who 'demande à rejoindre un vivier de candidats... (intégration de jobboards)' — and says: 'L'intégration du profil du candidat au sein d'une CVthèque étant réalisée à son initiative, celui-ci peut être considéré comme ayant consenti, par la même occasion.'
