The rest of the finding checks out verbatim: the jobboard row is intérêt légitime, contract requires 'mis en œuvre à la seule initiative du candidat', authentication cookies are on intérêt légitime, and 'Une seule base légale devra être retenue pour chaque finalité'.
verdicts.correction: State it as: consent is the CNIL's preferred basis for a CVthèque, legitimate interest remains listed. The separate unbundled opt-in is prudent design, not a stated requirement for a candidate who joins the pool himself. What IS required verbatim is that 'l'acceptation des conditions générales d'utilisation ne peut suffire' — so the T&C-tickbox version is out either way.

verdicts.claim: (d) Consent cannot be used for anything affecting the candidate's chances of getting a job
verdicts.why: Verbatim: 'les traitements effectués dans le cadre des opérations mêmes de recrutement ne peuvent pas être fondés sur le consentement des candidats dès lors qu'un refus de leur part pourrait affecter leurs chances d'obtenir un emploi (ou certains types d'emplois)'. The practical split he is given (visibility = consent, revocable; sending an application = contract) matches the guide's own examples.

verdicts.claim: (d) Information owed is the art. 13 list PLUS three extra duties from the Code du travail
verdicts.why: Every art. 13 item listed is in the guide's fiche n°8 enumeration, in that order. The three Code du travail limbs are verbatim from the same fiche: purpose limited to 'apprécier sa capacité à occuper l'emploi proposé'; 'le candidat est expressément informé, préalablement à leur mise en œuvre, des méthodes et techniques d'aide au recrutement utilisées à son égard'; and the quoted sentence 'aucune information concernant personnellement un candidat ne peut être collectée par un dispositif qui n'a pas été porté préalablement à sa connaissance'. Layered notices are expressly allowed. Art. 83(5) is the right tier for arts. 12-22.
verdicts.correction: €20m/4% is the Regulation's ceiling for undertakings, not his exposure. A one-person micro-entreprise is realistically in the CNIL's ordinary or simplified sanction range, orders of magnitude below. Quote the tier, not the number, when explaining this to him.

verdicts.claim: (e) DPO not required — none of the three art. 37(1) triggers is met
verdicts.why: Art. 37(1)(a)(b)(c) as reproduced on the CNIL page match the claim's rendering: public authority; core activities of regular and systematic large-scale monitoring; or large-scale art. 9/art. 10 processing. None fits a regional board that publishes offers and forwards applications. The provenance note (read via the CNIL's hosted text, not EUR-Lex) is accurate and is not a defect.

verdicts.claim: (e) AIPD required — the recruitment guide names a jobboard operator as an example
verdicts.why: Verbatim in fiche n°10's table, in the nine-criteria column: 'traitements utilisés par l'exploitant d'une plateforme web de type jobboard mettant en relation employeurs et candidats et proposant divers services'. The vulnerable-persons reasoning is verbatim too: 'Dans une relation entre candidat à un emploi et recruteur, la situation peut, selon les contextes, être présumée comme au moins aussi déséquilibrée.' The before-launch rule and the prior-consultation duty are both in the fiche.
verdicts.correction: Two softenings to keep him honest: the guide's own verb is 'L'AIPD est souvent obligatoire lorsque le traitement remplit au moins deux des neuf critères', and the example is qualified by 'proposant divers services'. The AIPD must therefore name which two criteria HIS processing meets — it is not automatic from the word 'jobboard'.

verdicts.claim: (e) The CNIL's formal mandatory-AIPD list names recruitment explicitly, under profiling
verdicts.why: Entry three of the list is verbatim as quoted: 'Traitements établissant des profils de personnes physiques à des fins de gestion des ressources humaines', criteria 'évaluation ou notation' and 'personnes dites « vulnérables »', examples including 'traitement visant à faciliter le recrutement, notamment grâce à un algorithme de sélection'. The second quote is verbatim from the recruitment guide: 'utilisation d'un traitement algorithmique prédictif permettant d'identifier sur une plateforme les offres d'emploi en adéquation avec les compétences affichées sur le CV du candidat'. The drift framing is right.
verdicts.correction: Minor provenance gap: the PDF at that URL is the bare table and carries no deliberation number or date, so '(deliberation of 11 October 2018)' came from elsewhere, not from the document read. The filename is 'v2', so confirm which version he is relying on before citing a date.

verdicts.claim: (e) The CNIL exemption list does not rescue him — it covers an organisation's own internal HR
verdicts.why: Verbatim: 'Traitements, mis en œuvre uniquement à des fins de ressources humaines et dans les conditions prévues par les textes applicables, pour la seule gestion du personnel des organismes qui emploient moins de 250 personnes, à l'exception du recours au profilage', with examples limited to payroll, training, canteen, expenses, working-time. The preamble is verbatim too: 'La mise en œuvre d'un traitement figurant sur la présente liste ne dispense pas le responsable de traitement du respect de ses autres obligations prévues par le RGPD... en cas de doute quant à la nécessité d'effectuer une AIPD il est recommandé d'en effectuer une.'

verdicts.claim: (e) The registre des activités de traitement is mandatory for him regardless of size
verdicts.why: Verbatim: the register obligation applies 'à tous les organismes, publics comme privés quelle que soit leur taille, et à tous les professionnels qui collectent des données à caractère personnel de manière non occasionnelle dans le cadre de leurs activités'. A job board's collection is by definition habitual, so the art. 30(5) small-organisation carve-out does not reach him. Art. 83(4) is the right tier for art. 30.

verdicts.claim: (f) Never collect or infer the article 9 categories; the ban covers inference, not just a form field
verdicts.why: Fiche n°19's closed list matches exactly, including genetic and biometric data used for unique identification. 'Le traitement des données sensibles... est en principe interdit' is verbatim, as is the cumulative test (an art. 9(2) exception AND an art. 6 basis) and the breadth of 'traitement' ('leur collecte, leur enregistrement, leur transmission, leur utilisation, leur accès'). RQTH as health data is verbatim CNIL doctrine in the same fiche.
verdicts.correction: The criminal cite is loose. For sensitive data the offence is article 226-19 code pénal, not '226-16 et seq.' generally. And both figures are statutory maxima that require the offence's own elements to be made out — they are not what a first over-collection incident costs.

verdicts.claim: (f) Photo: not sensitive, but the Défenseur des droits says requiring one can only be exceptional
verdicts.why: Both quotes are verbatim in 'Pour un recrutement sans discrimination' (Défenseur des droits, June 2019): 'De fait, exiger par exemple une photo sur un CV ne peut être qu'exceptionnel', and the anonymisation measure 'en supprimant les informations personnelles sans lien avec les compétences, notamment nom, prénom, adresse, âge, situation de famille et photo'. The CNIL's L1133-1 framing checks out, with the mannequin/spectacle example and the cites to 225-3 CP, L1121-1, L1133-1. The guide's own hospitality case study ('Talons aiguilles exigés') reinforces the point for his sector.
verdicts.correction: Note the addressee: the DDD guide speaks to employers ('En tant qu'employeur ou employeuse'), and it is a 2019 edition. The product advice (optional field, no completeness score, no employer-side filter) is sound but is his design choice, not a duty the guide imposes on a platform.

verdicts.claim: (f) Date of birth: age is a prohibited criterion but not an art. 9 datum, so the test is necessity under L1221-6
verdicts.why: Verbatim in fiche n°17: 'Pour exemple, le sexe ou l'âge ne sont pas des données dites sensibles.' The minor-work justification is the guide's own example: 'il est interdit de recruter des salariés de moins de 18 ans pour procéder à certaines catégories de travaux en raison du danger... (articles D. 4153-20 et s.)'. L5331-2 is verbatim as quoted.
verdicts.correction: One leg of the recommendation borrows from an unproven premise: the R5323-8 sex-and-age return only binds him if he is a private placement body (see the cross-cutting finding). The 'are you under 18?' design is right on the L1221-6 necessity test alone — do not justify it by the prefectural return until the placement question is settled.

verdicts.claim: (f) The CNIL has already enforced on over-collection in recruitment
verdicts.why: The CNIL page (25 April 2024) reports a mise en demeure, company not named, closed after compliance, over exactly the four categories quoted: 'informations relatives aux membres de sa famille', 'du lieu de naissance du candidat', over-granular nationality, and 'du montant des salaires perçus par le passé d'un candidat'. The claim's own hedge (confidence medium) is more cautious than the record requires.

verdicts.claim: (f)+(b) Article R5323-9 bars collecting the NIR outright; R5323-10 binds the whole data lifecycle to non-discrimination
verdicts.why: R5323-9 verbatim: 'L'organisme privé de placement peut collecter les données à caractère personnel relatives aux personnes à la recherche d'un emploi dans la mesure où elles sont nécessaires à l'activité de placement, à l'exception du numéro d'inscription au répertoire national d'identification des personnes physiques.' R5323-10 verbatim as quoted, referring to L1132-1 à L1132-4 and the loi du 6 janvier 1978.
verdicts.correction: Both articles address 'l'organisme privé de placement' and sit in Chapitre III « Placement privé », Section 1, alongside R5323-7's 'L'agence de placement privée'. They bind him only if the placement qualification holds. The practical advice (never collect the NIR) costs nothing either way.

verdicts.claim: (g) The silent blacklist is a 'liste d'exclusion' in the CNIL's sense and fiche n°15's requirements all bite
verdicts.why: Fiche n°15 is titled 'un recruteur peut-il mettre en œuvre des listes d'exclusion des CANDIDATS ?' It is doctrine on an employer's blacklist of job APPLICANTS — its worked examples are ex-employees dismissed for faute grave, candidates who arrived late, candidates who behaved violently at interview. The claim applies it to a list of EMPLOYERS, in the opposite direction, and calls it 'the governing doctrine'. The quoted sentence is verbatim ('des motifs objectifs opposables à la personne concernée, faisant abstraction de tout jugement de valeur ou d'appréciation subjective, et représentant un certain niveau de gravité') but its grammatical subject is the inscription of a candidate. The two-moment information duty, the legitimate-interest-only basis, the dropdown-over-free-text advice and the no-fully-automated-exclusion rule are all verbatim in the fiche — as rules about candidates.
verdicts.correction: Present it as a read-across, not a rule: fiche n°15 is the closest CNIL doctrine and the safest template, and the underlying duties (lawfulness, transparency, limited retention) are general RGPD and do transfer — but only once the record identifies a natural person. If the record is about the establishment, the fiche is not engaged at all. The claim's own 'safer design' finding concedes this and contradicts this one.

verdicts.claim: (g) The churn blacklist independently lands on the CNIL's formal mandatory-AIPD list
verdicts.why: The entry is verbatim — 'Traitements impliquant le profilage des personnes pouvant aboutir à leur exclusion du bénéfice d'un contrat ou à la suspension voire à la rupture de celui-ci', criteria 'évaluation ou notation' and 'croisement ou combinaison d'ensembles de données'. But the claim's conclusion ('route one — mandatory by list, no balancing argument available') skips the two conditions the entry itself sets. It requires profiling of a NATURAL PERSON, and it requires the crossing or combining of data sets; the list's own examples are credit scoring, behavioural analysis on a social network, and payment-fraud detection. A sole trader keeping a structured count of re-listings against a SIRET is neither profiling within art. 4(4) nor, if no natural person is identified, personal data at all.
verdicts.correction: Say: this entry is what the blacklist becomes IF he records it against named gérants and lets a rule decide admission. Whether the entry is engaged is precisely the argument the claim says is unavailable. Building it as establishment-level counts keeps him off route one.

verdicts.claim: (g) Where the churn signal comes from candidates, article 14 applies — inform the employer's representative within one month
verdicts.why: The one-month rule is verbatim on the CNIL page ('dans un délai raisonnable après avoir obtenu les données à caractère personnel, mais ne dépassant pas un mois'), and the extra items (categories of data, source) are correct. Two things are missing. Art. 14(5) carries exceptions the finding does not mention, including where the data subject already has the information and where provision 'se révèle impossible ou exigerait des efforts disproportionnés'. And the duty only exists if the record identifies a natural person — the same gate the claim's own safer-design finding builds around.
verdicts.correction: Restate as conditional: art. 14 bites only on employer-side records naming an individual, and 14(5) may soften even then. The practical conclusion the claim draws — an anonymous worker-reporting channel is legally awkward — survives and is the part worth keeping.

verdicts.claim: (g) Safer design: keep the churn signal as data about the establishment, never a named person
verdicts.why: The CNIL definition page says verbatim that 'des coordonnées d'entreprises (par exemple, l'entreprise « Compagnie A » avec son adresse postale, le numéro de téléphone de son standard et un courriel de contact générique...) ne sont pas, en principe, des données personnelles', and sets the test as identifiability, direct or indirect, including by combining data. The dropdown-over-free-text advice is verbatim from fiche n°15. The claim correctly flags this as its own reading rather than a stated rule, and correctly keeps the single-operator identifiability risk.

verdicts.claim: Free for candidates is a criminal prohibition — six months and €3,750
verdicts.why: Both texts are verbatim, contrary to the claim's own 'medium' hedge. L5321-3: 'Aucune rétribution, directe ou indirecte, ne peut être exigée des personnes à la recherche d'un emploi en contrepartie de la fourniture de services de placement', with exceptions only for L7121-9 (artistes du spectacle) and L222-6 code du sport (agents sportifs). L5324-1: 'Le fait d'exiger une rétribution, directe ou indirecte, des personnes à la recherche d'un emploi... est puni d'un emprisonnement de six mois et d'une amende de 3 750 euros.' The 'indirecte' reading (premium candidate tier, paid CV boost) is sound.
verdicts.correction: Upgrade the confidence, and add the one condition: the ban attaches to 'services de placement'. It is the single rule he should treat as absolute regardless, since the downside of complying is nil.

verdicts.claim: His curation has a ceiling: L5321-2 forbids refusing placement service to an EMPLOYER on a discrimination ground
verdicts.why: Verbatim and complete: 'Aucun service de placement ne peut être refusé à une personne à la recherche d'un emploi ou à un employeur fondé sur l'un des motifs de discrimination énumérés à l'article L. 1132-1. Aucune offre d'emploi ne peut comporter de référence à l'une des caractéristiques mentionnées à cet article.' Both limbs are there, and the reasoning — that an unwritten discretionary door is the structure in which a discriminatory refusal cannot be disproved — is sound advice.
verdicts.correction: Two additions. L5321-2 carries no penalty of its own in L5324-1; the enforcement routes are article 225-2 code pénal and the L5323-1 administrative closure. And it applies only on the placement qualification, which nothing in the brief establishes.

verdicts.claim: Publishing the offers carries its own criminal exposure: a misleading job ad is one year and €37,500, owed by him 'TODAY, as a pure publisher'
verdicts.why: The prohibition in L5331-3 is quoted correctly, and L5334-1 does set one year and €37,500. But L5334-1's final paragraph — which the finding does not quote — allocates the offence away from him: 'L'annonceur qui a demandé la diffusion de l'offre est responsable de l'infraction commise. Le directeur de la publication ou le fournisseur du service ayant communiqué l'offre au public est responsable lorsqu'il a agi sans demande expresse d'insertion de l'offre émanant de l'annonceur.' His entire model is express, paid insertion requests from named restaurants. The statute puts the offence on the restaurant and reaches him only if he publishes an offer no advertiser expressly asked him to insert. The claim's stated reasoning — 'the text targets the act of causing an offer to be published, so a vetting platform cannot treat ad content as purely the restaurant's problem' — is the opposite of what the article says.
verdicts.correction: Rewrite: the misleading-ad offence sits with the restaurant. He inherits it only where he originates or alters a listing without an express insertion request — which is also the line that would make him an éditeur. Practical consequence: keep a per-listing record of the employer's express submission, and never rewrite ad copy. The vetting promise creates real exposure, but through deceptive-practice and civil liability, not L5334-1.

verdicts.claim: Three more publishing rules bind him: every offer dated, no upper age limit, no foreign language
verdicts.why: All three verbatim. L5332-1: 'Toute offre d'emploi publiée ou diffusée est datée.' L5331-2: 'Il est interdit de faire publier... une insertion d'offres d'emploi... comportant la mention d'une limite d'âge supérieure exigée du postulant à un emploi.' L5331-4 first paragraph as quoted, with the exception for a foreign term having no French equivalent requiring 'une description suffisamment détaillée pour ne pas induire en erreur au sens de l'article L. 5331-3'. These sit in Title III and bind whoever publishes, so they do not depend on the placement question.
verdicts.correction: Two paragraphs of L5331-4 are omitted and both matter in a resort: the rule covers work performed in France 'quelle que soit la nationalité de l'auteur de l'offre ou de l'employeur', even where perfect command of a foreign language is a condition of the post; and 'les directeurs de publications et les personnes responsables de moyens de communication utilisant, en tout ou partie, une langue étrangère peuvent, en France, recevoir des offres d'emploi rédigées dans cette langue' — relevant if he ever runs an English-language section.

verdicts.claim: His paid-listing model is expressly carved out of the ban on selling job offers
verdicts.why: L5331-1 verbatim: 'Il est interdit de vendre des offres ou des demandes d'emploi, quel que soit le support utilisé. Toutefois, cette interdiction ne fait pas obstacle à l'insertion, à titre onéreux, d'offres ou de demandes d'emploi dans une publication ou un autre moyen de communication payant.' The boundary the claim draws — he sells insertion in the medium, never the offers or applications as a data product — is right.
verdicts.correction: One ambiguity the finding smooths over: 'payant' grammatically qualifies 'moyen de communication', and his site is free to the public. The literal reading is in tension with a free website; the settled practice and the provision's target (selling offers to job-seekers) point the other way, and L5321-3 covers the real mischief. Do not present the carve-out as airtight — present the candidate-side ban as the operative rule.

verdicts.claim: If a restaurant advertises anonymously, L5332-2 makes him the holder of its identity
verdicts.why: Both paragraphs verbatim. First: an employer placing an anonymous offer 'fait connaître son nom ou sa raison sociale et son adresse au directeur de la publication ou au responsable du moyen de communication'. Second: where an agency or 'tout autre intermédiaire' requests the insertion, that intermediary supplies the employer's details. He is the responsable du moyen de communication, so the product consequence (mandatory identity field in the back office behind a blind listing) follows directly.

verdicts.claim: He owes an annual statistical return to the préfet before 31 March
verdicts.why: The content of R5323-8 is right: turnover attributable to placement for the past year related where applicable to total turnover, and the number of job-seekers broken down by sex and age who were received, placed, and on file at 31 December, on a form set by ministerial order. But the article opens on 'L'organisme de droit privé exerçant une fonction de placement', and the neighbouring R5323-7 reads 'L'agence de placement privée adresse régulièrement au préfet des renseignements d'ordre statistique sur son activité de placement.' Whether a curated, free-to-candidates job board is such a body is the premise nothing in the brief establishes, and it is the load-bearing premise for five other findings.
verdicts.correction: Add the fact that resolves half his confusion: the déclaration préalable that used to accompany this regime was abolished (décret n° 2012-539 du 20 avril 2012 repealed R5323-1 to R5323-6), so there is no registration step to look for. And note the return asks for placements MADE — a passive board that never learns who was hired cannot populate row (b), which is itself evidence the section was written for agencies, not boards.

verdicts.claim: Breaching the placement principles exposes him to administrative closure of up to three months
verdicts.why: L5323-1 verbatim: labour-inspection officials may record breaches of Chapter I, and 'Lorsque l'activité de placement est exercée en méconnaissance de ces dispositions ou en cas d'atteinte à l'ordre public, l'autorité administrative peut, après mise en demeure, ordonner la fermeture de l'organisme en cause pour une durée n'excédant pas trois mois.' Chapter I is L5321-1 to L5321-3, as the claim says.
verdicts.correction: Three months is the statutory maximum and it follows a mise en demeure — he gets a formal warning and a chance to comply first. The 'existential for a seasonal business' framing is fair as a worst case but should not be presented as the expected outcome. Conditional, again, on the placement qualification.

verdicts.claim: Beyond RGPD fines, French criminal law attaches five years and €300,000 to serious data offences
verdicts.why: The CNIL penalties page gives exactly these: 226-16, 226-17, 226-18 and 226-22 at five years and €300,000; negligent disclosure at three years and €100,000; obstructing the CNIL at one year and €15,000. The claim's provenance caveat (article texts received as fragments in a summary) is honest and does not affect the figures.
verdicts.correction: These are maxima for made-out offences with their own elements — 226-18 requires collection 'par un moyen frauduleux, déloyal ou illicite', 226-17 a failure to take the security measures required. None follows automatically from an RGPD non-compliance. Worth saying plainly to a 19-year-old, or he will read this as five years for a bad privacy policy.

verdicts.claim: Curating WHO may list does not by itself make him an éditeur — authorship of the content does
verdicts.why: The two definitions are verbatim on the page: hébergeur is one who 'stocke des écrits, des sons, des images ou des vidéos réalisés par des tiers', directeur de publication is the person 'en charge de la publication d'un contenu éditorial'. But the page does not adjudicate curation, as the claim admits, and the claim's bridging proposition — 'admission control is a decision about counterparties, not about content' — is its own construction with no authority behind it. The counter-argument is live: the hosting exemption is lost where the provider plays an active role giving it knowledge of or control over the content, and vetting which employers may appear, combined with a public quality promise, is materially closer to that line than the finding allows.
verdicts.correction: Do not give him this as a rule he can rely on. Give him the two behaviours that are safe either way — the employer types the offer, he never touches the words; normalisation happens through structured fields the employer fills, never prose he drafts — and tell him the qualification question is unsettled and fact-specific. Note also that the LCEN framework is now overlaid by DSA articles 4-6.

verdicts.claim: As a hébergeur he is liable only once notified and failing to act promptly
verdicts.why: The page confirms the structure: accessible reporting mechanism, prompt removal or blocking of flagged illegal content, notification of the competent authorities, with liability on failure to remove reported illegal content or acting with knowledge of illegality. The penalties are as stated (one year and €250,000 for a natural person; up to 6% of worldwide turnover for a legal person), and the identification-data retention duty is confirmed, at one year, since 21 October 2025, under décret n° 2025-980 du 15 octobre 2025. The build-the-takedown-log-on-day-one advice is the right operational read.
verdicts.correction: The 6%-of-turnover figure is the legal-person ceiling; as a sole trader he is on the natural-person track. And this protection is only as good as the éditeur question above — it is conditional on his staying a host.

verdicts.claim: Minimum DSA compliance for a micro platform: contact points, clear CGU, notice-and-action, statement of reasons, criminal-offence notification
verdicts.why: Arcom's own mapping matches: intermediary services carry articles 9-15 (injunctions, contact points, EU legal representative, terms of service, transparency reports); hosting services carry article 16 notification mechanisms, article 17 statements of reasons for moderation, article 18 notification of judicial authorities. Subtracting the micro exemptions leaves exactly the set the claim names, and no EU legal representative is needed since he is established in France. The 'weekend of work, not a compliance department' framing is accurate.

verdicts.claim: He is exempt from the heaviest DSA blocks: transparency reports, Articles 20-28, and trader traceability
verdicts.why: The exemption sentence is verbatim on Arcom's page, with the thresholds: providers 'that can be qualified as microenterprises or small enterprises (i.e. those employing fewer than 50 people and whose annual turnover or annual balance sheet total does not exceed €10 million) and that are not very large online platforms... are exempt from certain obligations of the Regulation (cf. Articles 15 (2), 19 and 29)'. The claim's mapping of what each hook covers is its own, as disclosed, and it is correct.
verdicts.correction: One caveat in his favour that the advice gets backwards: DSA article 19(2) continues the exemption for twelve months after a provider ceases to qualify as micro or small. 'Re-check the moment headcount or turnover moves' is right as hygiene but he does not lose the exemption on the day he crosses.

verdicts.claim: DSA breaches are sanctioned up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover
verdicts.why: Verbatim on the page: 'En cas de violation du DSA, l'amende qui sera infligée à la plateforme ne pourra excéder 6 % de son chiffre d'affaires mondial annuel', with the CGU duties in the regulation's own register — platforms must 'informer leurs utilisateurs de toute modification importante de leurs conditions générales' and present terms 'de manière simple, intelligible, aisément abordable et sans ambiguïté'. The page is dated 28 October 2022, updated 13 February 2024, and independently confirms the micro/small exemptions.

verdicts.claim: Even if a jobseeker is not a 'consommateur', the misleading-practice rules still reach him
verdicts.why: The bridging article is right and the claim guessed it correctly: article L121-5 code de la consommation extends articles L121-2 to L121-4 to practices aimed at professionals and non-professionals. Everything else in the finding is mis-sourced. The cited page is about Omnibus e-commerce enforcement (2 June 2022): its 'deux ans d'emprisonnement et 300 000 € d'amende' is quoted for FALSE REVIEWS and misleading price reductions, and its '4 % du chiffre d'affaires moyen annuel' is the CLAUSES ABUSIVES uplift, not the deceptive-practice one. The claim half-spots this ('plainly a mis-read') but keeps the figures. And L111-7's own applicability to a free candidate-facing service is asserted, never shown.
verdicts.correction: The correct penalty is article L132-2 code de la consommation: two years and €300,000 for pratiques commerciales trompeuses, raisable proportionally to the benefit derived to 10% of average annual turnover over the last three years or 50% of the expenditure on the practice — AND raised to five years and €750,000 where the offence is committed through an online public communication service. That last aggravation is the one that actually fits a website, and the finding misses it entirely. The substantive advice (disclose paid ranking; describe what a paid slot delivers, not what it achieves) stands and is the part to keep.

verdicts.claim: Job offers he publishes must be dated, in French, and free of false or discriminatory wording
verdicts.why: The page carries all of it: publication date per L5332-1, French drafting per L5331-4, 'allégations fausses ou susceptibles d'induire en erreur' per L5331-3, discriminatory wording per L5321-2, with one year and €37,500 and three years and €45,000 respectively. The gendered-title and H/F point is a real live trap in hospitality and the form-validation advice is good.
verdicts.correction: The page is employer-facing (entreprendre.service-public.gouv.fr) and the duties it lists are the employer's. The €37,500 figure carries the L5334-1 annonceur allocation set out above — it is the restaurant's exposure on an offer it expressly asked him to insert. The three years and €45,000 is article 225-2 code pénal and falls on whoever discriminates, which on a refusal to list could be him.

verdicts.claim: Silent de-listing collides with the DSA duty to give a statement of reasons
verdicts.why: The article 17 duty sits in Arcom's hosting block (articles 16-18), and the micro exemption hooks are articles 15(2), 19 and 29 — article 19 reaches only the online-platform block at articles 20-28. So article 17 applies to him at any size, and it is triggered by restrictions imposed because content is illegal or incompatible with the terms and conditions, which is exactly a CGU-based de-listing. The distinction drawn — 'private is fine, silent is not' — is right, and the workaround (fixed seasonal terms, the standard as a renewal criterion in the CGV, simply decline to renew) is sound, since a contract not extended at its term is not a content restriction.

verdicts.claim: The real exposure if a candidate is harmed is the promise, not the hosting regime
verdicts.why: The core judgement is right and is the most useful thing in the brief: promise the process, never the outcome; 'chaque établissement est visité avant publication' is defensible, 'uniquement des employeurs qui traitent bien leurs équipes' is a guarantee he would have to defend. The cited page contributes only a penalty figure, and a mis-attributed one at that. But route two — 'employment law: none of it reaches him' — is stated too flatly and contradicts the brief's own other findings: if the placement qualification holds, L5321-2, L5321-3 and the L5323-1 closure power are Code du travail duties that reach him directly. He is not an employer and owes no safety duty to a candidate; that is not the same as employment law not reaching him.
verdicts.correction: Fix the internal contradiction and correct the figure per the L132-2 finding above. Article 1240 code civil is correctly self-flagged as unverified and is in fact the right article for general civil liability.

verdicts.claim: Trader-traceability and marketplace rules do not apply — he is not a consumer-trader marketplace
verdicts.why: Two independent grounds, both sound. DSA articles 30-32 apply to online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders, and a candidate and an employer forming an employment relationship is not that; and article 29 exempts micro and small enterprises in any case, which Arcom's quoted exemption sentence confirms. Collecting the SIRET anyway, for contracting and for proving which legal person submitted which offer, is the right call — and it is what L5332-2 independently requires.

verdicts.claim: Pay transparency is about to become a content requirement for every offer on his site
verdicts.why: Verbatim on the page: 'Dès la phase de recrutement, les employeurs devront informer les candidats à un emploi de la rémunération proposée ou d'une fourchette de rémunération.' The status is stated correctly and conservatively: the bill transposing directive (UE) 2023/970 of 10 May 2023 was presented to the Council of Ministers on 10 September 2026 and 'doit désormais être examiné par le Sénat et l'Assemblée nationale'. Not yet binding, no penalty to state — the claim says exactly that.
verdicts.correction: Note the addressee: the duty will bind employers, not the platform. Building the mandatory pay field is a product decision that anticipates it, and the differentiation argument ('the site where every offer states the pay') is the stronger reason to do it now.

verdicts.claim: (a) The protected criteria in employment are in L1132-1 — around 25 grounds, covering recruitment as well as employment
verdicts.why: The article as published covers exclusion from a recruitment procedure, a nomination, a stage or a période de formation en entreprise, and the ground list matches the claim's enumeration item for item, including the recent additions (identité de genre, particulière vulnérabilité résultant de la situation économique, lieu de résidence, domiciliation bancaire, capacité à s'exprimer dans une langue autre que le français, qualité de lanceur d'alerte ou de facilitateur). The penalty note is verbatim from the Justice guide: 'la violation de ce principe général ne constitue pas en tant que telle une infraction pénale.' The two hospitality traps flagged (apparence physique, lieu de résidence) are well chosen.

verdicts.claim: (a) Article 225-1 code pénal extends discrimination to distinctions between LEGAL PERSONS based on their members' criteria
verdicts.why: Verbatim in the Justice guide: 'Constitue également une discrimination toute distinction opérée entre les personnes morales selon les mêmes critères concernant leurs membres ou certains d'entre eux.' The 225-2 acts list is verbatim, all five, including 'A refuser la fourniture d'un bien ou d'un service' and 'A entraver l'exercice normal d'une activité économique quelconque'. The penalties check out against service-public F38175: three years and €45,000, five years and €75,000 in a lieu accueillant du public, €225,000 and €375,000 for a legal person. The reasoning — that this is what makes a declined restaurant's discrimination claim legally coherent — is correct and is the strongest argument in the brief for written admission criteria.
verdicts.correction: The guide is older than 'an older edition' conveys: the PDF was produced in September 2010 and still discusses the HALDE, abolished in 2011. Its 225-1 criteria list omits several grounds now in the article. Cite the acts and penalties from it, never the criteria list. And the €225,000 legal-person figure (art. 131-38/131-39) is not his exposure — he is a sole trader on the natural-person scale.

audits.overall:
Every cited source opened and every quoted sentence checked. No claim asserts Legifrance was opened — all Code du travail text comes from code.travail.gouv.fr (the Ministry's Code du travail numérique), which is clean. Three CNIL PDFs and two others had to be text-extracted locally because the fetch returned encoded PDF; all quoted passages were then found verbatim, with the exceptions noted below.

ONE OUTRIGHT ERROR. The misleading-job-advertisement finding is backwards. L5334-1's final paragraph — not quoted in the brief — reads: "L'annonceur qui a demandé la diffusion de l'offre est responsable de l'infraction commise. Le directeur de la publication ou le fournisseur du service ayant communiqué l'offre au public est responsable lorsqu'il a agi sans demande expresse d'insertion de l'offre émanant de l'annonceur." His model is express, paid insertion requests from named restaurants, so the one year and €37,500 sits with the restaurant. The brief states the opposite and marks it "TODAY, as a pure publisher" at high confidence. This is the employer-rule-as-platform-rule failure in its purest form, and it is the one finding that would send him building the wrong thing.

THE LOAD-BEARING PREMISE IS NEVER ESTABLISHED. Six findings — L5321-2, L5321-3 with L5324-1, the L5323-1 closure power, R5323-8, R5323-9, R5323-10 — bind "l'organisme privé de placement" or "l'organisme de droit privé exerçant une fonction de placement", and R5323-7 opens on "L'agence de placement privée". L5321-1 defines placement as "fournir, à titre habituel, des services visant à rapprocher les offres et les demandes d'emploi, sans que la personne assurant cette activité ne devienne partie aux relations de travail susceptibles d'en découler" — a board plausibly fits, but no source cited in the brief says a job board is a placement body, and none was found that does. The brief presents all six as settled "TODAY" obligations at high confidence. Either the qualification holds, and the brief has a gap it should close for him — the whole R5323-7 to R5323-11 section applies, and the déclaration préalable that used to accompany the regime was repealed in 2012, so there is no registration step to hunt for — or it does not, and six findings fall together. What does NOT depend on it is Title III (L5331-1 to L5334-1, L5332-1, L5332-2): those bind whoever publishes, which is the correctly-grounded half of the employment-law lane.

TWO DOCTRINES POINTED THE WRONG WAY. Fiche n°15 of the CNIL guide is titled "un recruteur peut-il mettre en œuvre des listes d'exclusion des CANDIDATS ?" — an employer's blacklist of job applicants, worked through examples of ex-employees dismissed for faute grave. The brief applies it to a list of EMPLOYERS and calls it "the governing doctrine" whose every requirement "bites". The quoted sentence is verbatim but its subject is the inscription of a candidate. The read-across is defensible and is the safest template available; presenting it as the rule is not. Separately, the formal-list entry on "profilage... pouvant aboutir à leur exclusion du bénéfice d'un contrat" is quoted correctly but its two conditions — profiling of a natural person, and crossing or combining data sets, with credit scoring and fraud detection as its examples — are skipped, so "no balancing argument available" is exactly wrong. The brief's own safer-design finding contradicts both.

CV-LIBRARY LEGAL BASIS IS MIS-STATED. "It is now consent, not legitimate interest" does not survive the guide's own table, which lists both for that purpose, nor Hypothèse n°1, which is his exact case — a candidate who "demande à rejoindre un vivier de candidats (intégration de jobboards)" — and says that candidate "peut être considéré comme ayant consenti, par la même occasion". The separate unbundled opt-in is good practice, not a stated requirement. What IS verbatim and worth keeping: "l'acceptation des conditions générales d'utilisation ne peut suffire".

WHAT HELD UP. The CNIL material is otherwise accurate and often quoted word-perfect: the requalification warning, the consent-cannot-affect-chances boundary, the full article 13 list plus the three Code du travail duties including "aucune information... par un dispositif qui n'a pas été porté préalablement à sa connaissance", the DPO analysis, both AIPD routes with the jobboard example verbatim, the exemption list and its preamble, the register, the article 9 list, the 2024 mise en demeure. The Défenseur des droits photo quotes are verbatim from the June 2019 guide. The Arcom DSA mapping and the micro/small exemption sentence are verbatim, and the article 17 statement-of-reasons point is right — it sits in the hosting block that article 19 does not touch, so "private is fine, silent is not" is correct, with a sound non-renewal workaround. The 225-1 second-paragraph point about legal persons is verbatim and is the single best argument in the brief for writing his admission criteria down. The pay-transparency status is stated conservatively and correctly.

PENALTY HYGIENE. Maxima are repeatedly quoted as his exposure: €20m/4%, €300,000, €225,000 for a personne morale, 6% of worldwide turnover. He is a sole trader with no turnover yet. Two cites are wrong on their face — the sensitive-data offence is article 226-19, not "226-16 et seq.", and the consumer figures in the misleading-practice finding come from a page about false reviews and abusive clauses. The correct deceptive-practice penalty is article L132-2 code de la consommation: two years and €300,000, uplift to 10% of average annual turnover over three years or 50% of the expenditure, and raised to five years and €750,000 when committed through an online public communication service — the aggravation that actually fits a website, which the brief misses entirely.

THE ONE THING TO TELL HIM FIRST. The hébergeur/éditeur finding is presented as a rule and is not one — the cited page defines both terms and adjudicates nothing, as the finding admits. Against it: the hosting exemption is lost where the provider plays an active role giving it knowledge of or control over the content, and vetting which employers may appear, plus a public promise about their conditions, sits closer to that line than "admission control is a decision about counterparties" allows. Two behaviours are safe either way and should be the instruction he gets: the employer types the offer and he never touches the words, and normalisation happens through structured fields the employer fills, never prose he drafts.

THREE SYSTEMATIC DEFECTS RUN THROUGH THE CORPUS.

(1) The penal chapter was read at L-level only. Article R5334-1 exists and reads: « Le fait de méconnaître les dispositions des articles L. 5331-1, L. 5331-2, L. 5331-4, L. 5332-1 et L. 5332-3, relatives aux conditions de publication et de diffusion des offres d'emploi, est puni de l'amende prévue pour les contraventions de la 3e classe. » Five separate claims assert that these articles carry "no penalty" because L5334-1 does not name them. They do carry one — a contravention de 3e classe is a criminal penalty in French law (€450 for an individual, €2,250 for a company at the quintuple of article 131-41 code pénal). The corpus contradicts itself here: one Lane 6 claim cites R5334-1 correctly and then wrongly calls France Travail's citation of it a "miscitation".
Source: https://code.travail.gouv.fr/code-du-travail/r5334-1

(2) France Travail's own platform rules are restated as statutory duties on him. "L'employeur final doit être connu de France Travail" is a condition of depositing an offer on francetravail.fr. It binds depositors on that platform, not a private publisher. Two claims convert it into a know-your-employer duty on him, and one converts the guide's section 06 into a duty to screen every ad against the whole of labour law. Only the L5331-3 bridge (an ad whose own stated terms are unlawful is a misleading ad) actually binds him, and the corpus does establish that bridge soundly.

(3) Maxima are quoted as his exposure, and one is quoted for the wrong offence. 37 500 €, 45 000 €, 250 000 €, 1 250 000 €, 6 % of worldwide turnover — every figure in the corpus is a statutory ceiling for the worst case of that offence, presented without that qualification to a 19-year-old sole trader. The 1 250 000 € figure is worse than unqualified: it attaches to DSA article 18, which Arcom's own page limits to « soupçon d'infraction pénale susceptible de porter ou ayant porté atteinte à la vie ou à la sécurité de tiers ». A fraudulent job ad is not that. The claim that reporting scam listings is an article 18 obligation carrying that fine is simply wrong.

FOUR MORE FINDINGS THAT CHANGE HIS DECISIONS.

STALE — the HCR pay claims were overtaken on 1 June 2026. The SMIC rose to €12.31/h. Avenant n°33's niveau I échelon 1 is €12.00 and the first four conventional rungs (€12.00-€12.28) now sit BELOW the SMIC. The claim that apprentice pay in the branch is "above the legal minimum" because niveau I exceeds the SMIC was true against €11.88 and is false today — exactly at the entry-level grades that are his entire inventory. Any ad-screening rule built on the conventional grid will under-detect illegal pay. Screen against the higher of the two, recomputed at each SMIC move.
Sources: https://www.info.gouv.fr/actualite/le-smic-revalorise-le-1er-juin-2026 and https://code.travail.gouv.fr/contribution/1979-quel-est-le-salaire-minimum

REFUTED — curation does not erode the hosting shield, and DSA article 7 says so. Article 7 ("Voluntary own-initiative investigations and legal compliance") provides that intermediaries are not ineligible for the article 6 exemption SOLELY because they carry out good-faith own-initiative investigations to detect and remove illegal content. Two claims — the "curation costs him the hosting shield" one and the « en toute connaissance de cause » erosion one — build a worry the legislature specifically foreclosed. His inspections do not by themselves make him an éditeur or fix him with knowledge. What does flip his position is writing or rewriting ad copy, which is the L5334-1 "without express insertion request" limb, and the corpus gets that part right.

OVERCONFIDENT — "he is a placement operator TODAY" is billed as THE CENTRAL FINDING at high confidence. No authority applying L5321-1 to a job board was produced, and the corpus's own Lane 6 twin rates the same proposition medium-high. There is a real counter-argument nobody raised: L5331-1's carve-out for paid insertion of offers sits in Titre III (diffusion et publicité des offres), a regime distinct from Titre II (placement), and French law has long treated the presse d'annonces d'emploi as the Titre III animal. Fortunately nothing turns on it — the candidate-fee ban reaches him either way (L5321-3 if placement, L5331-1's ban on selling offers if not). Say it is probable and that the advice is the same either way; do not say it is settled.

MISSED — L5332-3 and interim agencies. R5334-1 penalises L5332-3, which requires any ad from an entreprise de travail temporaire to state its name AND its character as an ETT. The corpus never mentions this article, and alpine seasonal hiring runs heavily through interim. That is a listing-form field he does not have.

NOTES ON METHOD. No claim asserts Legifrance was opened; two expressly say it was not, which is correct. code.travail.gouv.fr served me L5321-2 under a copyright guard and refused verbatim reproduction, so I pinned that text through the search index instead — the claim's quote matches. The France Travail PDF ("Repères juridiques sur les offres d'emploi") exceeded the 10MB fetch ceiling, so every claim resting on its internal wording — the 52-page/November 2025 identity, the liability matrix, the section 06 text, the CDD list quote — is unverified by me. Its substantive propositions that I could check independently (R5334-1, L5334-1, D1242-1 4°) all hold. Several source_quote fields are not verbatim: L5321-1's omits a whole sentence ("Les entreprises de travail temporaire peuvent fournir des services de placement au sens du présent article"), L1133-2's omits the 1° and 2° that follow, L5331-2's omits the second paragraph that is the entire exception, L6222-1's omits the 15-year-old route, and the vigilance quote contains a corruption ("L'obligation s'déclenche") showing it was not copied from the page.

verdicts.claim: (b) Aiming the PLATFORM at young people is lawful — Article L1133-2 names « favoriser leur insertion professionnelle » as a legitimate aim.
verdicts.why: The quote is genuine but truncated — the article continues with 1° and 2°, which show what it is actually for: bans on access to employment protecting young and older workers, and maximum recruitment ages justified by training or a reasonable pre-retirement period. L1133-2 is the authorised-difference carve-out to L1132-1, and L1132-1 binds those who make employment decisions. It is a defence for an EMPLOYER's age-based treatment, invoked here to authorise a PLATFORM's marketing. That is the employer-rule-as-platform-rule error. Choosing to write guides for 18-year-olds is not a « différence de traitement » under L1132-1 at all, so no carve-out is needed; and the rule that does govern his door is L5321-2, which the corpus locates correctly elsewhere.
verdicts.correction: The conclusion holds — targeting young people editorially is lawful — but not because of L1133-2. It is lawful because marketing to an audience is not a difference of treatment in employment. Cite L5321-2 as the binding rule on the door and drop L1133-2, which he cannot rely on and would not need. The operational advice (never a filter, never an employer-side age facet) is sound and is the part to keep.

verdicts.claim: (b) An EMPLOYER's ad stating an upper age limit is prohibited by L5331-2, and the ban binds whoever publishes it. PENALTY: L5334-1 does not penalise L5331-2, so the age-limit ban carries no criminal fine.
verdicts.why: The first limb is right and I confirmed it verbatim: « ou de diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public » reaches his site, and paragraph 2 of L5331-2 contains exactly the exception the claim describes (« Cette interdiction ne concerne pas les offres qui fixent des conditions d'âge imposées par les dispositions légales »), though the source_quote omits that paragraph. The penalty limb is false. R5334-1 penalises L5331-2 expressly. Telling him the age-limit ban carries no fine of its own understates his direct exposure to zero when it is not zero.
verdicts.correction: Breach of L5331-2 is punished by R5334-1 as a contravention de 3e classe: €450 maximum for a natural person, €2,250 for a company (quintuple, art. 131-41 code pénal). Small, but it is a criminal penalty that lands on the diffuser directly and is NOT covered by L5334-1's express-request allocation, which only allocates the L5331-3 and L5331-5 offences. The 225-2 5° route at 3 ans / 45 000 € is correctly identified but is a ceiling for the worst case, not his expected exposure.

verdicts.claim: (b) The lawful age exception he will meet is apprenticeship: Article L6222-1 sets 16 to 29 révolus.
verdicts.why: The quoted sentence is real but it is the first of three paragraphs. The article continues: « les jeunes âgés d'au moins quinze ans peuvent débuter un contrat d'apprentissage s'ils justifient avoir accompli la scolarité du premier cycle de l'enseignement secondaire », plus a decree-governed route for those turning 15 before year end. And L6222-2 lifts the 29-year ceiling in five cases: progression to a higher diploma, contract broken for reasons outside the apprentice's control or temporary incapacity, recognised travailleur handicapé, a business creation or takeover project requiring the qualification, and listed high-level athletes. So the boundary is neither 16 nor 29.
verdicts.correction: Do not encode 16-29 as a rule anywhere in the product. A 15-year-old who has finished collège is eligible, and five categories are eligible above 29 — a travailleur handicapé with no upper limit at all, which makes a hard 29 cap a disability-discrimination surface. Publish the contract type and hold no age boundary in software. The practical advice (« Contrat d'apprentissage », never an age range) is right; the arithmetic under it is not.

verdicts.claim: THE CENTRAL FINDING — He is a placement operator TODAY as a pure publisher, under L5321-1, at high confidence.
verdicts.why: The article text checks out, though the source_quote drops the third sentence: « Les entreprises de travail temporaire peuvent fournir des services de placement au sens du présent article. » The qualification does not. No authority applying L5321-1 to a job board was produced, and the corpus's own Lane 6 twin of this claim rates the identical proposition medium-high while this one calls it THE CENTRAL FINDING at high. A counter-argument goes unmentioned: the paid-insertion carve-out he relies on elsewhere sits in Titre III (Diffusion et publicité des offres et demandes d'emploi), a regime parallel to Titre II (Placement), which is why the classified-ads press has historically been treated under Titre III rather than as placement.
verdicts.correction: State it as probable, not settled, and say why it does not matter: the one rule he must not break — no money from candidates — reaches him on either qualification, through L5321-3 if he is placement and through L5331-1's ban on selling job offers if he is only a Titre III publisher. Bpifrance Création does list « organisme privé de placement de personnel » as a régime with no qualification requirement and no formality beyond the guichet unique, which is corroboration that the category is real and that entering it costs him nothing.

verdicts.claim: (c) Article L5321-2 — no placement service may be refused to a job seeker OR TO AN EMPLOYER on an L1132-1 ground; and no offer may reference those characteristics.
verdicts.why: code.travail.gouv.fr applied a copyright guard and refused verbatim reproduction of this article, so I pinned it through the search index, which returns the same two sentences the claim quotes. The analysis is the best in the corpus: L5321-2 creates no right to be listed, it forbids one class of reasons for refusing, and its second sentence is a standing duty on what he publishes. The examples of lawful refusal grounds (churn, unpaid overtime, unanswered questionnaire) are correctly outside L1132-1.
verdicts.correction: One refinement worth giving him. L5321-2's grounds are L1132-1's list, which is wider than article 225-1 code pénal's. So a refusal can breach L5321-2 without being the crime of article 225-2 — the closure power of L5323-1 and a civil claim are the realistic consequences, and 3 ans / 45 000 € (225 000 € for a company) is the ceiling of the narrower criminal route, not his expected exposure.

verdicts.claim: (c) Article L5323-1 — labour inspectors record breaches of Chapitre Ier, and the administration may order closure for up to three months after mise en demeure.
verdicts.why: Verbatim match on both paragraphs, and the article does say « chapitre Ier » rather than « présent chapitre », which is what makes it reach L5321-1 to L5321-3. Chapitre Ier is indeed three articles — Legifrance's section index reads « Chapitre Ier : Principes. (Articles L5321-1 à L5321-3) », so L5321-4 does not exist, as claimed. L5323-2 and L5323-3 return 404 on code.travail.gouv.fr, consistent with Chapitre III now containing this article alone.
verdicts.correction: None on the law. The seasonal-impact reasoning is his, not the statute's, and the mise en demeure step is correctly identified as the thing that makes this survivable.

verdicts.claim: (d) A French business is not obliged to serve any paying customer once that customer is itself a business — refus de vente between professionals free since the loi Galland 1996; the obligation exists only towards consumers under L121-11 code de la consommation.
verdicts.why: The core is confirmed on the INC page: the prohibition is « Il est interdit de refuser à un consommateur la vente d'un produit ou la prestation d'un service (…) », it is B2C only, professionals have been free to refuse other professionals since the loi Galland of 1 July 1996, and the penalties are a 5th-class contravention at €1,500 / €7,500 under articles 131-13 5° and 131-38 code pénal. The DGCCRF sourcing is honestly flagged as index-only. The defect is the closing 'mirror': treating his candidates as consumers of a free service and using L121-11 to argue the site must stay open to all ages.
verdicts.correction: Drop the mirror. L121-11 speaks to « la vente d'un produit ou la prestation d'un service » and carries a « sauf motif légitime » exception the quoted ellipsis hides; stretching a consumer sales rule over a free, non-contractual relationship to reach a conclusion L5321-2 already delivers directly is the reverse of the employer/platform error and weakens a finding that is otherwise solid. The obligation to keep the site open to candidates of every age comes from L5321-2, full stop.

verdicts.claim: (e) RGAA / article 47 loi 2005-102 does not bite him — the private-company threshold is €250M average annual French turnover over the last three closed financial years.
verdicts.why: Arcom's page matches on every element: the three categories (personnes morales de droit public, private bodies delegated a public service mission, « les entreprises dont le chiffre d'affaires excède un seuil fixé par décret (actuellement 250 millions d'euros) »), the calculation basis « la moyenne du chiffre d'affaires annuel réalisé en France des trois derniers exercices comptables clos », and the sanctions at €50,000 / €25,000 modulated by nature, gravity and duration. The page adds a detail the claim omits and that favours him: for groups the threshold is assessed on the entity designated as responsible for the service, not consolidated.
verdicts.correction: None. The practical warning — do not let an agency sell him an RGAA audit as a legal requirement — is correct and worth keeping. Note only that the sanction figures are ceilings for entities in scope; he is not one.

verdicts.claim: (e) The European Accessibility Act exempts micro-enterprises providing services entirely: fewer than 10 employees AND turnover or balance-sheet total under €2M.
verdicts.why: The thresholds and date are confirmed verbatim on the government page — « moins de 10 salariés avec un chiffre d'affaires annuel ou un total de bilan inférieur à 2 millions d'euros », applicable « depuis le 28 juin 2025 ». But the same page lists the services in scope and it is a closed list: computers and operating systems, payment terminals, smartphones, TV equipment, telephony, audiovisual media access, transport, consumer banking, e-books, e-commerce, and 112. E-commerce in the directive means services concluded at the individual request of a CONSUMER with a view to a consumer contract. His paying customers are businesses and his candidates pay nothing.
verdicts.correction: He is very probably out of scope entirely, before size is even reached — which makes the warning that 'this protection disappears if the business succeeds at scale' misleading, because scope, not headcount, is the first gate. The right framing: build accessibility because it is cheap now and expensive later, not because 10 employees / €2M is a compliance cliff he is approaching. The penalty figures in the claim are self-flagged as unverified and I could not verify them either — keep that flag.

verdicts.claim: HARD RULE — Article L5321-3: no direct or indirect payment may be required from job seekers. Six months and €3,750 under L5324-1.
verdicts.why: Both articles verified verbatim. L5321-3's prohibition reads as quoted and is subject only to L7121-9 (artistes du spectacle) and L222-6 code du sport (agents sportifs) — neither reaches hospitality, as claimed. L5324-1 exists and reads « est puni d'un emprisonnement de six mois et d'une amende de 3 750 euros ». The reading of « indirecte » as covering premium candidate tiers, paid CV boosts and fees from a first pay packet is the right reading of the word. This is the single best-sourced claim in the corpus.
verdicts.correction: None. Note for him that this is the one place where the corpus's penalty figure is not a distant ceiling — €3,750 is a small enough number that it describes a realistic outcome, and the six months is what makes it a line rather than a cost.

verdicts.claim: His model sits inside L5331-1's carve-out: selling job offers is banned on any medium, but paid insertion in a publication or other paid means of communication is permitted. PENALTY: no penalty attached to L5331-1 in L5334-1.
verdicts.why: The article text and the carve-out reading are right, and the self-flagged caveat is the best piece of intellectual honesty in the corpus: « une publication ou un autre moyen de communication payant » is not an obviously comfortable fit for a free-to-read site funded by advertisers, and no case law resolves it. The penalty statement is false for the same reason as the L5331-2 one — R5334-1 names L5331-1 expressly.
verdicts.correction: Breach of L5331-1 is a contravention de 3e classe under R5334-1 (€450 / €2,250 for a company). That matters more here than elsewhere, because the unresolved reading the claim honestly flags is precisely a reading on which he could be outside the carve-out — and if he is, there is a penalty waiting, not nothing. Keep the caveat and attach the right consequence to it.

verdicts.claim: LIABILITY SPLIT — L5334-1 final paragraph: the advertiser bears the offence; the publisher bears it only where he acted without an express insertion request.
verdicts.why: The allocation rule is real and I confirmed it on the page — the annonceur who requested publication is liable, and the directeur de la publication or service provider is liable when he acted without an express insertion request. The product advice built on it (provable, timestamped, per-offer submission; never rewrite an employer's copy; never auto-import) is excellent and is the single most useful thing in the corpus. What is overstated is the reach: calling it 'his most valuable procedural protection' implies it covers his publishing risk generally.
verdicts.correction: L5334-1 penalises only L5331-3 and L5331-5, and its allocation paragraph allocates only those two offences. It does nothing for the R5334-1 contraventions (L5331-1, L5331-2, L5331-4, L5332-1, L5332-3), nothing for article 225-2 code pénal, and nothing for L8221-1 2°. So the express-request evidence trail protects him against the misleading-offer offences and the marketing offence, and against nothing else. 37 500 € is the ceiling for those offences, not his exposure.

verdicts.claim: His own marketing claims are criminally policed — L5331-5 forbids misleading claims about an employment-related service, « notamment sur le caractère gratuit de ce service »; L5331-3 protects job existence, pay and place of work; DGCCRF investigates both under L5333-1.
verdicts.why: L5331-3's three numbered heads verified verbatim: « L'existence, le caractère effectivement disponible, l'origine, la nature et la description de l'emploi », « La rémunération et les avantages annexes proposés », « Le lieu du travail ». L5333-1 verified: it gives the concurrence, consommation et répression des fraudes agents investigation powers over L5331-3 and L5331-5 infractions, under article L511-5 code de la consommation. The insight that his 'decent conditions' promise is itself a claim about his service under L5331-5, and that pay and staff housing are the exact two things L5331-3 names, is correct and is the sharpest business point in the corpus.
verdicts.correction: None on the law. 1 an / 37 500 € is L5334-1's ceiling; say so when quoting it to him.

verdicts.claim: Three mechanical duties: date every listing (L5332-1), hold the employer's real identity behind anonymous offers (L5332-2), publish in French (L5331-4). PENALTY: no penalty attached to these three in L5334-1.
verdicts.why: The three duties are real and L5332-2's second paragraph does extend to intermediaries requesting insertion, as claimed. The penalty statement is false again: R5334-1 penalises L5331-4 AND L5332-1. Only L5332-2 escapes it. The claim also omits the fourth paragraph of L5331-4, which is a derogation directly relevant to an international resort: « les directeurs de publications et les personnes responsables de moyens de communication utilisant, en tout ou partie, une langue étrangère peuvent, en France, recevoir des offres d'emploi rédigées dans cette langue ».
verdicts.correction: Dating and French-language breaches are contraventions de 3e classe under R5334-1 (€450 / €2,250). Two further points: the L5331-4 derogation means a genuinely bilingual section of his site is a lawful route to English-language listings, not a prohibited one — worth knowing in Megève rather than building a French-mandatory field that turns away business he could lawfully take. And R5334-1 also penalises L5332-3, which the corpus never mentions: any ad from an entreprise de travail temporaire must state its name and its ETT status. Alpine seasonal hiring runs through interim; that is a missing field on his listing form.

verdicts.claim: He has no obligation to send his offers to France Travail; stating the salary is not compulsory.
verdicts.why: Both sentences verified verbatim on the service-public page: « L'employeur n'a pas l'obligation d'informer France Travail des offres de recrutement » and « Indiquer le salaire et, le cas échéant, les compléments de rémunération dans les offres d'emploi n'est pas obligatoire ». The same page also confirms the French-language and publication-date requirements the corpus asserts elsewhere.
verdicts.correction: None. The commercial reading — make pay disclosure a listing condition because it hardens the curation standard and because L5331-3 makes misstating pay an offence — is sound and is the right way round.

verdicts.claim: [Lane 6 duplicate] A job board is legally an « activité de placement » and may be run for profit; Chapter I binds him from the first listing.
verdicts.why: Same text, same qualification gap as the Lane 5 twin — but this one rates it medium-high on the qualification while the Lane 5 twin rates it high and calls it THE CENTRAL FINDING. Two claims in one corpus cannot carry different confidences on an identical proposition. This version's confidence note is the honest one.
verdicts.correction: Keep this version's calibration and discard the Lane 5 version's. Merge the two into one claim: probable qualification, no authority on job boards specifically, and no practical consequence because the candidate-fee ban reaches him on either reading.

verdicts.claim: [Lane 6 duplicate] He may never take money from a candidate. PENALTY: administrative closure up to 3 months after mise en demeure (L5323-1); also caught by France Travail doctrine on « la gratuité des offres d'emploi ».
verdicts.why: The prohibition is right but the penalty is materially understated on the one rule the corpus itself calls a hard line. L5324-1 punishes breach of L5321-3 with six months' imprisonment and €3,750 — the Lane 5 twin states this correctly and this version omits it entirely, offering only administrative closure. Understating a criminal prohibition to a closure power is the most consequential internal contradiction in the corpus. The appeal to unnamed 'France Travail doctrine' as an independent catch is unsourced and adds nothing.
verdicts.correction: The penalty for L5321-3 is L5324-1: six months and €3,750, on top of the L5323-1 closure power. Drop the France Travail doctrine reference — it has no citation and the statute is stronger than anything it could add.

verdicts.claim: [Lane 6 duplicate] His curated door is lawful but L5321-2 forbids refusing service to an employer on a discrimination ground; the criteria must be documented and must not proxy a protected characteristic.
verdicts.why: Same article, same reading as the Lane 5 twin, and the indirect-discrimination point about proxying is the correct refinement. The asymmetry it names — free to refuse on quality grounds, but must be able to show the ground — is the practical rule.
verdicts.correction: Merge with the Lane 5 twin rather than carrying both. Same caveat as there: L1132-1's list is wider than article 225-1's, so an L5321-2 breach is not automatically the crime of 225-2, and closure plus a civil claim is the realistic consequence.

verdicts.claim: There is no registration, licence or prior declaration to open a job board — the déclaration préalable was abrogated.
verdicts.why: The current L5323-1 contains no declaration duty, verified verbatim, and L5323-2 and L5323-3 now return 404 on code.travail.gouv.fr — consistent with the chapter having been emptied down to the enforcement article. Bpifrance Création's page for « organisme privé de placement de personnel », which I did open, confirms independently: no professional qualification is required (« Il n'est pas nécessaire de justifier d'une qualification professionnelle particulière pour ouvrir un organisme privé de placement de personnel ») and the only formality is the guichet unique declaration that gives the business legal existence. The décret n° 2012-539 du 20 avril 2012 title is confirmed through the search index as « portant modification des dispositions réglementaires relatives à la déclaration préalable d'exercice d'une activité de placement ».
verdicts.correction: One nuance on the abrogation history the claim gets slightly wrong: 2012-539 is titled a modification of the regulatory provisions, and the statutory duty went by legislative amendment. The claim's medium-high flag on the history is appropriate and should stay. Add the Bpifrance page as a second opened source — it is the one a sceptical adviser would want.

verdicts.claim: [Lane 6 duplicate] He owes France Travail nothing — no obligation to transmit, share or deposit offers.
verdicts.why: Verified verbatim, same page as the Lane 5 twin. The a fortiori reasoning is sound: if the employer owes no notification, a private publisher with no statutory relationship to France Travail plainly owes none.
verdicts.correction: None. Duplicate of an earlier claim — collapse them.

verdicts.claim: Publishing a false or misleading offer is a criminal offence that names the diffuser, not only the employer (L5331-3).
verdicts.why: Verified. The prohibition covers « de diffuser par tout autre moyen de communication accessible au public », and a website is squarely within it. The three protected heads are as quoted. The framing — that the hook pulling an employer's labour-law non-compliance into his lap is not a duty to audit but the fact that a non-compliant offer is a misleading offer — is the corpus's best structural insight and it survives scrutiny.
verdicts.correction: Quote 1 an / 37 500 € as L5334-1's statutory ceiling, and pair it with the allocation paragraph in the same breath: with an express insertion request on file, this offence sits on the advertiser.

verdicts.claim: [Lane 6 duplicate] L5334-1 puts the offence on the advertiser and on the publisher only where he published without an express request — his single best shield.
verdicts.why: This version flagged its own quote as blocked by the page's copyright guard and rated the allocation rule medium-high. I got the paragraph through: the page does state that advertisers requesting publication are liable, and that publication directors or service providers are liable when they acted without express insertion requests from the advertiser. The substance is confirmed, so the medium-high flag can be raised.
verdicts.correction: Raise the confidence on the allocation rule to high. But keep the reach honest, as flagged on the Lane 5 twin: it allocates the L5331-3 and L5331-5 offences only, and leaves the R5334-1 contraventions, article 225-2 and L8221-1 2° untouched. 'Single best shield' is true of misleading-offer risk and false of his publishing risk generally.

verdicts.claim: France Travail's current legal guide prints the diffuser's criminal exposure as a flat 37 500 € in every liability table; the guide itself miscites R.5334-1 where it means L.5334-1 for the 1-year custodial penalty.
verdicts.why: Two problems. First, I could not open the source: the PDF exceeds the 10MB fetch ceiling, so the guide's identity (November 2025, 52 pages), its liability matrix, and every verbatim quote drawn from it across four claims are unverified — the 'opened: true' flag on this item does not hold for my toolset, and older editions from September 2017 and February 2019 are also in circulation, so the version claim is a live risk. Second, the embedded correction is itself false. R5334-1 is a real article with a real penalty — a contravention de 3e classe for breach of L5331-1, L5331-2, L5331-4, L5332-1 and L5332-3. France Travail is citing it correctly. The guide is right and the audit of it is wrong.
verdicts.correction: Withdraw the 'miscitation' correction. The guide's three-row diffuser matrix — L5334-1 criminal, R5334-1 administrative/contraventionnel, article 1240 code civil for damages — is an accurate statement of French law on all three rows. The substantive propositions I could check independently (R5334-1's existence and content, L5334-1's figures, D1242-1 4°) all hold, which is reason to trust the guide; the version and pagination should be re-checked from the file itself before anything is built on it.

verdicts.claim: The offer's content must comply with labour law — working time, contract type, SMIC — and France Travail states this as a rule about the OFFER, not the employer.
verdicts.why: Unverifiable at source (the PDF exceeded the fetch ceiling), and structurally the France Travail rule-as-statute error. The guide's section 06 states conditions for offers deposited on francetravail.fr. It binds depositors on that platform; it is not a rule of general application to private publishers. The statutory bridge the claim then builds — an ad whose own stated terms are unlawful is by definition misleading under L5331-3 — is sound and is where the real duty lives. The framing that the check is on the four corners of the ad rather than on the payroll is exactly right.
verdicts.correction: Cite L5331-3 as the duty and France Travail's guide only as persuasive practice. Say which employer-side figures the claim names are ceilings against the employer, not him: R3233-1 (below-SMIC pay, 5e classe, €1,500) and R3124-3 (working time, 4e classe, €750) are the employer's exposure and reach him only derivatively through L5331-3.

verdicts.claim: He may not publish an offer whose final employer is unknown, or for which no real post exists — the closest thing in French law to a know-your-employer duty on a publisher.
verdicts.why: The claim's own quoted text refutes its framing: « l'employeur final doit être connu de France Travail ». That is France Travail's rule for offers deposited with France Travail, under France Travail's terms — not a duty on a private publisher, and not 'French law'. The claim also concedes its article mapping is imprecise (L5331-2 is the age-limit article). The reality-of-the-post limb does bind him, but through L5331-3's « l'existence, le caractère effectivement disponible », which I verified, not through the guide.
verdicts.correction: Restate as: no statutory know-your-employer duty exists; what binds him is L5331-3, under which advertising a post that does not exist is a criminal misleading allegation. Knowing who the employer is follows as the only way to prove the post is real, which makes it risk management with a statutory motive rather than a compliance obligation with an article number.

verdicts.claim: There is NO statutory duty on a job-offer publisher to verify that a listing employer is a registered business — no SIRET, no Kbis, no attestation de vigilance.
verdicts.why: I searched the same ground independently and found no general verification duty either, so the negative broadly holds and the claim's medium flag is appropriately calibrated. But it is not clean. The corpus missed L5332-3, penalised by R5334-1, which requires ads from an entreprise de travail temporaire to state the agency's name and its character as a temporary work agency — a status he cannot publish without verifying. The source_quote attached to this claim is also a non-sequitur: it quotes the French-language and dating rules, which have nothing to do with employer verification, and the first word is corrupted (« La offre »).
verdicts.correction: Narrow the negative: no general SIRET or Kbis duty, but an ETT advertiser triggers L5332-3, whose breach is a 3e-classe contravention under R5334-1. That is one verification he genuinely owes. Replace the source_quote, which does not support the claim it is attached to. The advice to check the SIRET anyway as good-faith evidence is right and is strengthened, not weakened, by having one real case where it is compulsory.

verdicts.claim: The obligation de vigilance runs the OTHER WAY: the restaurant is the donneur d'ordre and he is the prestataire, so HE may have to hand THEM an attestation de vigilance.
verdicts.why: The direction is right. L8222-1's own text covers « un contrat dont l'objet porte sur une obligation d'un montant minimum en vue de l'exécution d'un travail, de la fourniture d'une prestation de services ou de l'accomplissement d'un acte de commerce », so selling advertising is within scope and the buyer is the donneur d'ordre. Three defects sit on top. The €5,000 threshold is not in L8222-1, which says only « un montant minimum » and refers the modalities to décret — the figure is in D8222-1, so the claim cites the wrong article for its most concrete number. The service-public page frames the whole obligation around « contrat de sous-traitance », which is a narrower framing than L8222-1's text and is worth knowing before telling a restaurant it owes him vigilance. And the source_quote is not verbatim — it contains « L'obligation s'déclenche », a corruption showing it was not copied from the page.
verdicts.correction: Cite D8222-1 for the €5,000 HT threshold, not L8222-1. Soften 'there is no legal basis to demand one from them' — nothing prevents a contracting party from asking for documents as a condition of business, and his curation questionnaire is exactly such a condition. Keep the operational point, which is good: keep his own URSSAF account current from day one, because a single house crossing €5,000 of annual spend will ask him for an attestation.

verdicts.claim: Advertising that knowingly favours travail dissimulé is its own criminal offence (L8221-1 2°) — he does not need to be an accomplice to be a defendant.
verdicts.why: L8221-1's three prohibitions verified verbatim, including « La publicité, par quelque moyen que ce soit, tendant à favoriser, en toute connaissance de cause, le travail dissimulé ». L8224-1 verified at three years and €45,000 for breach of L8221-1's prohibitions. The analytical point — that the legislature already wrote the publisher's version of the offence, so complicity under article 121-7 code pénal is largely academic beside it — is correct and is a genuinely useful reframe.
verdicts.correction: Say that 3 ans / 45 000 € is L8224-1's ceiling.
