The aggravated tier at 10 ans / 100 000 € (minors, vulnerable persons, bande organisée) is quoted accurately but is a ceiling for organised exploitation, and quoting it beside a 19-year-old's advertising risk distorts the picture more than it informs.

verdicts.claim: « En toute connaissance de cause » is the entire defence, and his curation model erodes it — a business that inspects is a business that knows.
verdicts.why: The statutory knowledge element is certain and the claim's medium flag is honest. But the reasoning runs against a rule the corpus never reaches. DSA article 7 provides that intermediaries are not ineligible for the article 4, 5 and 6 liability exemptions SOLELY because they carry out, in good faith and diligently, voluntary own-initiative investigations aimed at detecting and removing illegal content. That is the Good Samaritan clause, enacted precisely so that inspecting does not convert into knowing. It does not decide the L8221-1 2° question — that is French criminal law with its own knowledge standard — but it is the strongest authority on the exact anxiety the claim raises, and it points the other way.
verdicts.correction: Reframe: good-faith curation is legally protected activity, not an evidential liability, and the legislature said so in DSA article 7. What creates real exposure under L8221-1 2° is continuing to publish after a credible report of undeclared work — that is actual knowledge, and the mitigation the claim proposes (dated intake file, immediate delisting reflex) is the right one. Curate more, not less; the record is what turns inspection into a defence.

verdicts.claim: As a hosting service he must run a notice-and-action mechanism from day one — the micro-enterprise exemption does not cover it.
verdicts.why: Arcom's page confirms every element: hosting is defined as services that « stockent des informations fournies par un destinataire du service à sa demande »; micro and small enterprises are those with « moins de 50 personnes » and turnover or balance sheet not exceeding €10 million; and they are exempt from « articles 15 (2), 19 et 29 ». Article 16 is not on that list, so the notice-and-action mechanism binds him at any size. The claim's honest flag that EUR-Lex returned empty bodies and the paragraph-level wording of articles 16-18 is unverified is appropriate and should stay.
verdicts.correction: One presentational fix: article 19 is not an obligation he is exempt from, it is the provision that grants micro and small platforms the exemption from Section 3, and article 29 does the same for Section 4. Arcom's shorthand reads as a list of exemptions; it is a list of the provisions that create them. The conclusion is unaffected.

verdicts.claim: No fixed statutory delay — the standard is immediate removal on actual knowledge; failure to remove is 1 an / 250 000 €, or up to 6 % of worldwide turnover for a company; failure to alert authorities is 1 an / 250 000 € and 1 250 000 € for a legal person.
verdicts.why: Every figure is confirmed on the service-public page. Two problems with how they are presented. The claim itself flags that the « immédiatement » sentence it quotes concerns a directeur de publication rather than an hébergeur, which means the host's own standard is asserted without being pinned — a real gap left open. And the figures are ceilings drawn from a regime that runs up to very large platforms: 6 % of annual worldwide turnover is the DSA's top-end sanction, quoted here beside a micro-enterprise's removal duty as though it described his exposure.
verdicts.correction: Mark the ceilings as ceilings. And correct the alert limb, which the next claim relies on: the 1 250 000 € figure attaches to the reporting duty whose trigger Arcom states as « soupçon d'infraction pénale susceptible de porter ou ayant porté atteinte à la vie ou à la sécurité de tiers ». That is a narrow trigger and it does not fire on an ordinary illegal listing.

verdicts.claim: His curation is what could cost him the hosting shield and make him the éditeur of every ad.
verdicts.why: The two definitions are quoted accurately from the service-public page and I confirmed both. But the claim is built without DSA article 7, which bears on it directly: a provider is not ineligible for the liability exemptions solely because it carries out good-faith, diligent own-initiative investigations or takes measures to comply with law. Choosing which advertisers may buy — a commercial gate — is further still from editorial control than the moderation article 7 protects. The claim's own 'on the better view, leaves him a host' instinct is right; the risk it attaches to that instinct is inflated.
verdicts.correction: Separate the two shields the claim bundles. The éditeur/hébergeur line is not endangered by curating the door — article 7 covers that, and a commercial gate is not editorial control of content. The L5334-1 express-request limb is a different test and is genuinely at risk from rewriting copy. Both point to the same design rule, which the claim states perfectly: he curates the door, the employer writes the ad. Keep the rule, drop the inflated warrant.

verdicts.claim: The DSA's know-your-business-customer rule (article 30) most likely does NOT apply to him.
verdicts.why: Arcom's page confirms the scope: article 30's traçabilité des vendeurs professionnels applies to « Fournisseurs de plateformes en ligne permettant aux consommateurs de conclure des contrats à distance avec des professionnels (places de marché) ». A jobseeker browsing free listings concludes no distance consumer contract, and an employment contract is not one. The claim's medium flag and its note that it could not open the recitals are appropriately cautious; the conclusion is nonetheless well supported by the scope wording itself.
verdicts.correction: The confidence can be raised from medium. The point the claim makes about why it matters — article 30 is the one provision that would otherwise force him to collect and verify each employer's registration data, and it is the rule people assume covers job boards — is correct and is worth keeping prominent.

verdicts.claim: Fraudulent job ads carry heavy criminal qualifications against their authors, and there is a State reporting channel he should use — and under the DSA, alerting the authorities to suspected criminal offences is itself an obligation (art. 18), separately sanctioned at 1 250 000 € for a company.
verdicts.why: The cybermalveillance half is confirmed verbatim: the scam purpose « soutirer de l'argent ou dérober des informations personnelles », escroquerie at 5 ans / 375 000 € (art. 313-1), usurpation d'identité at 1 an / 15 000 € (art. 226-4-1), collecte frauduleuse de données at 5 ans / 300 000 € (art. 226-18), and the PHAROS, France Victimes 116 006 and Info Escroqueries 0 805 805 817 channels. The DSA half is wrong. Arcom states article 18's trigger as « Notification aux autorités judiciaires en cas de soupçon d'infraction pénale susceptible de porter ou ayant porté atteinte à la vie ou à la sécurité de tiers ». A fraudulent job ad is neither. Attaching the 1 250 000 € corporate fine to failing to report one is a rule for a different offence applied to his facts.
verdicts.correction: Article 18 is a life-and-safety reporting duty, not a general crime-reporting duty. A scam listing triggers his article 16 notice-and-action duty — take it down — and reporting to PHAROS is good practice and good evidence, not a sanctioned obligation. Where article 18 WOULD fire on a job board is the case worth naming for him instead: a listing that is a front for trafficking or for luring a minor. Those are the things that put a threat to life or safety on his site, and in a seasonal resort market they are not fanciful.

verdicts.claim: Every offer must be in French and must carry its publication date (L5331-4, plus the dating rule).
verdicts.why: The first paragraph of L5331-4 is verbatim correct, and the third paragraph does confirm the two points the claim leans on — it applies to services performed in France « quelle que soit la nationalité de l'auteur de l'offre ou de l'employeur », and even where foreign-language knowledge is required for the post. This is also the one claim in the corpus that cites R5334-1 correctly. Two gaps. It omits the fourth paragraph, a derogation letting publication directors and those responsible for communications media operating wholly or partly in a foreign language receive job offers drafted in that language — directly relevant to an international resort. And it attributes the dating duty to « R.5332-1 et seq. per France Travail » when the duty is in L5332-1.
verdicts.correction: Cite L5332-1 for the dating duty. And give him the fourth-paragraph derogation, because it changes a product decision: rather than a mandatory French field that turns away English-language business, he can operate a genuinely bilingual section and take those offers lawfully. The contravention de 3e classe under R5334-1 is correctly identified here and should be propagated to the other claims that deny any penalty exists.

verdicts.claim: Discriminatory wording in an ad is the highest-penalty content risk, and L5331-2 targets age limits specifically; 3 ans / 45 000 € under articles 225-2 / 225-4 code pénal.
verdicts.why: L5331-2's first paragraph is verbatim correct and article 225-2 5° is confirmed — subordinating a job offer to a condition based on an article 225-1 criterion is punished by three years and €45,000. But the quote stops before paragraph 2, which is the exception that matters most to his inventory: « Cette interdiction ne concerne pas les offres qui fixent des conditions d'âge imposées par les dispositions légales. » Apprenticeship offers live in that exception. Quoting the ban without the exception, in a claim whose own stated audience is young people entering the trade, is the omission most likely to make him over-moderate lawful listings. The France Travail wording guidance (Débutant/Expérimenté, no « contrat étudiant », the Bilingue/Courant/Notions scale with its restaurant example) is unverifiable at source — the PDF exceeded the fetch ceiling.
verdicts.correction: Quote both paragraphs of L5331-2. And correct the penalty picture in both directions: his own direct exposure for diffusing an age-limited ad is the R5334-1 contravention de 3e classe, while 3 ans / 45 000 € (225 000 € for a company under 225-4) is the criminal ceiling on the narrower article 225-1 route, and L5334-1's express-request allocation does not shield him from the code pénal at all.

verdicts.claim: The sector has one extended convention collective binding every employer he lists: CCN HCR du 30 avril 1997, IDCC 1979, with minima from avenant n°33 du 19 juin 2024.
verdicts.why: The Code du travail numérique page confirms the convention's identity, avenant n°33 du 19 juin 2024 as the source of current minima, and the rule that the applicable floor is whichever is higher of the SMIC and the conventional minimum. The claim's own medium-high flag on avenant 33 still being current is right to be cautious but holds as of today. The scoping is also right: he is not bound by the convention, it operates on him only as a content check under L5331-3 and as a spine for his curation standard.
verdicts.correction: Add the fact that makes the higher-of rule bite rather than being a formality. Since the SMIC rose to €12.31/h on 1 June 2026, the bottom four conventional rungs (€12.00 at niveau I/1 up to €12.28) now sit BELOW the SMIC. For commis, plongeurs and débutants — his whole market — the operative floor today is the SMIC, not the grid. Any screening rule must recompute at every SMIC move rather than caching the grid.

verdicts.claim: Night work by under-18s in hotels and restaurants is permitted only between 22h00 and 23h30, by derogation from the labour inspector.
verdicts.why: R3163-2 verified verbatim: in the hôtellerie and restauration sectors, night work by young workers may only be authorised from twenty-two hours to twenty-three hours thirty. The framing is also right — this binds the employer, and reaches him only as an ad-screening rule through L5331-3, because advertising to an apprentice a closing shift the employer cannot lawfully staff is advertising something that misdescribes the job. In a Megève winter that is a live rather than a theoretical screen.
verdicts.correction: None. This is the best-constructed derivative claim in the corpus: employer duty, correct article, correct statutory bridge to his own exposure, and a concrete screening rule at the end.

verdicts.claim: Every maître d'apprentissage in the HCR branch must hold a valid « permis de former » before the apprenticeship contract is signed.
verdicts.why: UMIH's page confirms the substance verbatim — the obligation, 14 hours initial for anyone who has never supervised an alternant or has not in five years, 7 hours refresher every four years, and « À défaut de ce permis, un contrat d'apprentissage ou de professionnalisation ne peut être valablement conclu ». Three cautions. The page does not state the avenant number or date, so that citation remains from the search index. The date is wrong: avenant n°17 du 10 janvier 2013 was extended by arrêté of 22 July 2013, published 31 July 2013, in force 1 August 2013 — not 2014. And the two corroborating sources, UMIH and GHR, are the branch bodies that sell the training; a claim that a conventional obligation voids a contract is a strong legal proposition from an interested source.
verdicts.correction: Fix the date to 2013. Treat the contract-validity consequence as the branch bodies' position rather than established law — what is solid is that AKTO refuses funding without it, which is the commercially decisive fact anyway. The underlying point stands and is genuinely valuable: it is binary, verifiable with one question, and it separates houses that take young people seriously from houses that take them cheaply.

verdicts.claim: HCR apprentice pay was raised above the legal minimum by avenant n°35 du 27 février 2025, applicable 1 August 2025 — the niveau I conventional rates exceed the SMIC, so the branch minimum applies in practice.
verdicts.why: The avenant's identity, date, application date and published extension are all confirmed on AKTO's page. The operative conclusion is no longer true. AKTO's reasoning rests on niveau I hourly rates exceeding the SMIC at €11.88. The SMIC was revalued automatically on 1 June 2026 to €12.31/h — a 2,41 % rise triggered by the price index — and avenant n°33's niveau I échelon 1 is €12.00. The conventional floor is now BELOW the SMIC at the entry grades, so avenant 35's percentage base reverts to the SMIC and the branch uplift is neutralised exactly where his apprenticeship inventory sits.
verdicts.correction: Rewrite the screening rule. It is not 'an apprentice offer quoting percentage-of-SMIC is quoting too little' — as of 1 June 2026 percentage-of-SMIC is the correct and higher basis at niveau I. The durable rule is avenant 35's own: a percentage of whichever is higher of the conventional minimum and the SMIC, recomputed at each SMIC revaluation. Anything hard-coded from the 2025 position will now under-detect rather than over-detect.

verdicts.claim: CDD is normal in his sector, not a warning sign — hôtellerie and restauration are listed CDD d'usage sectors and seasonal work is its own lawful ground; but « CDD puis CDI » is a proscribed mention.
verdicts.why: D1242-1 verified directly rather than through the France Travail guide: « 4° L'hôtellerie et la restauration, les centres de loisirs et de vacances » appears in the list of sectors where CDD d'usage is permitted under L1242-2. The saisonnier ground is separately lawful. The calibration point is the useful one and it is right — treating CDD as a red flag would gut his inventory for no legal reason in an alpine resort, while the wording that sounds generous is the one that is actually unlawful.
verdicts.correction: One sourcing note: the « CDD puis CDI » proscription is France Travail's editorial rule for its own platform, and I could not open the guide to verify its wording. The legal substance behind it is sound — promising a permanent job at the end contradicts the temporary-task condition and invites requalification under L1245-1, and as a statement in an ad it is caught by L5331-3 as misdescribing the nature of the job. Cite L1242-1 and L1245-1 rather than the guide.
